abstract: We present a new hypothesis that the cerebellum plays a key role in ac(cid:173) tively controlling the acquisition of sensory infonnation by the nervous system. In this paper we explore this idea by examining the function of a simple cerebellar-related behavior, the vestibula-ocular reflex or VOR, in which eye movements are generated to minimize image slip on the retina during rapid head movements. Considering this system from the point of view of statistical estimation theory, our results sug(cid:173) gest that the transfer function of the VOR, often regarded as a static or slowly modifiable feature of the system, should actually be continu(cid:173) ously and rapidly changed during head movements. We further suggest that these changes are under the direct control of the cerebellar cortex and propose experiments to test this hypothesis.

paragraphs: The vestibulo-ocular reflex stabilizes retinal images by moving the eyes during rapid head motion. This paper uses that behavior to investigate a broader hypothesis: the cerebellum actively controls the acquisition of sensory information. The question is whether eye-movement control should change dynamically even within a head movement.

Viewing the system through statistical estimation theory leads the authors to argue that the reflex’s transfer function should be adjusted rapidly and continuously. That differs from treating it as a fixed or only slowly adaptable feature. They propose that the cerebellar cortex directly controls these changes.

The paper develops a testable physiological hypothesis and proposes experiments to assess it. Its significance is a shift from treating sensory input as something the nervous system simply receives to considering how motor control shapes the quality of that input. The theoretical proposal is not presented as an already confirmed experimental account of cerebellar function.
summary.tldr: A statistical-estimation account proposes that the cerebellum rapidly adjusts the vestibulo-ocular reflex to improve sensory acquisition.

title: Neural Control of Sensory Acquisition: The Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex

abstract: The existence of modularity in the organization of nervous systems (e.g. cortical columns and olfactory glomeruli) is well known. We show that localized activity patterns in a layer of cells, collective excitations, can induce the formation of modular structures in the anatomical connections via a Hebbian learning mechanism. The networks are spatially homogeneous before learning, but the spontaneous emergence of localized collective excitations and subsequently modularity in the connection patterns breaks translational symmetry. This spontaneous symmetry breaking phenomenon is similar to those which drive pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems. We have identified requirements on the patterns of lateral connections and on the gains of internal units which are essential for the development of modularity. These essential requirements will most likely remain operative when more complicated (and biologically realistic) models are considered.

paragraphs: This paper asks how modular connection patterns can develop in a neural network that initially has no preferred spatial locations. It takes biological structures such as cortical columns and olfactory glomeruli as motivation. The proposed explanation begins with localized patterns of collective activity in a layer of interacting cells.

These activity patterns shape anatomical connections through Hebbian learning. Although the network starts spatially homogeneous, localized collective excitations emerge spontaneously and are followed by modular connectivity. The authors describe this as breaking translational symmetry: locations that were initially equivalent acquire different roles as organized spatial structure develops. They relate the process to pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems.

The analysis identifies requirements involving lateral connection patterns and the gains of individual units that are essential for modularity to develop. Thus, the explanation depends on specific properties of network interaction and responsiveness. The authors expect these requirements to remain relevant in more biologically realistic models, presenting the simple system as a way to isolate conditions underlying modular organization.
summary.tldr: Localized collective activity can organize an initially uniform neural network into modules through Hebbian learning.

title: Note on Development of Modularity in Simple Cortical Models

abstract: We propose a new parallel-hierarchical neural network model to enable motor learning for simultaneous control of both trajectory and force. by integrating Hogan's control method and our previous neural network control model using a feedback-error-learning scheme. Furthermore. two hierarchical control laws which apply to the model, are derived by using the Moore-Penrose pseudo(cid:173) inverse matrix. One is related to the minimum muscle-tension-change trajectory and the other is related to the minimum motor-command-change trajectory. The human arm is redundant at the dynamics level since joint torque is generated by agonist and antagonist muscles. Therefore, acquisition of the inverse model is an ill-posed problem. However. the combination of these control laws and feedback-error-learning resolve the ill-posed problem. Finally. the efficiency of the parallel-hierarchical neural network model is shown by learning experiments using an artificial muscle arm and computer simulations.

paragraphs: An arm must often control both where it moves and the forces it applies. Muscle redundancy complicates learning because several agonist–antagonist combinations can produce the same joint torque. This paper proposes a parallel-hierarchical neural controller that addresses trajectory and force learning together.

The model combines Hogan’s control method with feedback-error learning. Two hierarchical laws derived using the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse favor either small changes in muscle tension or small changes in motor commands. Those choices resolve ambiguity in the inverse model by specifying how the redundant control possibilities should be used.

Artificial-muscle-arm experiments and computer simulations demonstrate the approach. The contribution is a coordination of learning and control constraints: feedback errors train the model, while the hierarchical laws make the inverse problem better defined. This provides a practical route to simultaneous motion and force control rather than treating redundancy only as an obstacle to learning.
summary.tldr: A parallel-hierarchical controller combines feedback-error learning and redundancy-resolving control laws for joint trajectory and force control.

title: Learning Trajectory and Force Control of an Artificial Muscle Arm by Parallel-hierarchical Neural Network Model

paragraphs: This paper studies how to reduce a network's error without explicitly knowing its internal structure. The adjustable quantities can include connection strengths, thresholds, and other parameters. The proposed stochastic procedure applies to deterministic networks with arbitrary connection layouts, making its learning mechanism independent of a particular network architecture.

The central change is a revised parameter update rule within an existing distributed learning method. The authors arrange for each individual perturbation of the parameter vector to contribute an error decrease. This makes the information obtained from perturbations more directly useful for optimization, and the abstract reports substantially faster learning as a result.

The method also supports learning features that vary over time in dynamical networks. The authors analyze convergence and scaling and present simulations involving recurrent networks learning trajectories. These components connect the update rule to both its mathematical behavior and a temporal learning task: the target is a pattern of activity over time, rather than just a single output.
summary.tldr: A revised stochastic update rule speeds error reduction without requiring explicit knowledge of a network's internal structure.

title: A Fast Stochastic Error-Descent Algorithm for Supervised Learning and Optimization

abstract: Using a quasi-realistic model of the feedback inhibition ofmotoneurons (MNs) by Renshaw cells, we show that weak inhibition is sufficient to maximally desynchronize MNs, with negligible effects on total MN activity. MN synchrony can produce a 20 - 30 Hz peak in the force power spectrum, which may cause instability in feedback loops.
originalAbstract: Using a quasi-realistic model of the feedback inhibition ofmotoneurons (MNs) by Renshaw cells, we show that weak inhibition is sufficient to maximally desynchronize MNs, with negligible effects on total MN activity. MN synchrony can produce a 20 - 30 Hz peak in the force power spectrum, which may cause instability in feedback loops.

paragraphs: The paper studies how feedback inhibition from Renshaw cells changes the coordination of motoneuron activity. Its central distinction is between how much the motoneurons are active overall and how synchronized their activity is. The authors use a quasi-realistic model to examine whether inhibition can substantially change synchrony while leaving total activity largely intact.

The reported result is that weak inhibition is sufficient to produce maximal desynchronization in the model, with negligible effects on total motoneuron activity. This means the modeled inhibitory feedback has a strong effect on coordination without requiring a comparable reduction in overall activity. The strength needed to disrupt synchrony is therefore a key feature of the finding.

The motivation comes from the consequences of synchronized motoneuron activity for force. Synchrony can produce a peak between 20 and 30 Hz in the force power spectrum, potentially causing instability in feedback loops. The model's result identifies a way that weak inhibitory feedback could address the synchrony associated with that peak while preserving the overall level of motoneuron activity.
summary.tldr: A model shows that weak Renshaw-cell inhibition can maximally desynchronize motoneurons with little change in their total activity.

title: Lower Boundaries of Motoneuron Desynchronization via Renshaw Interneurons

abstract: Selective suppression of transmission at feedback synapses during learning is proposed as a mechanism for combining associative feed(cid:173) back with self-organization of feed forward synapses. Experimental data demonstrates cholinergic suppression of synaptic transmission in layer I (feedback synapses), and a lack of suppression in layer IV (feed(cid:173) forward synapses). A network with this feature uses local rules to learn mappings which are not linearly separable. During learning, sensory stimuli and desired response are simultaneously presented as input. Feedforward connections form self-organized representations of input, while suppressed feedback connections learn the transpose of feedfor(cid:173) ward connectivity. During recall, suppression is removed, sensory input activates the self-organized representation, and activity generates the learned response.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a mechanism that lets a neural network both organize sensory representations and recall learned associations. Its key idea is to suppress transmission through feedback connections during learning. The biological motivation is experimental evidence of cholinergic suppression at feedback synapses in cortical layer I, without corresponding suppression at feedforward synapses in layer IV.

During learning, the network receives both the sensory stimulus and the desired response as inputs. Feedforward connections organize representations of the stimuli, while feedback connections learn connectivity corresponding to the transpose of the feedforward connections. Suppressing feedback transmission changes how those connections influence ongoing activity while the associations are being learned.

During recall, the suppression is lifted. A sensory input activates its organized representation, and network activity produces the learned response. Using local learning rules, the network learns mappings that are not linearly separable. The contribution is a concrete proposal for coordinating representation learning and associative recall through different transmission conditions during learning and retrieval.
summary.tldr: Suppressing feedback transmission during learning may let cortical networks combine self-organized representations with associative recall.

title: Cholinergic suppression of transmission may allow combined associative memory function and self-organization in the neocortex

paragraphs: This paper presents an algorithm for approximating functions with a neural network containing one hidden layer. Its nodes use piecewise-linear sigmoidal functions. The network grows one node at a time, with each new node fitted to the residual: the part of the target function that the current network has not yet explained.

The main innovation is the procedure for fitting an individual node. It searches for a good fit by solving a sequence of quadratic programming problems. This gives the node-fitting process a structured optimization approach and provides an alternative to derivative-based training methods such as backpropagation and its extensions.

The authors report finite-step convergence, a straightforward stopping criterion, and a deterministic way to seek good local minima. They also emphasize favorable scaling and numerical robustness. These properties matter because a constructive network method repeatedly solves the node-fitting problem as it grows. The stated guarantee concerns a controlled search for local solutions; the abstract characterizes the resulting minima as good, without claiming a globally optimal network.
summary.tldr: The sweeping hinge algorithm builds a network incrementally by fitting residuals through sequences of quadratic programming problems.

title: Function Approximation with the Sweeping Hinge Algorithm

abstract: A new method for multivariate density estimation is developed based on the Support Vector Method (SVM) solution of inverse ill-posed problems. The solution has the form of a mixture of den(cid:173) sities. This method with Gaussian kernels compared favorably to both Parzen's method and the Gaussian Mixture Model method. For synthetic data we achieve more accurate estimates for densities of 2, 6, 12, and 40 dimensions.

The solution has the form of a mixture of den(cid:173) sities. This method with Gaussian kernels compared favorably to both Parzen's method and the Gaussian Mixture Model method. For synthetic data we achieve more accurate estimates for densities of 2, 6, 12, and 40 dimensions.

paragraphs: This paper develops a method for estimating a probability density over several variables from data. Density estimation describes how probability is distributed across possible observations, including which combinations of variable values are more likely. The proposed approach uses the support vector method to formulate the estimation problem.

Specifically, the authors connect density estimation to solving an ill-posed inverse problem and obtain a solution expressed as a mixture of densities. That mixture form represents the estimated distribution by combining component densities. The contribution is a support-vector-based route to determining such an estimate, with Gaussian kernels used in the reported comparisons.

The method compares favorably with Parzen density estimation and Gaussian mixture modeling. On synthetic data, the authors report more accurate density estimates in 2, 6, 12, and 40 dimensions. Those results show the method being evaluated across several dimensionalities, including a substantially multivariate case. The stated evidence concerns estimation accuracy in those synthetic experiments and supports the approach as a useful alternative in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A support-vector density estimator produces mixture densities and reports improved synthetic-data accuracy over Parzen and Gaussian mixture methods.

title: Support Vector Method for Multivariate Density Estimation

abstract: We present a local learning approach for clustering. The basic idea is that a good clustering result should have the property that the cluster label of each data point can be well predicted based on its neighboring data and their cluster labels, using current supervised learning methods. An optimization problem is formulated such that its solution has the above property. Relaxation and eigen-decomposition are applied to solve this optimization problem. We also briefly investigate the parameter selection issue and provide a simple parameter selection method for the proposed algorithm. Experimental results are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
originalAbstract: We present a local learning approach for clustering. The basic idea is that a good clustering result should have the property that the cluster label of each data point can be well predicted based on its neighboring data and their cluster labels, using current supervised learning methods. An optimization problem is formulated such that its solution has the above property. Relaxation and eigen-decomposition are applied to solve this optimization problem. We also briefly investigate the parameter selection issue and provide a simple parameter selection method for the proposed algorithm. Experimental results are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: This paper proposes judging a clustering by how predictable its labels are within local neighborhoods. If a point belongs to a particular cluster, the nearby data and their assigned labels should help a supervised learning method predict that assignment. This turns local predictability into a criterion for discovering groups in unlabeled data.

The authors formulate an optimization problem that seeks cluster assignments with this property. Supervised learning methods provide the local prediction machinery, while the overall optimization determines the labels those predictors should explain. To solve the problem, the approach uses a relaxation and eigen-decomposition, connecting the local learning criterion to a tractable computational procedure.

The paper also briefly examines parameter selection and supplies a simple method for choosing parameters. Experiments support the effectiveness of the resulting clustering approach. Its central contribution is a way to make neighborhood-based prediction guide the formation of clusters, rather than using prediction only after cluster labels have already been established.
summary.tldr: The method discovers clusters by seeking labels that supervised learners can predict well from neighboring points.

title: A Local Learning Approach for Clustering

abstract: We consider the problem of constructing a function whose zero set is to represent a surface, given sample points with surface normal vectors. The contributions include a novel means of regularising multi-scale compactly supported basis functions that leads to the desirable properties previously only associated with fully supported bases, and show equivalence to a Gaussian process with modified covariance function. We also provide a regularisation framework for simpler and more direct treatment of surface normals, along with a corresponding generalisation of the representer theorem. We demonstrate the techniques on 3D problems of up to 14 million data points, as well as 4D time series data.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of constructing a function whose zero set is to represent a surface, given sample points with surface normal vectors. The contributions include a novel means of regularising multi-scale compactly supported basis functions that leads to the desirable properties previously only associated with fully supported bases, and show equivalence to a Gaussian process with modified covariance function. We also provide a regularisation framework for simpler and more direct treatment of surface normals, along with a corresponding generalisation of the representer theorem. We demonstrate the techniques on 3D problems of up to 14 million data points, as well as 4D time series data.

paragraphs: The paper reconstructs a surface from sample points and their normal vectors, which describe local surface orientation. It represents the surface implicitly: a function is learned, and the locations where that function equals zero form the surface. The central issue is how to construct and regularize this function using the supplied geometric evidence.

The authors introduce a way to regularize compactly supported basis functions at multiple scales. Such functions act within limited regions, yet the proposed regularization gives them desirable properties previously associated with fully supported bases. They also establish equivalence to a Gaussian process with a modified covariance function, linking the construction to a probabilistic representation.

A further regularization framework handles surface normals more directly and is supported by a generalized representer theorem. This integrates information about surface orientation into the mathematical treatment of reconstruction. Demonstrations include three-dimensional problems with up to 14 million data points and four-dimensional time-series data. These examples show the techniques applied to large geometric datasets and to data with a temporal component.
summary.tldr: A regularization framework reconstructs implicit surfaces using local basis functions, surface normals, and a Gaussian process connection.

title: Implicit Surfaces with Globally Regularised and Compactly Supported Basis Functions

abstract: The task of assigning a set of relevant tags to an image is challenging due to the size and variability of tag vocabularies. Consequently, most existing algorithms focus on tag assignment and fix an often large number of hand-crafted features to describe image characteristics. In this paper we introduce a hierarchical model for learning representations of full sized color images from the pixel level, removing the need for engineered feature representations and subsequent feature selection. We benchmark our model on the STL-10 recognition dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance. When our features are combined with TagProp (Guillaumin et al.), we outperform or compete with existing annotation approaches that use over a dozen distinct image descriptors. Furthermore, using 256-bit codes and Hamming distance for training TagProp, we exchange only a small reduction in performance for efficient storage and fast comparisons. In our experiments, using deeper architectures always outperform shallow ones.

paragraphs: Automatically assigning tags to images requires handling a large and varied vocabulary. Many approaches concentrate on the tag assignment step while relying on an extensive collection of manually designed image features. This paper instead learns a hierarchical representation directly from the pixels of full-sized color images, removing the need to engineer and subsequently select those features.

The learned representation is evaluated in both image recognition and annotation. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on STL-10. When combined with TagProp for annotation, it outperforms or competes with approaches that use more than a dozen distinct image descriptors. These results show that learning the image representation can support the downstream task without assembling that collection of handcrafted descriptions.

The authors also investigate a compact version using 256-bit codes and Hamming distance to train TagProp. This trades a small performance reduction for efficient storage and fast comparisons. Deeper architectures outperform shallow ones throughout the reported experiments. The findings connect representation learning, annotation quality, and compact coding, with the depth advantage stated for the experiments performed.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical image features learned from pixels support strong annotation performance, while compact binary codes trade a small accuracy reduction for efficiency.

title: Deep Representations and Codes for Image Auto-Annotation

abstract: Multiple hypothesis testing is a significant problem in nearly all neuroimaging studies. In order to correct for this phenomena, we require a reliable estimate of the Family-Wise Error Rate (FWER). The well known Bonferroni correction method, while being simple to implement, is quite conservative, and can substantially under-power a study because it ignores dependencies between test statistics. Permutation testing, on the other hand, is an exact, non parametric method of estimating the FWER for a given α threshold, but for acceptably low thresholds the computational burden can be prohibitive. In this paper, we observe that permutation testing in fact amounts to populating the columns of a very large matrix P. By analyzing the spectrum of this matrix, under certain conditions, we see that P has a low-rank plus a low-variance residual decomposition which makes it suitable for highly sub–sampled — on the order of 0.5% — matrix completion methods. Thus, we propose a novel permutation testing methodology which offers a large speedup, without sacrificing the fidelity of the estimated FWER. Our valuations on four different neuroimaging datasets show that a computational speedup factor of roughly 50× can be achieved while recovering the FWER distribution up to very high accuracy. Further, we show that the estimated α threshold is also recovered faithfully, and is stable.

paragraphs: Neuroimaging studies often test many hypotheses, making family-wise error control important. Permutation testing can account for dependencies between test statistics, but its computational cost can become prohibitive at low thresholds. This paper seeks to reduce that cost while preserving the accuracy of the error-rate estimates used for statistical decisions.

The authors view permutation testing as filling a large matrix. Under certain conditions, analysis of its spectrum reveals a low-rank component plus a residual with low variance. This structure supports matrix completion from a very small fraction of entries, on the order of 0.5%, allowing the procedure to avoid computing the entire matrix directly.

Evaluations on four neuroimaging datasets report roughly a 50-fold computational speedup while recovering the family-wise error distribution with high accuracy. The estimated significance threshold is also recovered faithfully and remains stable. These findings support the proposed acceleration in the evaluated settings, with its matrix-completion rationale depending on the stated low-rank-plus-residual structure rather than applying unconditionally to every permutation-testing problem.
summary.tldr: A matrix-completion approach achieves roughly 50-fold faster permutation testing on four neuroimaging datasets while preserving accurate error-rate estimates.

title: Speeding up Permutation Testing in Neuroimaging

abstract: We consider a setting in which low-power distributed sensors are each making highly noisy measurements of some unknown target function. A center wants to accurately learn this function by querying a small number of sensors, which ordinarily would be impossible due to the high noise rate. The question we address is whether local communication among sensors, together with natural best-response dynamics in an appropriately-deﬁned game, can denoise the system without destroying the true signal and allow the center to succeed from only a small number of active queries. We prove positive (and negative) results on the denoising power of several natural dynamics, and also show experimentally that when combined with recent agnostic active learning algorithms, this process can achieve low error from very few queries, performing substantially better than active or passive learning without these denoising dynamics as well as passive learning with denoising.
originalAbstract: We consider a setting in which low-power distributed sensors are each making highly noisy measurements of some unknown target function. A center wants to accurately learn this function by querying a small number of sensors, which ordinarily would be impossible due to the high noise rate. The question we address is whether local communication among sensors, together with natural best-response dynamics in an appropriately-deﬁned game, can denoise the system without destroying the true signal and allow the center to succeed from only a small number of active queries. We prove positive (and negative) results on the denoising power of several natural dynamics, and also show experimentally that when combined with recent agnostic active learning algorithms, this process can achieve low error from very few queries, performing substantially better than active or passive learning without these denoising dynamics as well as passive learning with denoising.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a central learner can recover an unknown function by querying only a few sensors when individual sensor measurements are highly noisy. With that much noise, a small number of direct queries would ordinarily be insufficient. The proposed opportunity is to let sensors communicate locally before the center requests their information.

The authors formulate this local interaction as a game and study natural best-response dynamics, in which sensors update according to their incentives. The crucial issue is whether these updates remove noise while retaining the underlying signal. Simply making sensors agree would not establish that their agreement reflects the function the center wants to learn.

The theoretical results include both successful and unsuccessful cases for the denoising power of different dynamics. Experiments then combine denoising with agnostic active learning, which selects informative queries while accommodating imperfect data. The combined process achieves low error from very few queries in the reported experiments, outperforming the stated alternatives with or without denoising. The findings support carefully chosen local dynamics, rather than a universal benefit from sensor interaction.
summary.tldr: Local sensor interactions can support accurate learning from few queries, but their ability to remove noise depends on the update dynamics.

title: Active Learning and Best-Response Dynamics

abstract: We extend the theory of boosting for regression problems to the online learning setting. Generalizing from the batch setting for boosting, the notion of a weak learning algorithm is modeled as an online learning algorithm with linear loss functions that competes with a base class of regression functions, while a strong learning algorithm is an online learning algorithm with smooth convex loss functions that competes with a larger class of regression functions. Our main result is an online gradient boosting algorithm which converts a weak online learning algorithm into a strong one where the larger class of functions is the linear span of the base class. We also give a simpler boosting algorithm that converts a weak online learning algorithm into a strong one where the larger class of functions is the convex hull of the base class, and prove its optimality.
originalAbstract: We extend the theory of boosting for regression problems to the online learning setting. Generalizing from the batch setting for boosting, the notion of a weak learning algorithm is modeled as an online learning algorithm with linear loss functions that competes with a base class of regression functions, while a strong learning algorithm is an online learning algorithm with smooth convex loss functions that competes with a larger class of regression functions. Our main result is an online gradient boosting algorithm which converts a weak online learning algorithm into a strong one where the larger class of functions is the linear span of the base class. We also give a simpler boosting algorithm that converts a weak online learning algorithm into a strong one where the larger class of functions is the convex hull of the base class, and prove its optimality.

paragraphs: Boosting combines weaker learning procedures into a stronger one. This paper extends that theory for regression to online learning, where predictions and updates occur over time. It makes the distinction between weak and strong learners precise through the losses they handle and the classes of regression functions against which they compete.

A weak learner handles linear losses and competes with a base class of functions. The main algorithm converts such a learner into one that handles smooth convex losses and competes with the linear span of the base class. This expands the comparison class to linear combinations of the original functions, giving a formal meaning to stronger predictive capability in the online setting.

The authors also provide a simpler algorithm whose comparison class is the convex hull of the base class, corresponding to convex combinations of its functions. They prove this simpler algorithm optimal. The two results offer different scopes of strengthening: the main construction reaches the linear span, while the simpler construction comes with an optimality result for the convex-hull setting.
summary.tldr: Online gradient boosting converts weak regression learners into stronger learners competing with linear or convex combinations of their base functions.

title: Online Gradient Boosting

abstract: Solving statistical learning problems often involves nonconvex optimization. Despite the empirical success of nonconvex statistical optimization methods, their global dynamics, especially convergence to the desirable local minima, remain less well understood in theory. In this paper, we propose a new analytic paradigm based on diffusion processes to characterize the global dynamics of nonconvex statistical optimization. As a concrete example, we study stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for the tensor decomposition formulation of independent component analysis. In particular, we cast different phases of SGD into diffusion processes, i.e., solutions to stochastic differential equations. Initialized from an unstable equilibrium, the global dynamics of SGD transit over three consecutive phases: (i) an unstable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process slowly departing from the initialization, (ii) the solution to an ordinary differential equation, which quickly evolves towards the desirable local minimum, and (iii) a stable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process oscillating around the desirable local minimum. Our proof techniques are based upon Stroock and Varadhan’s weak convergence of Markov chains to diffusion processes, which are of independent interest.

paragraphs: Nonconvex learning methods often work well empirically, but explaining their full optimization trajectory remains difficult. This paper introduces an analysis based on diffusion processes, using stochastic gradient descent for a tensor-decomposition formulation of independent component analysis as its concrete setting. The aim is to describe how the algorithm moves toward a desirable local minimum over time.

Starting from an unstable equilibrium, the analyzed dynamics pass through three phases. First, an unstable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process describes a slow departure from initialization. Next, an ordinary differential equation describes rapid movement toward the desirable minimum. Finally, a stable Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process describes fluctuations around that minimum.

This phase-by-phase account distinguishes the roles of random fluctuations and systematic motion along the trajectory. The proof uses weak convergence of Markov chains to diffusion processes to connect the discrete optimization algorithm with continuous mathematical descriptions. summary.tldr: A diffusion-based analysis describes three phases of SGD for tensor-based ICA, from leaving an unstable equilibrium to fluctuating around a desirable minimum.

title: Online ICA: Understanding Global Dynamics of Nonconvex Optimization via Diffusion Processes

abstract: We propose introspective convolutional networks (ICN) that emphasize the importance of having convolutional neural networks empowered with generative capabilities. We employ a reclassification-by-synthesis algorithm to perform training using a formulation stemmed from the Bayes theory. Our ICN tries to iteratively: (1) synthesize pseudo-negative samples; and (2) enhance itself by improving the classification. The single CNN classifier learned is at the same time generative --- being able to directly synthesize new samples within its own discriminative model. We conduct experiments on benchmark datasets including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN using state-of-the-art CNN architectures, and observe improved classification results.

paragraphs: A convolutional classifier is usually trained to distinguish examples, but this paper gives the classifier a generative role as well. The proposed introspective convolutional network can synthesize new samples within its own discriminative model. The authors use that capability as part of training, linking sample generation directly to improving classification.

Training follows an iterative reclassification-by-synthesis procedure derived from a Bayesian formulation. The network first generates pseudo-negative examples and then improves its classification using the resulting training process. Repeating these steps lets synthesis and discrimination contribute to the development of the same model. The final learned CNN retains both classification and sample-generation capabilities.

The authors evaluate the approach on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN using state-of-the-art CNN architectures and observe improved classification results. The findings support the value of adding this generative training mechanism to a classifier in the tested settings. The central contribution is the integration: the model’s own ability to produce examples becomes a resource for learning to distinguish them.
summary.tldr: Introspective convolutional networks alternate between synthesizing pseudo-negative samples and improving classification, with reported gains on three image benchmarks.

title: Introspective Classification with Convolutional Nets

abstract: Many problems in machine learning are naturally expressed in the language of undirected graphical models. Here, we propose black-box learning and inference algorithms for undirected models that optimize a variational approximation to the log-likelihood of the model. Central to our approach is an upper bound on the log-partition function parametrized by a function q that we express as a flexible neural network. Our bound makes it possible to track the partition function during learning, to speed-up sampling, and to train a broad class of hybrid directed/undirected models via a unified variational inference framework. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several popular generative modeling datasets.

Our bound makes it possible to track the partition function during learning, to speed-up sampling, and to train a broad class of hybrid directed/undirected models via a unified variational inference framework. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several popular generative modeling datasets.

paragraphs: Undirected graphical models express relationships among variables without assigning a direction to each connection. Learning them involves the partition function, which normalizes the model’s probabilities. This paper proposes black-box learning and inference algorithms that work by optimizing a variational approximation to the model’s log-likelihood, bringing this normalization quantity into the approximation.

The central construction is an upper bound on the log-partition function. A function q parameterizes the bound, and the authors represent q with a flexible neural network. This makes the bound part of a trainable framework and allows the partition function to be tracked while the model itself is being learned.

The framework also enables faster sampling and unified variational training for a broad class of models that combine directed and undirected components. Experiments on several generative modeling datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution is thus broader than a single model architecture: the neural parameterization supports a shared approach to normalization, inference, and learning across the stated model classes.
summary.tldr: A neural variational bound on the log-partition function supports learning, inference, and faster sampling in undirected and hybrid graphical models.

title: Neural Variational Inference and Learning in Undirected Graphical Models

abstract: We consider estimating the parametric components of semiparametric multi-index models in high dimensions. To bypass the requirements of Gaussianity or elliptical symmetry of covariates in existing methods, we propose to leverage a second-order Stein’s method with score function-based corrections. We prove that our estimator achieves a near-optimal statistical rate of convergence even when the score function or the response variable is heavy-tailed. To establish the key concentration results, we develop a data-driven truncation argument that may be of independent interest. We supplement our theoretical findings with simulations.
originalAbstract: We consider estimating the parametric components of semiparametric multi-index models in high dimensions. To bypass the requirements of Gaussianity or elliptical symmetry of covariates in existing methods, we propose to leverage a second-order Stein’s method with score function-based corrections. We prove that our estimator achieves a near-optimal statistical rate of convergence even when the score function or the response variable is heavy-tailed. To establish the key concentration results, we develop a data-driven truncation argument that may be of independent interest. We supplement our theoretical findings with simulations.

paragraphs: Semiparametric multi-index models combine a finite-dimensional component with a more flexible relationship between inputs and responses. This paper studies how to estimate the parametric component when the input dimension is high. Existing approaches can require covariates to be Gaussian or elliptically symmetric, restricting which input distributions their methods accommodate.

The proposed estimator uses a second-order Stein method with corrections based on score functions. These corrections provide a way to move beyond the Gaussianity and elliptical-symmetry requirements identified in earlier methods. The work also addresses heavy tails, which can make estimation difficult because unusually large observations can interfere with reliable statistical control.

The authors prove a near-optimal convergence rate even when the score function or response is heavy-tailed. To obtain the concentration results needed for that proof, they develop a data-driven truncation argument, which they suggest may have uses beyond this estimator. Simulations supplement the theory. Together, these results broaden the distributional settings addressed by high-dimensional multi-index estimation while retaining a strong statistical rate guarantee.
summary.tldr: A score-corrected second-order Stein estimator achieves near-optimal rates for high-dimensional multi-index models beyond Gaussian covariates, including stated heavy-tailed settings.

title: Estimating High-dimensional Non-Gaussian Multiple Index Models via Stein’s Lemma

abstract: In the online multiple testing problem, p-values corresponding to different null hypotheses are presented one by one, and the decision of whether to reject a hypothesis must be made immediately, after which the next p-value is presented. Alpha-investing algorithms to control the false discovery rate were first formulated by Foster and Stine and have since been generalized and applied to various settings, varying from quality-preserving databases for science to multiple A/B tests for internet commerce. This paper improves the class of generalized alpha-investing algorithms (GAI) in four ways : (a) we show how to uniformly improve the power of the entire class of GAI procedures under independence by awarding more alpha-wealth for each rejection, giving a near win-win resolution to a dilemma raised by Javanmard and Montanari, (b) we demonstrate how to incorporate prior weights to indicate domain knowledge of which hypotheses are likely to be null or non-null, (c) we allow for differing penalties for false discoveries to indicate that some hypotheses may be more meaningful/important than others, (d) we define a new quantity called the \emph{decaying memory false discovery rate, or $\memfdr$} that may be more meaningful for applications with an explicit time component, using a discount factor to incrementally forget past decisions and alleviate some potential problems that we describe and name ``piggybacking'' and ``alpha-death''. Our GAI++ algorithms incorporate all four generalizations (a, b, c, d) simulatenously, and reduce to more powerful variants of earlier algorithms when the weights and decay are all set to unity.

paragraphs: Online multiple testing requires a decision about each hypothesis as its p-value arrives, before seeing the next one. Generalized alpha-investing procedures manage this sequence using alpha-wealth. This paper expands that framework so testing can account for prior knowledge, differing consequences of mistakes, and the changing relevance of decisions over time.

Under independence, the authors show that awarding more alpha-wealth after each rejection uniformly improves the power of the existing procedure class. They also incorporate prior weights indicating which hypotheses are more likely to be null or non-null, plus separate penalties reflecting that false discoveries can have different importance. These additions make the testing rules responsive to distinctions among hypotheses.

This alternative quantity may better suit applications with an explicit time component and alleviates problems the authors call piggybacking and alpha-death. Their GAI++ algorithms combine all four extensions. Setting every weight and decay factor to one recovers more powerful variants of earlier algorithms without those adjustments.
summary.tldr: GAI++ extends online false-discovery control with improved power under independence, hypothesis weights, unequal error penalties, and discounted memory.

title: Online control of the false discovery rate with decaying memory

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) are an effective method for training generative models of complex data such as natural images. However, they are notoriously hard to train and can suffer from the problem of missing modes where the model is not able to produce examples in certain regions of the space. We propose an iterative procedure, called AdaGAN, where at every step we add a new component into a mixture model by running a GAN algorithm on a re-weighted sample. This is inspired by boosting algorithms, where many potentially weak individual predictors are greedily aggregated to form a strong composite predictor. We prove analytically that such an incremental procedure leads to convergence to the true distribution in a finite number of steps if each step is optimal, and convergence at an exponential rate otherwise. We also illustrate experimentally that this procedure addresses the problem of missing modes.

We also illustrate experimentally that this procedure addresses the problem of missing modes.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce convincing examples while still failing to represent parts of the data distribution. This missing-modes problem means that some kinds of examples never appear in its output. AdaGAN addresses this issue by building a mixture of generators incrementally, rather than relying on a single GAN to capture the entire distribution.

At each step, the method reweights the training sample, runs a GAN algorithm on that sample, and adds the resulting generator to the mixture. The approach draws on boosting: several individually imperfect components can contribute to a stronger combined model. Reweighting gives successive training stages a way to change which examples receive attention.

The authors prove convergence to the true distribution in finitely many steps when every step is optimal, and establish exponential convergence otherwise in their analysis. Their experiments also illustrate improvements in coverage of missing modes. The result connects an incremental mixture-building procedure with both a convergence argument and empirical evidence addressing a specific weakness of GAN training.
summary.tldr: AdaGAN incrementally combines GANs trained on reweighted samples to improve distribution coverage and address missing modes.

title: AdaGAN: Boosting Generative Models

abstract: Unsupervised image-to-image translation aims at learning a joint distribution of images in different domains by using images from the marginal distributions in individual domains. Since there exists an infinite set of joint distributions that can arrive the given marginal distributions, one could infer nothing about the joint distribution from the marginal distributions without additional assumptions. To address the problem, we make a shared-latent space assumption and propose an unsupervised image-to-image translation framework based on Coupled GANs. We compare the proposed framework with competing approaches and present high quality image translation results on various challenging unsupervised image translation tasks, including street scene image translation, animal image translation, and face image translation. We also apply the proposed framework to domain adaptation and achieve state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets. Code and additional results are available in https://github.com/mingyuliutw/unit.
originalAbstract: Unsupervised image-to-image translation aims at learning a joint distribution of images in different domains by using images from the marginal distributions in individual domains. Since there exists an infinite set of joint distributions that can arrive the given marginal distributions, one could infer nothing about the joint distribution from the marginal distributions without additional assumptions. To address the problem, we make a shared-latent space assumption and propose an unsupervised image-to-image translation framework based on Coupled GANs. We compare the proposed framework with competing approaches and present high quality image translation results on various challenging unsupervised image translation tasks, including street scene image translation, animal image translation, and face image translation. We also apply the proposed framework to domain adaptation and achieve state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets. Code and additional results are available in https://github.com/mingyuliutw/unit.

paragraphs: Unsupervised image translation learns relationships between image domains using separate image collections. The difficulty is that these collections reveal each domain's distribution but do not uniquely determine how images across domains should correspond. Infinitely many joint distributions can share the same individual distributions, so additional assumptions are needed.

The paper introduces a shared-latent-space assumption and builds a translation framework based on Coupled GANs. The assumption supplies a common underlying representation through which the domains can be related. This is central to the method: it gives structure to a correspondence problem that the separate image collections alone cannot resolve.

Comparisons with competing approaches show high-quality translations for street scenes, animals, and faces. The framework is also applied to domain adaptation, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets. These findings demonstrate useful translations and adaptation under the proposed modeling approach. They support the shared representation as a productive assumption for the evaluated tasks, while preserving the paper's distinction between learning individual image distributions and specifying relationships between them.
summary.tldr: A shared-latent-space assumption enables a Coupled GAN framework to learn image translation from separate domain collections.

title: Unsupervised Image-to-Image Translation Networks

abstract: We study the interplay between sequential decision making and avoiding discrimination against protected groups, when examples arrive online and do not follow distributional assumptions. We consider the most basic extension of classical online learning: Given a class of predictors that are individually non-discriminatory with respect to a particular metric, how can we combine them to perform as well as the best predictor, while preserving non-discrimination? Surprisingly we show that this task is unachievable for the prevalent notion of "equalized odds" that requires equal false negative rates and equal false positive rates across groups. On the positive side, for another notion of non-discrimination, "equalized error rates", we show that running separate instances of the classical multiplicative weights algorithm for each group achieves this guarantee. Interestingly, even for this notion, we show that algorithms with stronger performance guarantees than multiplicative weights cannot preserve non-discrimination.

Interestingly, even for this notion, we show that algorithms with stronger performance guarantees than multiplicative weights cannot preserve non-discrimination.

paragraphs: Combining individually non-discriminatory predictors may seem like a straightforward way to obtain both good predictions and fair treatment. This paper tests that intuition in online learning, where examples arrive sequentially without assumptions about their distribution. The objective is to perform as well as the best available predictor while preserving the predictors' non-discrimination guarantee.

For equalized odds, the authors prove that this objective cannot be achieved in the setting studied. Equalized odds requires equal false positive rates and equal false negative rates across protected groups. The result shows that this property of the individual predictors does not suffice to make it compatible with the desired online performance guarantee.

A different criterion, equalized overall error rates, admits a positive result: separate multiplicative weights learners for each group can provide the required guarantee. Even then, the paper establishes a boundary, showing that algorithms with stronger performance guarantees than multiplicative weights cannot preserve non-discrimination. The findings make the specific fairness definition central to what sequential predictor combination can achieve.
summary.tldr: Online predictor combination cannot preserve equalized odds with the desired performance guarantee, while group-specific multiplicative weights can preserve equalized error rates.

title: On preserving non-discrimination when combining expert advice

abstract: In high dimensional settings, density estimation algorithms rely crucially on their inductive bias. Despite recent empirical success, the inductive bias of deep generative models is not well understood. In this paper we propose a framework to systematically investigate bias and generalization in deep generative models of images by probing the learning algorithm with carefully designed training datasets. By measuring properties of the learned distribution, we are able to find interesting patterns of generalization. We verify that these patterns are consistent across datasets, common models and architectures.
originalAbstract: In high dimensional settings, density estimation algorithms rely crucially on their inductive bias. Despite recent empirical success, the inductive bias of deep generative models is not well understood. By measuring properties of the learned distribution, we are able to find interesting patterns of generalization. We verify that these patterns are consistent across datasets, common models and architectures.

paragraphs: Estimating a distribution over high-dimensional images depends heavily on a learning algorithm's inductive bias: the tendencies that guide what it learns from available examples. Successful image generation alone does not explain those tendencies. This paper develops an empirical framework for investigating how deep generative models generalize and what their learned distributions reveal about their bias.

The approach probes learning algorithms with carefully constructed training datasets. After training, the researchers measure properties of the resulting distribution and look for patterns in how the model generalizes. Designing the training evidence is central to the method: it provides a controlled way to investigate how what a model learns relates to the examples it receives.

The authors identify interesting generalization patterns and verify that they recur across the datasets, common models, and architectures examined. This consistency gives the observations significance beyond a single tested model configuration. The contribution is a systematic way to study generative learning behavior, together with empirical evidence of recurring patterns across the investigated settings.
summary.tldr: Carefully designed training datasets expose recurring patterns of bias and generalization in image-generating models.

title: Bias and Generalization in Deep Generative Models: An Empirical Study

abstract: In multiagent domains, coping with non-stationary agents that change behaviors from time to time is a challenging problem, where an agent is usually required to be able to quickly detect the other agent's policy during online interaction, and then adapt its own policy accordingly. This paper studies efficient policy detecting and reusing techniques when playing against non-stationary agents in Markov games. We propose a new deep BPR+ algorithm by extending the recent BPR+ algorithm with a neural network as the value-function approximator. To detect policy accurately, we propose the \textit{rectified belief model} taking advantage of the \textit{opponent model} to infer the other agent's policy from reward signals and its behaviors. Instead of directly storing individual policies as BPR+, we introduce \textit{distilled policy network} that serves as the policy library in BPR+, using policy distillation to achieve efficient online policy learning and reuse. Deep BPR+ inherits all the advantages of BPR+ and empirically shows better performance in terms of detection accuracy, cumulative rewards and speed of convergence compared to existing algorithms in complex Markov games with raw visual inputs.

paragraphs: When another agent changes its behavior during interaction, a previously effective response may stop working. This paper studies that problem in Markov games, focusing on how an agent can recognize its counterpart's current policy and reuse an appropriate response. The challenge combines identifying behavior with adapting quickly enough to benefit from that identification.

The proposed deep BPR+ algorithm extends Bayesian policy reuse with a neural network that approximates the value function. Its rectified belief model uses an opponent model to infer the other agent's policy from both observed behavior and reward signals. These two evidence sources inform the agent's beliefs about which policy it is facing.

The method also replaces separately stored policies with a distilled policy network serving as a policy library. This supports online learning and reuse within the same approach. In complex Markov games using raw visual inputs, the authors report better policy detection accuracy, cumulative reward, and convergence speed than existing algorithms. The findings support combining richer opponent inference with a compact reusable policy representation for the evaluated changing-agent settings.
summary.tldr: Deep BPR+ combines opponent inference and distilled policy reuse to improve adaptation to changing agents in evaluated Markov games.

title: A Deep Bayesian Policy Reuse Approach Against Non-Stationary Agents

abstract: Existing methods for interactive image retrieval have demonstrated the merit of integrating user feedback, improving retrieval results. However, most current systems rely on restricted forms of user feedback, such as binary relevance responses, or feedback based on a fixed set of relative attributes, which limits their impact. In this paper, we introduce a new approach to interactive image search that enables users to provide feedback via natural language, allowing for more natural and effective interaction. We formulate the task of dialog-based interactive image retrieval as a reinforcement learning problem, and reward the dialog system for improving the rank of the target image during each dialog turn. To mitigate the cumbersome and costly process of collecting human-machine conversations as the dialog system learns, we train our system with a user simulator, which is itself trained to describe the differences between target and candidate images. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated in a footwear retrieval application. Experiments on both simulated and real-world data show that 1) our proposed learning framework achieves better accuracy than other supervised and reinforcement learning baselines and 2) user feedback based on natural language rather than pre-specified attributes leads to more effective retrieval results, and a more natural and expressive communication interface.

paragraphs: Interactive image search can improve results by asking users for feedback, but a yes-or-no judgment or a fixed menu of attributes limits what they can communicate. This paper lets users describe their preferences in natural language over successive dialog turns. The search system can therefore use more expressive feedback when moving toward a target image.

The authors formulate the dialog as reinforcement learning. At each turn, the system receives a reward for improving the target image's rank. Because collecting human conversations throughout training would be costly, they train with a simulated user. That simulator learns to describe differences between a candidate image and the target, supplying feedback for the retrieval system's learning process.

Experiments in footwear retrieval use both simulated and real-world data. The proposed framework achieves better accuracy than the compared supervised and reinforcement learning baselines. Natural-language feedback also produces more effective retrieval than predefined attributes. These results support both the learning framework and the choice of an expressive conversational interface within the evaluated application.
summary.tldr: A retrieval system trained through simulated dialog uses natural-language feedback to improve footwear image search.

title: Dialog-based Interactive Image Retrieval

abstract: Multitask learning has shown promising performance in many applications and many multitask models have been proposed. In order to identify an effective multitask model for a given multitask problem, we propose a learning framework called Learning to MultiTask (L2MT). To achieve the goal, L2MT exploits historical multitask experience which is organized as a training set consisting of several tuples, each of which contains a multitask problem with multiple tasks, a multitask model, and the relative test error. Based on such training set, L2MT first uses a proposed layerwise graph neural network to learn task embeddings for all the tasks in a multitask problem and then learns an estimation function to estimate the relative test error based on task embeddings and the representation of the multitask model based on a unified formulation. Given a new multitask problem, the estimation function is used to identify a suitable multitask model. Experiments on benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed L2MT framework.

To achieve the goal, L2MT exploits historical multitask experience which is organized as a training set consisting of several tuples, each of which contains a multitask problem with multiple tasks, a multitask model, and the relative test error. Based on such training set, L2MT first uses a proposed layerwise graph neural network to learn task embeddings for all the tasks in a multitask problem and then learns an estimation function to estimate the relative test error based on task embeddings and the representation of the multitask model based on a unified formulation. Given a new multitask problem, the estimation function is used to identify a suitable multitask model. Experiments on benchmark datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed L2MT framework.

Learning to MultiTask, or L2MT, addresses this choice by using experience from previous multitask problems instead of treating every model-selection decision independently.

Its training examples pair a multitask problem with a model and the relative test error that model achieved. A proposed layerwise graph neural network learns representations of the tasks. An estimation function then combines these task representations with a representation of the candidate model, expressed through a unified formulation, to predict relative test error.

For a new multitask problem, L2MT uses that learned estimator to identify a suitable model. The approach makes historical model performance part of the information used for future selection, linking characteristics of the tasks with characteristics of the learning method. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness, supporting this learned model-selection strategy in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: L2MT learns from past multitask problems to predict model performance and select a suitable model for new tasks.

title: Learning to Multitask

abstract: We implement gradient-based variational inference routines for Wishart and inverse Wishart processes, which we apply as Bayesian models for the dynamic, heteroskedastic covariance matrix of a multivariate time series. The Wishart and inverse Wishart processes are constructed from i.i.d. Gaussian processes, existing variational inference algorithms for which form the basis of our approach. These methods are easy to implement as a black-box and scale favorably with the length of the time series, however, they fail in the case of the Wishart process, an issue we resolve with a simple modification into an additive white noise parameterization of the model. This modification is also key to implementing a factored variant of the construction, allowing inference to additionally scale to high-dimensional covariance matrices. Through experimentation, we demonstrate that some (but not all) model variants outperform multivariate GARCH when forecasting the covariances of returns on financial instruments.

This paper models those changes using Bayesian Wishart and inverse Wishart processes. The goal is to infer a changing covariance matrix while keeping computation manageable for long series and large collections of variables.

These processes are built from independent, identically distributed Gaussian processes, allowing the authors to draw on existing gradient-based variational inference algorithms. Applying those algorithms directly fails for the Wishart process. The paper resolves this issue through an additive white-noise parameterization, which also enables a factored construction that scales inference to higher-dimensional covariance matrices.

That distinction matters: the results support particular variants of the scalable Bayesian construction, rather than establishing an advantage for every Wishart or inverse Wishart model considered.
summary.tldr: A modified variational inference construction makes dynamic Bayesian covariance modeling scalable, with some variants outperforming multivariate GARCH.

title: Scalable Bayesian dynamic covariance modeling with variational Wishart and inverse Wishart processes

abstract: In this work, we consider the problem of model selection for deep reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world environments. Typically, the performance of deep RL algorithms is evaluated via on-policy interactions with the target environment. However, comparing models in a real-world environment for the purposes of early stopping or hyperparameter tuning is costly and often practically infeasible. This leads us to examine off-policy policy evaluation (OPE) in such settings. We focus on OPE of value-based methods, which are of particular interest in deep RL with applications like robotics, where off-policy algorithms based on Q-function estimation can often attain better sample complexity than direct policy optimization. Furthermore, existing OPE metrics either rely on a model of the environment, or the use of importance sampling (IS) to correct for the data being off-policy. However, for high-dimensional observations, such as images, models of the environment can be difficult to fit and value-based methods can make IS hard to use or even ill-conditioned, especially when dealing with continuous action spaces. In this paper, we focus on the specific case of MDPs with continuous action spaces and sparse binary rewards, which is representative of many important real-world applications. We propose an alternative metric that relies on neither models nor IS, by framing OPE as a positive-unlabeled (PU) classification problem. We experimentally show that this metric outperforms baselines on a number of tasks. Most importantly, it can reliably predict the relative performance of different policies in a number of generalization scenarios, including the transfer to the real-world of policies trained in simulation for an image-based robotic manipulation task.

summary.tldr: A positive-unlabeled classification metric predicts relative policy performance off-policy for continuous-action tasks with sparse binary rewards.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation via Off-Policy Classification

abstract: Adversarial training is a popular method to give neural nets robustness against adversarial perturbations. In practice adversarial training leads to low robust training loss. However, a rigorous explanation for why this happens under natural conditions is still missing. Recently a convergence theory of standard (non-adversarial) supervised training was developed by various groups for {\em very overparametrized} nets. It is unclear how to extend these results to adversarial training because of the min-max objective. Recently, a first step towards this direction was made by Gao et al. using tools from online learning, but they require the width of the net to be \emph{exponential} in input dimension $d$, and with an unnatural activation function. Our work proves convergence to low robust training loss for \emph{polynomial} width instead of exponential, under natural assumptions and with ReLU activations. A key element of our proof is showing that ReLU networks near initialization can approximate the step function, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Adversarial training seeks network parameters that perform well even under adversarial input perturbations. Although it often achieves low robust training loss in practice, explaining that success theoretically is difficult. Its min-max objective complicates the extension of convergence arguments developed for ordinary supervised training of highly over-parameterized neural networks.

This paper proves convergence to low robust training loss for ReLU networks with width polynomial in the input dimension, under assumptions described by the authors as natural. The earlier result discussed in the abstract required width exponential in that dimension and an unusual activation function. Replacing exponential width with polynomial width substantially improves the dimensional dependence of the theoretical requirement.

A key step shows that ReLU networks near their initialization can approximate a step function, supplying an ingredient for the convergence proof. The result helps explain optimization success in adversarial training within the stated theoretical setting. Its guarantee concerns low robust loss on the training data; that is the specific achievement established by the analysis, alongside the potentially useful approximation result near initialization.
summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, adversarial training of ReLU networks reaches low robust training loss with polynomial rather than exponential width.

title: Over-parameterized Adversarial Training: An Analysis Overcoming the Curse of Dimensionality

abstract: One of the main strengths of online algorithms is their ability to adapt to arbitrary data sequences. This is especially important in nonparametric settings, where performance is measured against rich classes of comparator functions that are able to fit complex environments. Although such hard comparators and complex environments may exhibit local regularities, efficient algorithms, which can provably take advantage of these local patterns, are hardly known. We fill this gap by introducing efficient online algorithms (based on a single versatile master algorithm) each adapting to one of the following regularities: (i) local Lipschitzness of the competitor function, (ii) local metric dimension of the instance sequence, (iii) local performance of the predictor across different regions of the instance space. Extending previous approaches, we design algorithms that dynamically grow hierarchical ε-nets on the instance space whose prunings correspond to different “locality profiles” for the problem at hand. Using a technique based on tree experts, we simultaneously and efficiently compete against all such prunings, and prove regret bounds each scaling with a quantity associated with a different type of local regularity. When competing against “simple” locality profiles, our technique delivers regret bounds that are significantly better than those proven using the previous approach. On the other hand, the time dependence of our bounds is not worse than that obtained by ignoring any local regularities.

paragraphs: Online learners must adapt as data arrive, potentially in arbitrary sequences. Even when the overall prediction problem is complex, particular regions can have useful regularities. This paper develops efficient algorithms that exploit such local structure while comparing their performance with rich classes of functions capable of fitting complicated environments.

A shared master algorithm supports adaptations to three different properties: local smoothness of the comparator function, local metric dimension of the observed instances, and local predictor performance. The algorithms grow hierarchical nets that organize the input space at different resolutions. Pruning those hierarchies produces different descriptions of where finer or coarser treatment is useful.

A tree-expert technique lets the learner efficiently compete with all these prunings at once. The authors prove regret bounds that depend on the relevant form of local regularity. For simple locality profiles, the bounds improve significantly on the earlier approach. Their dependence on time is also no worse than bounds that ignore local regularity, supporting adaptation without worsening that aspect of the guarantee.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical online learners exploit local regularity to improve regret guarantees while preserving the time dependence of bounds that ignore it.

title: Locally-Adaptive Nonparametric Online Learning

abstract: The state-of-the-art approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) algorithms face a fundamental tradeoff between query latency and accuracy, because of small main memory capacity: To store indices in main memory for short query latency, the ANNS algorithms have to limit dataset size or use a quantization scheme which hurts search accuracy. The emergence of heterogeneous memory (HM) brings a solution to significantly increase memory capacity and break the above tradeoff: Using HM, billions of data points can be placed in the main memory on a single machine without using any data compression. However, HM consists of both fast (but small) memory and slow (but large) memory, and using HM inappropriately slows down query significantly. In this work, we present a novel graph-based similarity search algorithm called HM-ANN, which takes both memory and data heterogeneity into consideration and enables billion-scale similarity search on a single node without using compression. On two billion-sized datasets BIGANN and DEEP1B, HM-ANN outperforms state-of-the-art compression-based solutions such as L&C and IMI+OPQ in recall-vs-latency by a large margin, obtaining 46% higher recall under the same search latency. We also extend existing graph-based methods such as HNSW and NSG with two strong baseline implementations on HM. At billion-point scale, HM-ANN is 2X and 5.8X faster than our HNSWand NSG baselines respectively to reach the same accuracy.

Heterogeneous memory offers another option: combine a small amount of fast memory with a larger amount of slow memory, allowing billions of uncompressed points on one machine.

summary.tldr: HM-ANN uses heterogeneous memory for uncompressed billion-point search and improves measured recall–latency tradeoffs over the evaluated alternatives.

title: HM-ANN: Efficient Billion-Point Nearest Neighbor Search on Heterogeneous Memory

abstract: Deep Generative Networks (DGNs) with probabilistic modeling of their output and latent space are currently trained via Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). In the absence of a known analytical form for the posterior and likelihood expectation, VAEs resort to approximations, including (Amortized) Variational Inference (AVI) and Monte-Carlo sampling. We exploit the Continuous Piecewise Affine property of modern DGNs to derive their posterior and marginal distributions as well as the latter's first two moments. These findings enable us to derive an analytical Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for gradient-free DGN learning. We demonstrate empirically that EM training of DGNs produces greater likelihood than VAE training. Our new framework will guide the design of new VAE AVI that better approximates the true posterior and open new avenues to apply standard statistical tools for model comparison, anomaly detection, and missing data imputation.
