paragraphs: Probabilistic deep generative networks connect hidden variables to observed outputs, but training requires reasoning about distributions that can be difficult to calculate. Variational autoencoders address this difficulty using approximate inference and sampling. This paper investigates whether the mathematical structure of the generator can instead provide analytical access to the relevant distributions.

The authors exploit the continuous piecewise affine structure of modern generative networks: the mapping consists of affine pieces joined continuously. From this structure, they derive posterior and marginal distributions, together with the marginal distribution's first two moments. These results support an analytical expectation-maximization algorithm that learns the generative network without gradient-based training.

In the reported experiments, expectation-maximization training achieves greater likelihood than VAE training. That is empirical evidence for the proposed learning approach, rather than a universal ranking of the methods. The analytical framework also offers a basis for designing better variational approximations and for applying statistical tools to model comparison, anomaly detection, and missing-data imputation; these are presented as avenues opened by the work.
summary.tldr: The paper uses piecewise affine network structure to derive analytical distributions and a gradient-free expectation-maximization training method.

title: Analytical Probability Distributions and Exact Expectation-Maximization for Deep Generative Networks

abstract: The Schatten-$p$ quasi-norm with $p\in(0,1)$ has recently gained considerable attention in various low-rank matrix estimation problems offering significant benefits over relevant convex heuristics such as the nuclear norm. However, due to the nonconvexity of the Schatten-$p$ quasi-norm, minimization suffers from two major drawbacks: 1) the lack of theoretical guarantees and 2) the high computational cost which is demanded for the minimization task even for trivial tasks such as finding stationary points. In an attempt to reduce the high computational cost induced by Schatten-$p$ quasi-norm minimization, variational forms, which are defined over smaller-size matrix factors whose product equals the original matrix, have been proposed. Here, we propose and analyze a novel {\it variational form of Schatten-$p$ quasi-norm} which, for the first time in the literature, is defined for any continuous value of $p\in(0,1]$ and decouples along the columns of the factorized matrices. The proposed form can be considered as the natural generalization of the well-known variational form of the nuclear norm to the nonconvex case i.e., for $p\in(0,1)$. Notably, low-rankness is now imposed via a group-sparsity promoting regularizer. The resulting formulation gives way to SVD-free algorithms thus offering lower computational complexity than the one that is induced by the original definition of the Schatten-$p$ quasi-norm. A local optimality analysis is provided which shows~that we can arrive at a local minimum of the original Schatten-$p$ quasi-norm problem by reaching a local minimum of the matrix factorization based surrogate problem. In addition, for the case of the squared Frobenious loss with linear operators obeying the restricted isometry property (RIP), a rank-one update scheme is proposed, which offers a way to escape poor local minima. Finally, the efficiency of our approach is empirically shown on a matrix completion problem.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix estimation seeks a compact matrix description that still explains the data. The Schatten-p quasi-norm encourages this structure and can offer benefits over convex alternatives, but its nonconvex optimization is computationally demanding. This paper develops a different mathematical expression for the penalty, using smaller matrices whose product represents the matrix being estimated.

The new expression works for every continuous choice of p between zero and one, including one, and separates across columns of the factors. It encourages groups of factor entries to disappear together, imposing low rank through group sparsity. This structure enables algorithms that avoid singular value decomposition, reducing computational complexity relative to working directly with the original penalty.

The analysis connects local minima of the factorized surrogate to local minima of the original problem. For squared Frobenius loss and linear operators satisfying the restricted isometry property, the authors also propose rank-one updates that offer an escape from poor local minima. Matrix-completion experiments demonstrate efficiency, complementing the mathematical justification for the reformulation.
summary.tldr: A factorized Schatten-p penalty enables cheaper low-rank optimization while connecting surrogate local minima to those of the original problem.

title: A novel variational form of the Schatten-$p$ quasi-norm

abstract: Hypergraphs are important objects to model ternary or higher-order relations of objects, and have a number of applications in analysing many complex datasets occurring in practice. In this work we study a new heat diffusion process in hypergraphs, and employ this process to design a polynomial-time algorithm that approximately finds bipartite components in a hypergraph. We theoretically prove the performance of our proposed algorithm, and compare it against the previous state-of-the-art through extensive experimental analysis on both synthetic and real-world datasets. We find that our new algorithm consistently and significantly outperforms the previous state-of-the-art across a wide range of hypergraphs.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships involving three or more objects, making them useful for datasets whose interactions cannot be captured fully by ordinary pairwise connections. This paper studies how to find bipartite components within such structures. Its goal is approximate discovery, allowing an algorithm to identify this organization without requiring an exact solution to the component-finding problem.

The central construction is a new heat diffusion process on a hypergraph. The authors use that process to design a polynomial-time algorithm for approximately finding bipartite components. Diffusion is therefore the basis of the computational method, connecting a process on the hypergraph to the task of identifying its internal structure.

The paper provides a theoretical performance guarantee and compares the algorithm with the previous state of the art on synthetic and real-world datasets. Across the tested range of hypergraphs, the authors report consistent and significant improvements. The combination of a proved guarantee and broad experimental comparison supports the new diffusion process as a useful tool for this particular structural analysis task.
summary.tldr: A new hypergraph heat diffusion process yields a polynomial-time approximation algorithm with theoretical guarantees and strong experimental results.

title: Finding Bipartite Components in Hypergraphs

abstract: We study pure exploration in bandits, where the dimension of the feature representation can be much larger than the number of arms. To overcome the curse of dimensionality, we propose to adaptively embed the feature representation of each arm into a lower-dimensional space and carefully deal with the induced model misspecifications. Our approach is conceptually very different from existing works that can either only handle low-dimensional linear bandits or passively deal with model misspecifications. We showcase the application of our approach to two pure exploration settings that were previously under-studied: (1) the reward function belongs to a possibly infinite-dimensional Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space, and (2) the reward function is nonlinear and can be approximated by neural networks. Our main results provide sample complexity guarantees that only depend on the effective dimension of the feature spaces in the kernel or neural representations. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our methods.

paragraphs: In bandit pure exploration, an algorithm collects observations to learn about available choices. A challenge arises when each choice has a feature representation far larger than the number of choices themselves. This paper develops an approach for avoiding the resulting dependence on a very large ambient feature space.

The method adaptively embeds each arm's features into a lower-dimensional space and explicitly handles the model mismatch introduced by that compression. This is central to the approach: reducing dimension changes how rewards can be represented, so the algorithm must account for those errors while deciding how to explore.

The authors apply the method to rewards belonging to a potentially infinite-dimensional kernel function space and to nonlinear rewards that neural networks can approximate. Their sample-complexity guarantees depend on the effective dimension of these representations rather than their full feature dimension. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate efficacy. The results show how adaptive representation reduction can make exploration tractable in these settings while retaining theoretical control over the induced approximation.
summary.tldr: Adaptive feature compression enables kernel and neural bandit exploration with guarantees governed by effective representation dimension.

title: Pure Exploration in Kernel and Neural Bandits

abstract: We present a new second-order oracle bound for the expected risk of a weighted majority vote. The bound is based on a novel parametric form of the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality (a.k.a. one-sided Chebyshev’s), which is amenable to efficient minimization. The new form resolves the optimization challenge faced by prior oracle bounds based on the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality, the C-bounds [Germain et al., 2015], and, at the same time, it improves on the oracle bound based on second order Markov’s inequality introduced by Masegosa et al. [2020]. We also derive a new concentration of measure inequality, which we name PAC-Bayes-Bennett, since it combines PAC-Bayesian bounding with Bennett’s inequality. We use it for empirical estimation of the oracle bound. The PAC-Bayes-Bennett inequality improves on the PAC-Bayes-Bernstein inequality of Seldin et al. [2012]. We provide an empirical evaluation demonstrating that the new bounds can improve on the work of Masegosa et al. [2020]. Both the parametric form of the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality and the PAC-Bayes-Bennett inequality may be of independent interest for the study of concentration of measure in other domains.

We use it for empirical estimation of the oracle bound. The PAC-Bayes-Bennett inequality improves on the PAC-Bayes-Bernstein inequality of Seldin et al. [2012]. Both the parametric form of the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality and the PAC-Bayes-Bennett inequality may be of independent interest for the study of concentration of measure in other domains.

paragraphs: A weighted majority vote combines predictions from several models, giving some models more influence than others. This paper develops a new bound on its expected prediction risk. The bound uses second-order information and is designed to address both the quality of the guarantee and the difficulty of optimizing it.

The first contribution is a parameterized version of the Chebyshev-Cantelli inequality, which controls deviations in one direction. Its form permits efficient minimization, resolving an optimization obstacle in earlier bounds known as C-bounds. The resulting oracle bound also improves on a previous bound derived from the second-order Markov inequality.

To estimate that oracle bound from data, the authors introduce PAC-Bayes-Bennett, combining PAC-Bayesian reasoning with Bennett's concentration inequality. They show that it improves on an earlier PAC-Bayes-Bernstein inequality. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that the new bounds can improve on prior work, rather than establishing improvement in every setting. Both mathematical inequalities may also prove useful for studying concentration outside weighted voting.
summary.tldr: New concentration inequalities provide improved, efficiently optimizable risk bounds for weighted majority votes.

title: Chebyshev-Cantelli PAC-Bayes-Bennett Inequality for the Weighted Majority Vote

abstract: In view of training increasingly complex learning architectures, we establish a nonsmooth implicit function theorem with an operational calculus. Our result applies to most practical problems (i.e., definable problems) provided that a nonsmooth form of the classical invertibility condition is fulfilled. This approach allows for formal subdifferentiation: for instance, replacing derivatives by Clarke Jacobians in the usual differentiation formulas is fully justified for a wide class of nonsmooth problems. Moreover this calculus is entirely compatible with algorithmic differentiation (e.g., backpropagation). We provide several applications such as training deep equilibrium networks, training neural nets with conic optimization layers, or hyperparameter-tuning for nonsmooth Lasso-type models. To show the sharpness of our assumptions, we present numerical experiments showcasing the extremely pathological gradient dynamics one can encounter when applying implicit algorithmic differentiation without any hypothesis.

paragraphs: Some learning systems contain components defined implicitly, such as an equilibrium or the solution of an optimization problem. Training requires tracking how those solutions change when parameters change. This becomes harder when the underlying functions are nonsmooth, because ordinary derivative formulas may no longer apply.

The paper establishes a nonsmooth implicit function theorem together with calculus rules that can be used in computations. The result applies to definable problems, a broad class covering many practical cases, provided a nonsmooth version of an invertibility condition holds. Within the supported setting, substituting Clarke Jacobians for ordinary derivatives in familiar formulas is mathematically justified and compatible with backpropagation.

These examples explain why the assumptions matter: the paper supplies conditions under which a convenient differentiation procedure has a sound mathematical foundation.
summary.tldr: A nonsmooth implicit function theorem justifies backpropagation-compatible differentiation rules under definability and generalized invertibility conditions.

title: Nonsmooth Implicit Differentiation for Machine-Learning and Optimization

abstract: Partial domain adaptation (PDA) has gained much attention due to its practical setting. The current PDA methods usually adapt the feature extractor by aligning the target and reweighted source domain distributions. In this paper, we experimentally find that the feature adaptation by the reweighted distribution alignment in some state-of-the-art PDA methods is not robust to the ``noisy'' weights of source domain data, leading to negative domain transfer on some challenging benchmarks. To tackle the challenge of negative domain transfer, we propose a novel Adversarial Reweighting (AR) approach that adversarially learns the weights of source domain data to align the source and target domain distributions, and the transferable deep recognition network is learned on the reweighted source domain data. Based on this idea, we propose a training algorithm that alternately updates the parameters of the network and optimizes the weights of source domain data. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the benchmarks of ImageNet-Caltech, Office-Home, VisDA-2017, and DomainNet. Ablation studies also confirm the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper examines a failure mode in partial domain adaptation: adapting a recognition model by aligning target data with weighted source data can go wrong when the source weights are unreliable. The authors experimentally find this sensitivity in some leading methods, where noisy weights lead to negative transfer on challenging benchmarks. In these cases, the adaptation process harms the transfer it is meant to support.

It learns weights adversarially to bring source and target distributions into alignment, then learns the transferable recognition network from the reweighted source data. These findings show the practical value of reconsidering how source examples receive weight, because those choices determine which source information shapes the transferred model.
summary.tldr: Adversarial Reweighting alternates between learning source-example weights and a recognition network to improve partial domain adaptation.

title: Adversarial Reweighting for Partial Domain Adaptation

abstract: The incorporation of appropriate inductive bias plays a critical role in learning dynamics from data. A growing body of work has been exploring ways to enforce energy conservation in the learned dynamics by encoding Lagrangian or Hamiltonian dynamics into the neural network architecture. These existing approaches are based on differential equations, which do not allow discontinuity in the states and thereby limit the class of systems one can learn. However, in reality, most physical systems, such as legged robots and robotic manipulators, involve contacts and collisions, which introduce discontinuities in the states. In this paper, we introduce a differentiable contact model, which can capture contact mechanics: frictionless/frictional, as well as elastic/inelastic. This model can also accommodate inequality constraints, such as limits on the joint angles. The proposed contact model extends the scope of Lagrangian and Hamiltonian neural networks by allowing simultaneous learning of contact and system properties. We demonstrate this framework on a series of challenging 2D and 3D physical systems with different coefficients of restitution and friction. The learned dynamics can be used as a differentiable physics simulator for downstream gradient-based optimization tasks, such as planning and control.

paragraphs: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian neural networks encode physical structure into learned dynamics, including energy conservation. The differential-equation approaches discussed in this paper do not allow state discontinuities, restricting their ability to describe contacts and collisions. Those events are central to physical systems such as legged robots and manipulators.

The authors introduce a differentiable contact model that covers frictionless and frictional interactions as well as elastic and inelastic contacts. It also supports inequality constraints, including joint-angle limits. Incorporating this model extends the networks so that contact properties and other system properties can be learned simultaneously from data.

The framework is demonstrated on challenging two-dimensional and three-dimensional systems with different friction and restitution coefficients. The contribution connects structured dynamics learning with physical events involving abrupt changes.

title: Extending Lagrangian and Hamiltonian Neural Networks with Differentiable Contact Models

abstract: Loss functions play an important role in training deep-network-based object detectors. The most widely used evaluation metric for object detection is Average Precision (AP), which captures the performance of localization and classification sub-tasks simultaneously. However, due to the non-differentiable nature of the AP metric, traditional object detectors adopt separate differentiable losses for the two sub-tasks. Such a mis-alignment issue may well lead to performance degradation. To address this, existing works seek to design surrogate losses for the AP metric manually, which requires expertise and may still be sub-optimal. In this paper, we propose Parameterized AP Loss, where parameterized functions are introduced to substitute the non-differentiable components in the AP calculation. Different AP approximations are thus represented by a family of parameterized functions in a unified formula. Automatic parameter search algorithm is then employed to search for the optimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the COCO benchmark with three different object detectors (i.e., RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, and Deformable DETR) demonstrate that the proposed Parameterized AP Loss consistently outperforms existing handcrafted losses. Code shall be released.

paragraphs: Object detectors are commonly evaluated using Average Precision, which combines localization and classification performance. Because AP is not differentiable, training often uses separate differentiable objectives for those tasks. This creates a mismatch between what the detector optimizes and how it is evaluated, which can reduce performance.

The paper proposes Parameterized AP Loss to make the choice of approximation searchable. Parameterized functions replace the non-differentiable components of the AP calculation, placing different approximations within one unified formula. An automatic search algorithm then selects the parameters. This makes the construction of the training objective part of the optimization process instead of relying entirely on a manually designed surrogate.

Experiments on COCO cover RetinaNet, Faster R-CNN, and Deformable DETR. Across those detectors, the proposed loss consistently outperforms the handcrafted losses used for comparison. These results support searching over AP approximations as a useful way to align training with evaluation. The empirical breadth across three detectors is part of the evidence for the approach’s usefulness.
summary.tldr: Automatically searching a parameterized approximation to Average Precision improves detection performance over compared handcrafted losses on COCO.

title: Searching Parameterized AP Loss for Object Detection

abstract: Online imitation learning is the problem of how best to mimic expert demonstrations, given access to the environment or an accurate simulator. Prior work has shown that in the \textit{infinite} sample regime, exact moment matching achieves value equivalence to the expert policy. However, in the \textit{finite} sample regime, even if one has no optimization error, empirical variance can lead to a performance gap that scales with $H^2 / N_{\text{exp}}$ for behavioral cloning and $H / N_{\text{exp}}$ for online moment matching, where $H$ is the horizon and $N_{\text{exp}}$ is the size of the expert dataset. We introduce the technique of ``replay estimation'' to reduce this empirical variance: by repeatedly executing cached expert actions in a stochastic simulator, we compute a smoother expert visitation distribution estimate to match. In the presence of general function approximation, we prove a meta theorem reducing the performance gap of our approach to the \textit{parameter estimation error} for offline classification (i.e. learning the expert policy). In the tabular setting or with linear function approximation, our meta theorem shows that the performance gap incurred by our approach achieves the optimal $\widetilde{O} \left( \min( H^{3/2} / N_{\text{exp}}, H / \sqrt{N_{\text{exp}}} \right)$ dependency, under significantly weaker assumptions compared to prior work. We implement multiple instantiations of our approach on several continuous control tasks and find that we are able to significantly improve policy performance across a variety of dataset sizes.

paragraphs: Online imitation learning uses expert demonstrations together with access to an environment or accurate simulator. Even when optimization is exact, a finite demonstration set introduces sampling variance that can leave a performance gap. This paper targets that statistical problem by improving the estimate of where the expert's behavior takes it.

Replay estimation repeatedly executes cached expert actions in a stochastic simulator. These replays produce a smoother estimate of the expert visitation distribution for the learner to match. summary.tldr: Replaying expert actions in a stochastic simulator reduces estimation variance and yields optimal imitation-learning guarantees in tabular and linear settings.

title: Minimax Optimal Online Imitation Learning via Replay Estimation

abstract: Simulation-based Bayesian inference (SBI) can be used to estimate the parameters of complex mechanistic models given observed model outputs without requiring access to explicit likelihood evaluations. A prime example for the application of SBI in neuroscience involves estimating the parameters governing the response dynamics of Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) models from electrophysiological measurements, by inferring a posterior over the parameters that is consistent with a set of observations. To this end, many SBI methods employ a set of summary statistics or scientifically interpretable features to estimate a surrogate likelihood or posterior. However, currently, there is no way to identify how much each summary statistic or feature contributes to reducing posterior uncertainty. To address this challenge, one could simply compare the posteriors with and without a given feature included in the inference process. However, for large or nested feature sets, this would necessitate repeatedly estimating the posterior, which is computationally expensive or even prohibitive. Here, we provide a more efficient approach based on the SBI method neural likelihood estimation (NLE): We show that one can marginalize the trained surrogate likelihood post-hoc before inferring the posterior to assess the contribution of a feature. We demonstrate the usefulness of our method by identifying the most important features for inferring parameters of an example HH neuron model. Beyond neuroscience, our method is generally applicable to SBI workflows that rely on data features for inference used in other scientific fields.

paragraphs: Simulation-based Bayesian inference estimates model parameters from observations when explicit likelihood evaluation is unavailable. Many workflows summarize observations using scientifically meaningful features. This paper addresses how to determine which features actually reduce uncertainty about parameters, rather than treating every supplied summary statistic as equally informative.

A straightforward comparison would infer parameters with and without each feature, but repeated posterior estimation becomes expensive for large or nested feature sets. The authors instead build on neural likelihood estimation. They show that a trained surrogate likelihood can be marginalized after training, allowing selected features to be integrated out before the posterior is inferred.

This reuse of the trained likelihood provides a more efficient route to assessing feature contributions. The authors demonstrate it by identifying informative features for parameter inference in an example Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model using electrophysiological observations. The contribution connects feature importance to posterior uncertainty and is presented as applicable beyond neuroscience to simulation-based inference workflows that rely on data features.
summary.tldr: Marginalizing a trained neural likelihood enables more efficient assessment of which features reduce uncertainty in simulation-based inference.

title: Efficient identification of informative features in simulation-based inference

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO), which uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a surrogate to model its objective function, is popular for black-box optimization. However, due to the limitations of GPs, BO underperforms in some problems such as those with categorical, high-dimensional or image inputs. To this end, recent works have used the highly expressive neural networks (NNs) as the surrogate model and derived theoretical guarantees using the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). However, these works suffer from the limitations of the requirement to invert an extremely large parameter matrix and the restriction to the sequential (rather than batch) setting. To overcome these limitations, we introduce two algorithms based on the Thompson sampling (TS) policy named Sample-Then-Optimize Batch Neural TS (STO-BNTS) and STO-BNTS-Linear. To choose an input query, we only need to train an NN (resp. a linear model) and then choose the query by maximizing the trained NN (resp. linear model), which is equivalently sampled from the GP posterior with the NTK as the kernel function. As a result, our algorithms sidestep the need to invert the large parameter matrix yet still preserve the validity of the TS policy. Next, we derive regret upper bounds for our algorithms with batch evaluations, and use insights from batch BO and NTK to show that they are asymptotically no-regret under certain conditions. Finally, we verify their empirical effectiveness using practical AutoML and reinforcement learning experiments.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimisation uses a surrogate model to decide which inputs of an unknown objective to evaluate. Gaussian-process surrogates can struggle with categorical, high-dimensional, or image inputs, motivating neural alternatives. However, existing theoretically supported neural approaches can require inversion of an extremely large parameter matrix and restrict evaluations to a sequential setting.

The paper introduces two batch Thompson-sampling algorithms, STO-BNTS and STO-BNTS-Linear. Selecting a query involves training a neural network or a linear model and then maximising that trained model. The authors connect this procedure to sampling from a Gaussian-process posterior with a neural tangent kernel. That connection preserves the Thompson-sampling interpretation while avoiding the large matrix inversion.

The authors derive regret upper bounds for batch evaluations and establish asymptotically no-regret behaviour under certain conditions. This conditional guarantee describes how performance compares with the best choices over time, rather than ensuring every selected query is optimal. Experiments in automated machine learning and reinforcement learning support the algorithms' practical effectiveness, linking their computational construction to applications that benefit from batch evaluation.
summary.tldr: Two neural Thompson-sampling algorithms enable batch optimisation without large parameter-matrix inversion and provide conditional no-regret guarantees.

title: Sample-Then-Optimize Batch Neural Thompson Sampling

abstract: In this work, we study data-driven decision-making and depart from the classical identically and independently distributed (i.i.d.) assumption. We present a new framework in which historical samples are generated from unknown and different distributions, which we dub \textit{heterogeneous environments}. These distributions are assumed to lie in a heterogeneity ball with known radius and centered around the (also) unknown future (out-of-sample) distribution on which the performance of a decision will be evaluated. We quantify the asymptotic worst-case regret that is achievable by central data-driven policies such as Sample Average Approximation, but also by rate-optimal ones, as a function of the radius of the heterogeneity ball. Our work shows that the type of achievable performance varies considerably across different combinations of problem classes and notions of heterogeneity. We demonstrate the versatility of our framework by comparing achievable guarantees for the heterogeneous version of widely studied data-driven problems such as pricing, ski-rental, and newsvendor. En route, we establish a new connection between data-driven decision-making and distributionally robust optimization.

paragraphs: Decisions based on historical data are often analyzed as though every sample came independently from the same distribution. This paper studies a different situation: historical observations come from unknown, different distributions, while the decision will be judged under another unknown future distribution. That distinction makes the relationship between past evidence and future performance central to the analysis.

The framework assumes that all historical distributions lie within a heterogeneity ball centered on the future distribution, with a known radius. This radius expresses how much mismatch is allowed. The authors characterize asymptotic worst-case regret as a function of that radius, considering both familiar policies such as Sample Average Approximation and policies that achieve optimal rates.

The resulting guarantees vary substantially with the decision problem and the definition of heterogeneity. Comparisons across pricing, ski-rental, and newsvendor problems illustrate that there is no single performance pattern covering all combinations. The work also establishes a connection to distributionally robust optimization, linking decisions from heterogeneous observations with optimization that explicitly accounts for uncertainty about distributions.
summary.tldr: A framework for heterogeneous historical data characterizes how distribution mismatch affects achievable decision-making regret.

title: Beyond IID: data-driven decision-making in heterogeneous environments

abstract: Free-form text prompts allow users to describe their intentions during image manipulation conveniently. Based on the visual latent space of StyleGAN[21] and text embedding space of CLIP[34], studies focus on how to map these two latent spaces for text-driven attribute manipulations. Currently, the latent mapping between these two spaces is empirically designed and confines that each manipulation model can only handle one fixed text prompt. In this paper, we propose a method named Free-Form CLIP (FFCLIP), aiming to establish an automatic latent mapping so that one manipulation model handles free-form text prompts. Our FFCLIP has a cross-modality semantic modulation module containing semantic alignment and injection. The semantic alignment performs the automatic latent mapping via linear transformations with a cross attention mechanism. After alignment, we inject semantics from text prompt embeddings to the StyleGAN latent space. For one type of image (e.g., `human portrait'), one FFCLIP model can be learned to handle free-form text prompts. Meanwhile, we observe that although each training text prompt only contains a single semantic meaning, FFCLIP can leverage text prompts with multiple semantic meanings for image manipulation. In the experiments, we evaluate FFCLIP on three types of images (i.e., `human portraits', `cars', and `churches'). Both visual and numerical results show that FFCLIP effectively produces semantically accurate and visually realistic images. Project page: https://github.com/KumapowerLIU/FFCLIP.

paragraphs: Text-guided image editing requires connecting the meaning of a prompt to changes in an image representation. Earlier approaches linking CLIP text embeddings with StyleGAN's visual latent space use mappings that restrict each manipulation model to a fixed prompt. FFCLIP aims to learn that connection automatically so one model can respond to free-form text for a given image category.

Its semantic modulation module first aligns the text and visual spaces using linear transformations and cross-attention. It then injects information from the text embedding into StyleGAN's latent space. This separates the process of establishing a correspondence between modalities from applying the prompt's meaning to the image representation.

The authors evaluate the method on portraits, cars, and churches, reporting semantically accurate and visually realistic edits through visual and numerical results. They also observe edits from prompts combining multiple meanings, although individual training prompts contain only one meaning. The scope remains one learned model per image type, with flexibility across prompts within that type.
summary.tldr: FFCLIP learns to align text and StyleGAN representations so one model per image type can perform edits from free-form prompts.

title: One Model to Edit Them All: Free-Form Text-Driven Image Manipulation with Semantic Modulations

abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning algorithms provide a data-driven way to acquire policies that quickly adapt to many tasks with varying rewards or dynamics functions. However, learned meta-policies are often effective only on the exact task distribution on which they were trained and struggle in the presence of distribution shift of test-time rewards or transition dynamics. In this work, we develop a framework for meta-RL algorithms that are able to behave appropriately under test-time distribution shifts in the space of tasks. Our framework centers on an adaptive approach to distributional robustness that trains a population of meta-policies to be robust to varying levels of distribution shift. When evaluated on a potentially shifted test-time distribution of tasks, this allows us to choose the meta-policy with the most appropriate level of robustness, and use it to perform fast adaptation. We formally show how our framework allows for improved regret under distribution shift, and empirically show its efficacy on simulated robotics problems under a wide range of distribution shifts.

In this work, we develop a framework for meta-RL algorithms that are able to behave appropriately under test-time distribution shifts in the space of tasks. Our framework centers on an adaptive approach to distributional robustness that trains a population of meta-policies to be robust to varying levels of distribution shift. When evaluated on a potentially shifted test-time distribution of tasks, this allows us to choose the meta-policy with the most appropriate level of robustness, and use it to perform fast adaptation. We formally show how our framework allows for improved regret under distribution shift, and empirically show its efficacy on simulated robotics problems under a wide range of distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning trains policies that can quickly adapt to tasks with different rewards or dynamics. That adaptability can remain tied to the particular task distribution used during training. This paper addresses what happens when test tasks come from a shifted distribution, so fast adaptation alone may no longer provide appropriate behavior.

The framework trains a population of meta-policies with different levels of distributional robustness. When presented with a potentially shifted distribution at test time, it selects the policy whose robustness level is most appropriate and uses that policy for fast adaptation. The population therefore provides multiple responses to the possible severity of task distribution shift.

The authors formally show how the framework allows improved regret under distribution shift and demonstrate its effectiveness on simulated robotics problems across a wide range of shifts. The contribution connects robustness selection with meta-learning: preparing policies for different shift levels gives the system a way to adjust its adaptation strategy to the test distribution.
summary.tldr: A population of differently robust meta-policies enables adaptation to shifted task distributions with formal and simulated support.

title: Distributionally Adaptive Meta Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent action recognition models have achieved impressive results by integrating objects, their locations and interactions. However, obtaining dense structured annotations for each frame is tedious and time-consuming, making these methods expensive to train and less scalable. At the same time, if a small set of annotated images is available, either within or outside the domain of interest, how could we leverage these for a video downstream task? We propose a learning framework StructureViT (SViT for short), which demonstrates how utilizing the structure of a small number of images only available during training can improve a video model. SViT relies on two key insights. First, as both images and videos contain structured information, we enrich a transformer model with a set of object tokens that can be used across images and videos. Second, the scene representations of individual frames in video should ``align'' with those of still images. This is achieved via a Frame-Clip Consistency loss, which ensures the flow of structured information between images and videos. We explore a particular instantiation of scene structure, namely a Hand-Object Graph, consisting of hands and objects with their locations as nodes, and physical relations of contact/no-contact as edges. SViT shows strong performance improvements on multiple video understanding tasks and datasets, including the first place in the Ego4D CVPR'22 Point of No Return Temporal Localization Challenge. For code and pretrained models, visit the project page at https://eladb3.github.io/SViT/.

title: Bringing Image Scene Structure to Video via Frame-Clip Consistency of Object Tokens

abstract: Bayesian optimization over the latent spaces of deep autoencoder models (DAEs) has recently emerged as a promising new approach for optimizing challenging black-box functions over structured, discrete, hard-to-enumerate search spaces (e.g., molecules). Here the DAE dramatically simplifies the search space by mapping inputs into a continuous latent space where familiar Bayesian optimization tools can be more readily applied. Despite this simplification, the latent space typically remains high-dimensional. Thus, even with a well-suited latent space, these approaches do not necessarily provide a complete solution, but may rather shift the structured optimization problem to a high-dimensional one. In this paper, we propose LOL-BO, which adapts the notion of trust regions explored in recent work on high-dimensional Bayesian optimization to the structured setting. By reformulating the encoder to function as both an encoder for the DAE globally and as a deep kernel for the surrogate model within a trust region, we better align the notion of local optimization in the latent space with local optimization in the input space. LOL-BO achieves as much as 20 times improvement over state-of-the-art latent space Bayesian optimization methods across six real-world benchmarks, demonstrating that improvement in optimization strategies is as important as developing better DAE models.

That maximum describes the reported results rather than a uniform gain on every benchmark. The broader finding is that search strategy deserves attention alongside representation quality: a useful latent space still needs an optimization method suited to its geometry and dimensionality.
summary.tldr: LOL-BO improves structured-object optimization by aligning local latent-space search with local changes in the original inputs.

title: Local Latent Space Bayesian Optimization over Structured Inputs

abstract: Vision transformers have recently achieved competitive results across various vision tasks but still suffer from heavy computation costs when processing a large number of tokens. Many advanced approaches have been developed to reduce the total number of tokens in the large-scale vision transformers, especially for image classification tasks. Typically, they select a small group of essential tokens according to their relevance with the [\texttt{class}] token, then fine-tune the weights of the vision transformer. Such fine-tuning is less practical for dense prediction due to the much heavier computation and GPU memory cost than image classification.In this paper, we focus on a more challenging problem, \ie, accelerating large-scale vision transformers for dense prediction without any additional re-training or fine-tuning. In response to the fact that high-resolution representations are necessary for dense prediction, we present two non-parametric operators, a \emph{token clustering layer} to decrease the number of tokens and a \emph{token reconstruction layer} to increase the number of tokens. The following steps are performed to achieve this: (i) we use the token clustering layer to cluster the neighboring tokens together, resulting in low-resolution representations that maintain the spatial structures; (ii) we apply the following transformer layers only to these low-resolution representations or clustered tokens; and (iii) we use the token reconstruction layer to re-create the high-resolution representations from the refined low-resolution representations. The results obtained by our method are promising on five dense prediction tasks including object detection, semantic segmentation, panoptic segmentation, instance segmentation, and depth estimation. Accordingly, our method accelerates $40\%\uparrow$ FPS and saves $30\%\downarrow$ GFLOPs of ``Segmenter+ViT-L/$16$'' while maintaining $99.5\%$ of the performance on ADE$20$K without fine-tuning the official weights.

paragraphs: Vision transformers become expensive when they process many image tokens. Reducing token counts is useful, but dense prediction tasks still need detailed spatial representations. This paper addresses the additional practical difficulty of accelerating an existing large model without retraining or fine-tuning, which can be particularly costly for dense prediction.

The method introduces two operators with no learned parameters. A clustering layer groups neighboring tokens into a lower-resolution representation while preserving spatial structure. Subsequent transformer layers process these grouped tokens, reducing computation. A reconstruction layer then expands the refined representation back to high resolution so that it can support detailed predictions.

This illustrates that temporarily reducing spatial resolution inside the model can offer a useful efficiency tradeoff without additional training.
summary.tldr: Clustering and reconstructing image tokens accelerates dense-prediction transformers without fine-tuning while preserving nearly all performance in a reported example.

title: Expediting Large-Scale Vision Transformer for Dense Prediction without Fine-tuning

abstract: Diffusion models are powerful generative models but suffer from slow sampling, often taking 1000 sequential denoising steps for one sample. As a result, considerable efforts have been directed toward reducing the number of denoising steps, but these methods hurt sample quality. Instead of reducing the number of denoising steps (trading quality for speed), in this paper we explore an orthogonal approach: can we run the denoising steps in parallel (trading compute for speed)? In spite of the sequential nature of the denoising steps, we show that surprisingly it is possible to parallelize sampling via Picard iterations, by guessing the solution of future denoising steps and iteratively refining until convergence. With this insight, we present ParaDiGMS, a novel method to accelerate the sampling of pretrained diffusion models by denoising multiple steps in parallel. ParaDiGMS is the first diffusion sampling method that enables trading compute for speed and is even compatible with existing fast sampling techniques such as DDIM and DPMSolver. Using ParaDiGMS, we improve sampling speed by 2-4x across a range of robotics and image generation models, giving state-of-the-art sampling speeds of 0.2s on 100-step DiffusionPolicy and 14.6s on 1000-step StableDiffusion-v2 with no measurable degradation of task reward, FID score, or CLIP score.

This paper explores accelerating those steps through parallel computation. Its central tradeoff is spending more compute to reduce elapsed time while retaining the denoising sequence, instead of relying solely on shortening that sequence.

It guesses the results of future denoising steps, processes multiple steps in parallel, and repeatedly refines the guesses until convergence. They observe no measurable degradation in task reward, FID, or CLIP score in these evaluations. The results demonstrate a practical compute-for-speed option while preserving the measured quality of the tested models.
summary.tldr: ParaDiGMS parallelizes diffusion sampling through iterative refinement, reporting two-to-fourfold speedups without measurable degradation on the evaluated metrics.

title: Parallel Sampling of Diffusion Models

abstract: Successful graph generation depends on the accurate estimation of the joint distribution of graph components such as nodes and edges from training data. While recent deep neural networks have demonstrated sampling of realistic graphs together with diffusion models, however, they still suffer from oversmoothing problems which are inherited from conventional graph convolution and thus high-frequency characteristics of nodes and edges become intractable. To overcome such issues and generate graphs with high fidelity, this paper introduces a novel approach that captures the dependency between nodes and edges at multiple resolutions in the spectral space. By modeling the joint distribution of node and edge signals in a shared graph wavelet space, together with a score-based diffusion model, we propose a Wavelet Graph Diffusion Model (Wave-GD) which lets us sample synthetic graphs with real-like frequency characteristics of nodes and edges. Experimental results on four representative benchmark datasets validate the superiority of the Wave-GD over existing approaches, highlighting its potential for a wide range of applications that involve graph data.

paragraphs: Generating realistic graphs requires capturing how nodes and edges depend on one another. The paper identifies oversmoothing as a problem in existing neural graph generators: graph convolution can blur distinctions and make high-frequency node and edge characteristics difficult to preserve. Realism therefore depends on more than representing broad graph structure.

Wave-GD models node and edge signals together in a shared graph wavelet space. Wavelets provide multiple resolutions for describing variation, letting the model capture dependencies at different scales. A score-based diffusion model operates with this representation to generate synthetic graphs whose node and edge frequency characteristics resemble those of real graphs.

Experiments on four representative benchmark datasets report better performance than existing approaches. These results support the value of jointly modeling nodes and edges while preserving information across resolutions. The contribution is specifically aimed at the loss of fine variation through oversmoothing, and the reported findings suggest that spectral structure is useful for improving graph generation fidelity across the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Wave-GD combines graph wavelets and diffusion to preserve node–edge dependencies and frequency characteristics across multiple resolutions.

title: Multi-resolution Spectral Coherence for Graph Generation with Score-based Diffusion

abstract: While deep learning techniques have become extremely popular for solving a broad range of optimization problems, methods to enforce hard constraints during optimization, particularly on deep neural networks, remain underdeveloped. Inspired by the rich literature on meshless interpolation and its extension to spectral collocation methods in scientific computing, we develop a series of approaches for enforcing hard constraints on neural fields, which we refer to as Constrained Neural Fields (CNF). The constraints can be specified as a linear operator applied to the neural field and its derivatives. We also design specific model representations and training strategies for problems where standard models may encounter difficulties, such as conditioning of the system, memory consumption, and capacity of the network when being constrained. Our approaches are demonstrated in a wide range of real-world applications. Additionally, we develop a framework that enables highly efficient model and constraint specification, which can be readily applied to any downstream task where hard constraints need to be explicitly satisfied during optimization.

This paper develops Constrained Neural Fields, or CNF, to enforce such hard constraints. Its focus is on conditions expressed through linear operators acting on the field and its derivatives, including constraints of arbitrary differential order.

The approaches draw inspiration from meshless interpolation and spectral collocation methods in scientific computing. The authors also design model representations and training strategies for difficulties that arise when networks are constrained. These include numerical conditioning, memory use, and the network’s remaining capacity to represent the desired field while meeting the imposed conditions.

Demonstrations cover a range of real-world applications, and an accompanying framework makes models and constraints efficient to specify. The contribution brings exact constraint satisfaction into the design of neural-field optimization, together with practical strategies for making it workable. Its stated constraint language is central: the conditions are represented as linear operators on the field and its derivatives, providing a concrete mathematical form for the requirements being enforced.
summary.tldr: Constrained Neural Fields enforce hard linear-operator constraints on neural fields and their derivatives while addressing practical training difficulties.

title: Neural Fields with Hard Constraints of Arbitrary Differential Order

abstract: High-definition (HD) vectorized map is essential for autonomous driving, providing detailed and precise environmental information for advanced perception and planning. However, current map vectorization methods often exhibit deviations, and the existing evaluation metric for map vectorization lacks sufficient sensitivity to detect these deviations. To address these limitations, we propose integrating the philosophy of rasterization into map vectorization. Specifically, we introduce a new rasterization-based evaluation metric, which has superior sensitivity and is better suited to real-world autonomous driving scenarios. Furthermore, we propose MapVR (Map Vectorization via Rasterization), a novel framework that applies differentiable rasterization to vectorized outputs and then performs precise and geometry-aware supervision on rasterized HD maps. Notably, MapVR designs tailored rasterization strategies for various geometric shapes, enabling effective adaptation to a wide range of map elements. Experiments show that incorporating rasterization into map vectorization greatly enhances performance with no extra computational cost during inference, leading to more accurate map perception and ultimately promoting safer autonomous driving. Codes are available at https://github.com/ZhangGongjie/MapVR. A standalone map vectorization evaluation toolkit is available at https://github.com/jiahaoLjh/MapVectorizationEvalToolkit.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving uses detailed vector maps to support perception and planning. The paper identifies two related problems: predicted map geometry can deviate from the intended shapes, and the existing evaluation metric may not detect those deviations sensitively enough. It introduces rasterization into both evaluation and model training to address these issues.

The new evaluation metric measures maps through a rasterized representation and is reported to be more sensitive to geometric deviations. The training framework, MapVR, also converts predicted vectors into rasterized maps, using a differentiable operation so that supervision can guide the vector-producing model. Different geometric shapes receive tailored rasterization strategies.

This lets training assess the geometry expressed by the output map in a form suited to precise supervision. Experiments show substantial performance improvements without additional computation at inference time. The stated practical benefit is more accurate map perception, which can support safer driving. The results establish improvements in map vectorization; the safety motivation explains why detecting and correcting geometric deviations matters for the broader application.
summary.tldr: MapVR uses differentiable rasterization to improve vector-map geometry, alongside a more sensitive evaluation metric, without extra inference computation.

title: Online Map Vectorization for Autonomous Driving: A Rasterization Perspective

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the impact of numerical instability on the reliability of sampling, density evaluation, and evidence lower bound (ELBO) estimation in variational flows. We first empirically demonstrate that common flows can exhibit a catastrophic accumulation of error: the numerical flow map deviates significantly from the exact map---which affects sampling---and the numerical inverse flow map does not accurately recover the initial input---which affects density and ELBO computations. Surprisingly though, we find that results produced by flows are often accurate enough for applications despite the presence of serious numerical instability. In this work, we treat variational flows as chaotic dynamical systems, and leverage shadowing theory to elucidate this behavior via theoretical guarantees on the error of sampling, density evaluation, and ELBO estimation. Finally, we develop and empirically test a diagnostic procedure that can be used to validate results produced by numerically unstable flows in practice.

paragraphs: Variational flows depend on numerical transformations for sampling, evaluating densities, and estimating the evidence lower bound, or ELBO. This paper shows empirically that errors in common flows can accumulate catastrophically. The computed forward transformation can depart substantially from the exact transformation, and the computed inverse may fail to recover its starting input.

Those failures threaten different parts of the calculation: forward errors affect samples, while inverse errors affect density and ELBO computations. Yet the authors observe that outputs can remain accurate enough for applications despite serious instability. They investigate this apparent tension by treating variational flows as chaotic dynamical systems and applying shadowing theory.

The analysis provides theoretical guarantees on errors in sampling, density evaluation, and ELBO estimation. The authors also develop and empirically test a diagnostic procedure for validating results from unstable flows. The contribution is a way to assess the consequences of numerical instability, rather than treating instability alone as proof that every resulting quantity is unusable.
summary.tldr: Shadowing theory helps explain why numerically unstable variational flows can remain useful and supports a practical diagnostic for their outputs.

title: Embracing the chaos: analysis and diagnosis of numerical instability in variational flows

abstract: In recent years, AI-assisted drug design methods have been proposed to generate molecules given the pockets' structures of target proteins. Most of them are {\em atom-level-based} methods, which consider atoms as basic components and generate atom positions and types. In this way, however, it is hard to generate realistic fragments with complicated structures. To solve this, we propose \textsc{D3FG}, a {\em functional-group-based} diffusion model for pocket-specific molecule generation and elaboration. \textsc{D3FG} decomposes molecules into two categories of components: functional groups defined as rigid bodies and linkers as mass points. And the two kinds of components can together form complicated fragments that enhance ligand-protein interactions. To be specific, in the diffusion process, \textsc{D3FG} diffuses the data distribution of the positions, orientations, and types of the components into a prior distribution; In the generative process, the noise is gradually removed from the three variables by denoisers parameterized with designed equivariant graph neural networks. In the experiments, our method can generate molecules with more realistic 3D structures, competitive affinities toward the protein targets, and better drug properties. Besides, \textsc{D3FG} as a solution to a new task of molecule elaboration, could generate molecules with high affinities based on existing ligands and the hotspots of target proteins.

paragraphs: Generating molecules for a protein pocket requires producing realistic three-dimensional structures. Approaches that generate individual atom types and positions can struggle with complicated molecular fragments. D3FG changes the basic representation by treating functional groups as rigid bodies and linkers as point-like components, allowing these pieces to form more complex fragments.

The diffusion model adds noise to component positions, orientations, and types. During generation, denoisers built from equivariant graph neural networks gradually remove that noise from all three variables. This representation lets the model work with the placement and orientation of structured groups while also generating the components that connect them.

Experiments report more realistic 3D molecular structures, competitive affinity toward protein targets, and improved drug properties. The authors also introduce a molecule-elaboration task in which generation builds on existing ligands and protein hotspots. D3FG can generate high-affinity molecules in that setting, extending its use from creating pocket-specific candidates to elaborating candidates from existing molecular and target information.
summary.tldr: D3FG generates and elaborates pocket-specific molecules by diffusing functional-group positions, orientations, and types rather than treating every atom independently.

title: Functional-Group-Based Diffusion for Pocket-Specific Molecule Generation and Elaboration

abstract: The distillation of ranking models has become an important topic in both academia and industry. In recent years, several advanced methods have been proposed to tackle this problem, often leveraging ranking information from teacher rankers that is absent in traditional classification settings. To date, there is no well-established consensus on how to evaluate this class of models. Moreover, inconsistent benchmarking on a wide range of tasks and datasets make it difficult to assess or invigorate advances in this field. This paper first examines representative prior arts on ranking distillation, and raises three questions to be answered around methodology and reproducibility. To that end, we propose a systematic and unified benchmark, Ranking Distillation Suite (RD-Suite), which is a suite of tasks with 4 large real-world datasets, encompassing two major modalities (textual and numeric) and two applications (standard distillation and distillation transfer). RD-Suite consists of benchmark results that challenge some of the common wisdom in the field, and the release of datasets with teacher scores and evaluation scripts for future research. RD-Suite paves the way towards better understanding of ranking distillation, facilities more research in this direction, and presents new challenges.
originalAbstract: The distillation of ranking models has become an important topic in both academia and industry. In recent years, several advanced methods have been proposed to tackle this problem, often leveraging ranking information from teacher rankers that is absent in traditional classification settings. To date, there is no well-established consensus on how to evaluate this class of models. Moreover, inconsistent benchmarking on a wide range of tasks and datasets make it difficult to assess or invigorate advances in this field. This paper first examines representative prior arts on ranking distillation, and raises three questions to be answered around methodology and reproducibility. To that end, we propose a systematic and unified benchmark, Ranking Distillation Suite (RD-Suite), which is a suite of tasks with 4 large real-world datasets, encompassing two major modalities (textual and numeric) and two applications (standard distillation and distillation transfer). RD-Suite consists of benchmark results that challenge some of the common wisdom in the field, and the release of datasets with teacher scores and evaluation scripts for future research. RD-Suite paves the way towards better understanding of ranking distillation, facilities more research in this direction, and presents new challenges.

paragraphs: Ranking distillation transfers knowledge from teacher ranking models to other models. Unlike ordinary classification, this can use information about the ordering of items. Although many methods have been proposed, inconsistent tasks, datasets, and evaluation practices make it difficult to determine which advances hold up under comparable conditions.

RD-Suite provides a systematic benchmark for this problem. The authors first examine representative prior methods and raise three questions about methodology and reproducibility. Their benchmark then brings together four large real-world datasets, covering textual and numeric inputs as well as standard distillation and distillation transfer.

The suite includes benchmark results, datasets with teacher scores, and evaluation scripts. Its findings challenge some common assumptions in ranking distillation, making the evaluation framework itself a contribution to understanding the field. Providing shared teacher outputs and evaluation procedures gives future studies a more consistent basis for comparison, helping distinguish methodological improvements from differences in how experiments are set up.
summary.tldr: RD-Suite standardizes ranking-distillation evaluation across four real-world datasets, with teacher scores, evaluation scripts, and results that challenge existing assumptions.

title: RD-Suite: A Benchmark for Ranking Distillation

abstract: Recent studies on Graph Neural Networks(GNNs) provide both empirical and theoretical evidence supporting their effectiveness in capturing structural patterns on both homophilic and certain heterophilic graphs. Notably, most real-world homophilic and heterophilic graphs are comprised of a mixture of nodes in both homophilic and heterophilic structural patterns, exhibiting a structural disparity. However, the analysis of GNN performance with respect to nodes exhibiting different structural patterns, e.g., homophilic nodes in heterophilic graphs, remains rather limited. In the present study, we provide evidence that Graph Neural Networks(GNNs) on node classification typically perform admirably on homophilic nodes within homophilic graphs and heterophilic nodes within heterophilic graphs while struggling on the opposite node set, exhibiting a performance disparity. We theoretically and empirically identify effects of GNNs on testing nodes exhibiting distinct structural patterns. We then propose a rigorous, non-i.i.d PAC-Bayesian generalization bound for GNNs, revealing reasons for the performance disparity, namely the aggregated feature distance and homophily ratio difference between training and testing nodes. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical implications of our new findings via (1) elucidating the effectiveness of deeper GNNs; and (2) revealing an over-looked distribution shift factor on graph out-of-distribution problem and proposing a new scenario accordingly.

paragraphs: A graph can contain nodes whose neighbors are mostly similar to them and nodes whose neighbors are mostly different. These are homophilic and heterophilic local patterns, respectively. The paper argues that treating an entire graph as one type can obscure important differences in how well a graph neural network classifies individual nodes.

The authors find that GNNs typically perform well on homophilic nodes in homophilic graphs and heterophilic nodes in heterophilic graphs, while struggling with nodes showing the opposite local pattern. They investigate this disparity both theoretically and empirically, shifting attention from graph-wide performance to the relationship between local structure and prediction quality.

Their analysis develops a PAC-Bayesian generalization bound that accommodates non-independent, non-identically distributed data. It identifies aggregated feature distance and differences in homophily ratios between training and testing nodes as explanations for the disparity. The authors use these findings to explain the effectiveness of deeper GNNs and identify an overlooked source of distribution shift, motivating a new graph out-of-distribution scenario.
summary.tldr: GNN performance varies with local node structure, and a new generalization analysis links this disparity to training–testing differences.

title: Demystifying Structural Disparity in Graph Neural Networks: Can One Size Fit All?

abstract: A common assumption in causal inference from observational data is that there is no hidden confounding. Yet it is, in general, impossible to verify the presence of hidden confounding factors from a single dataset. Under the assumption of independent causal mechanisms underlying the data-generating process, we demonstrate a way to detect unobserved confounders when having multiple observational datasets coming from different environments. We present a theory for testable conditional independencies that are only absent when there is hidden confounding and examine cases where we violate its assumptions: degenerate & dependent mechanisms, and faithfulness violations. Additionally, we propose a procedure to test these independencies and study its empirical finite-sample behavior using simulation studies and semi-synthetic data based on a real-world dataset. In most cases, the proposed procedure correctly predicts the presence of hidden confounding, particularly when the confounding bias is large.

paragraphs: Causal analyses of observational data often assume that no unmeasured factor influences the variables in a way that confounds their relationship. A single dataset generally cannot establish whether such hidden confounding is present. This paper investigates what becomes detectable when researchers have observational datasets from several different environments.

The approach assumes independent causal mechanisms in the process generating the data. Under its assumptions, the theory identifies conditional independence relationships whose absence can signal hidden confounding. The authors develop a procedure for testing these relationships and examine what happens when assumptions fail, including dependent or degenerate mechanisms and violations of faithfulness.

The proposed test is evaluated with simulations and semi-synthetic data derived from a real dataset. In most evaluated cases, it correctly identifies the presence of hidden confounding, particularly when confounding produces a large bias. The contribution is an assumption-dependent route to detecting an otherwise elusive problem, using information across environments and examining how the procedure behaves with finite samples.
summary.tldr: Multiple observational environments can reveal hidden confounding through conditional independence tests under independent causal mechanism assumptions.

title: Detecting hidden confounding in observational data using multiple environments

abstract: Linear scalarization, i.e., combining all loss functions by a weighted sum, has been the default choice in the literature of multi-task learning (MTL) since its inception. In recent years, there is a surge of interest in developing Specialized Multi-Task Optimizers (SMTOs) that treat MTL as a multi-objective optimization problem. However, it remains open whether there is a fundamental advantage of SMTOs over scalarization. In fact, heated debates exist in the community comparing these two types of algorithms, mostly from an empirical perspective. To approach the above question, in this paper, we revisit scalarization from a theoretical perspective. We focus on linear MTL models and study whether scalarization is capable of fully exploring the Pareto front. Our findings reveal that, in contrast to recent works that claimed empirical advantages of scalarization, scalarization is inherently incapable of full exploration, especially for those Pareto optimal solutions that strike the balanced trade-offs between multiple tasks. More concretely, when the model is under-parametrized, we reveal a multi-surface structure of the feasible region and identify necessary and sufficient conditions for full exploration. This leads to the conclusion that scalarization is in general incapable of tracing out the Pareto front. Our theoretical results partially answer the open questions in Xin et al. (2021), and provide a more intuitive explanation on why scalarization fails beyond non-convexity. We additionally perform experiments on a real-world dataset using both scalarization and state-of-the-art SMTOs. The experimental results not only corroborate our theoretical findings, but also unveil the potential of SMTOs in finding balanced solutions, which cannot be achieved by scalarization.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning often combines task losses into a weighted sum, a procedure called linear scalarization. Changing those weights is a natural way to seek different compromises between tasks. This paper asks whether that procedure can reach every Pareto-optimal compromise, where improving one task would require worsening another.

The analysis focuses on linear multi-task models. In the under-parameterized setting, the authors identify a feasible region with multiple surfaces and establish necessary and sufficient conditions for full exploration of the Pareto front. Their results show that scalarization generally cannot reach the entire front, particularly balanced trade-offs among tasks.

Experiments on a real-world dataset compare scalarization with specialized multi-task optimizers. They corroborate the theoretical findings and show the potential of those optimizers to find balanced solutions inaccessible to scalarization. The contribution gives a geometric explanation for the shortfall beyond a general appeal to nonconvexity, while grounding its theoretical conclusions in the linear-model setting studied.
summary.tldr: For the studied linear multi-task models, weighted loss sums generally miss parts of the Pareto front, including balanced trade-offs.

title: Revisiting Scalarization in Multi-Task Learning: A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Learning causal structures from interventional data is a fundamental problem with broad applications across various fields. While many previous works have focused on recovering the entire causal graph, in practice, there are scenarios where learning only part of the causal graph suffices. This is called \emph{targeted} causal discovery. In our work, we focus on two such well-motivated problems: subset search and causal matching. We aim to minimize the number of interventions in both cases.Towards this, we introduce the \emph{Meek separator}, which is a subset of vertices that, when intervened, decomposes the remaining unoriented edges into smaller connected components. We then present an efficient algorithm to find Meek separators that are of small sizes. Such a procedure is helpful in designing various divide-and-conquer-based approaches. In particular, we propose two randomized algorithms that achieve logarithmic approximation for subset search and causal matching, respectively. Our results provide the first known average-case provable guarantees for both problems. We believe that this opens up possibilities to design near-optimal methods for many other targeted causal structure learning problems arising from various applications.

paragraphs: Recovering an entire causal graph can require more interventions than a particular question needs. Targeted causal discovery instead seeks only the relevant part of the structure. This paper studies two such problems, subset search and causal matching, with the goal of reducing how many interventions they require.

Its main tool is a Meek separator: a set of vertices whose intervention splits the remaining edges with unresolved directions into smaller connected components. The authors give an efficient algorithm for finding small separators. This decomposition supports divide-and-conquer strategies by breaking unresolved structure into pieces that can be handled separately.

summary.tldr: Meek separators divide unresolved causal structure into smaller pieces, enabling randomized approximation algorithms for two targeted discovery problems.

title: Meek Separators and Their Applications in Targeted Causal Discovery

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) alleviates the problem of designing a task-specific reward function in reinforcement learning by learning it from human preference. However, existing RLHF models are considered inefficient as they produce only a single preference data from each human feedback. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel RLHF framework called SeqRank, that uses sequential preference ranking to enhance the feedback efficiency. Our method samples trajectories in a sequential manner by iteratively selecting a defender from the set of previously chosen trajectories $\mathcal{K}$ and a challenger from the set of unchosen trajectories $\mathcal{U}\setminus\mathcal{K}$, where $\mathcal{U}$ is the replay buffer. We propose two trajectory comparison methods with different defender sampling strategies: (1) sequential pairwise comparison that selects the most recent trajectory and (2) root pairwise comparison that selects the most preferred trajectory from $\mathcal{K}$. We construct a data structure and rank trajectories by preference to augment additional queries. The proposed method results in at least 39.2% higher average feedback efficiency than the baseline and also achieves a balance between feedback efficiency and data dependency. We examine the convergence of the empirical risk and the generalization bound of the reward model with Rademacher complexity. While both trajectory comparison methods outperform conventional pairwise comparison, root pairwise comparison improves the average reward in locomotion tasks and the average success rate in manipulation tasks by 29.0% and 25.0%, respectively. The source code and the videos are provided in the supplementary material.
