paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback learns a reward signal from people's preferences, reducing the need to hand-design rewards. SeqRank seeks to make that feedback more productive by organizing comparisons into a sequential ranking of trajectories. This structure allows additional preference queries to be derived from the collected ranking information.

Each comparison pairs a defender from previously selected trajectories with a challenger from the remaining replay buffer. One strategy chooses the most recently selected trajectory as defender; another chooses the most preferred trajectory so far. The paper also examines reward-model empirical risk convergence and generalization using Rademacher complexity, addressing the dependence created by reusing comparison information.

The reported average feedback efficiency is at least 39.2% higher than the baseline. Both strategies outperform conventional pairwise comparison, while the preferred-defender strategy improves average locomotion reward and manipulation success rate by 29.0% and 25.0%, respectively. The results support structured reuse of human comparisons while accounting for the relationship between feedback efficiency and data dependency.
summary.tldr: SeqRank organizes sequential trajectory comparisons into preference rankings to extract more learning value from human feedback.

title: Sequential Preference Ranking for Efficient Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

abstract: We consider the problem of mixed linear regression (MLR), where each observed sample belongs to one of $K$ unknown linear models. In practical applications, the mixture of the $K$ models may be imbalanced with a significantly different number of samples from each model. Unfortunately, most MLR methods do not perform well in such settings. Motivated by this practical challenge, in this work we propose Mix-IRLS, a novel, simple and fast algorithm for MLR with excellent performance on both balanced and imbalanced mixtures.In contrast to popular approaches that recover the $K$ models simultaneously, Mix-IRLS does it sequentially using tools from robust regression. Empirically, beyond imbalanced mixtures, Mix-IRLS succeeds in a broad range of additional settings where other methods fail, including small sample sizes, presence of outliers, and an unknown number of models $K$. Furthermore, Mix-IRLS outperforms competing methods on several real-world datasets, in some cases by a large margin. We complement our empirical results by deriving a recovery guarantee for Mix-IRLS, which highlights its advantage on imbalanced mixtures.

paragraphs: Mixed linear regression assumes that each observation comes from one of several unknown linear models. The difficulty increases when some models contribute many more observations than others. This paper introduces Mix-IRLS to address that imbalance, while also aiming to perform well when the groups have similar sizes.

Mix-IRLS recovers the component models sequentially using robust regression tools. This changes the organization of the problem from estimating all models simultaneously to recovering them one after another. The authors describe the resulting algorithm as simple and fast, and derive a recovery guarantee that highlights its advantage for imbalanced mixtures.

The empirical evaluation finds strong performance across balanced and imbalanced mixtures. It also reports success in settings with few samples, outliers, or an unknown number of component models, where competing approaches fail in the evaluated cases. On several real-world datasets, Mix-IRLS outperforms competing methods, sometimes by a large margin. The combination of empirical results and a recovery guarantee supports sequential robust regression as a useful approach to mixture estimation.
summary.tldr: Mix-IRLS sequentially recovers linear models using robust regression, with strong empirical performance and a recovery guarantee highlighting imbalanced mixtures.

title: Imbalanced Mixed Linear Regression

abstract: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) has enabled novel view synthesis with high fidelity given images and camera poses. Subsequent works even succeeded in eliminating the necessity of pose priors by jointly optimizing NeRF and camera pose. However, these works are limited to relatively simple settings such as photometrically consistent and occluder-free image collections or a sequence of images from a video. So they have difficulty handling unconstrained images with varying illumination and transient occluders. In this paper, we propose **UP-NeRF** (**U**nconstrained **P**ose-prior-free **Ne**ural **R**adiance **F**ields) to optimize NeRF with unconstrained image collections without camera pose prior. We tackle these challenges with surrogate tasks that optimize color-insensitive feature fields and a separate module for transient occluders to block their influence on pose estimation. In addition, we introduce a candidate head to enable more robust pose estimation and transient-aware depth supervision to minimize the effect of incorrect prior. Our experiments verify the superior performance of our method compared to the baselines including BARF and its variants in a challenging internet photo collection, *Phototourism dataset*. The code of UP-NeRF is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/UP-NeRF.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields usually need images and camera poses to reconstruct scenes and generate new views. Methods that estimate poses jointly with the scene have often relied on simpler image collections. UP-NeRF targets collections with changing illumination and temporary occluders, while removing the need for prior camera poses.

The method uses surrogate tasks that optimize feature fields insensitive to color, reducing the dependence of pose estimation on consistent image appearance. A separate module handles transient occluders so they do not distort pose estimates. A candidate head further supports robust pose estimation, while transient-aware depth supervision reduces the effect of incorrect prior information.

Experiments on the Phototourism internet photo collection show superior performance relative to the reported baselines, including BARF and its variants. The contribution brings several sources of uncertainty into the joint reconstruction process. By treating appearance variation, transient content, and unreliable depth information explicitly, UP-NeRF makes pose-free radiance-field optimization more effective in the challenging image-collection setting studied.
summary.tldr: UP-NeRF jointly estimates camera poses and scene representations from photo collections with varying illumination and transient occluders.

title: UP-NeRF: Unconstrained Pose Prior-Free Neural Radiance Field

abstract: Generative protein language models are a natural way to design new proteins with desired functions. However, current models are either difficult to direct to produce a protein from a specific family of interest, or must be trained on a large multiple sequence alignment (MSA) from the specific family of interest, making them unable to benefit from transfer learning across families. To address this, we propose **P**r**o**tein **E**volutionary **T**ransformer (PoET), an autoregressive generative model of whole protein families that learns to generate sets of related proteins as sequences-of-sequences across tens of millions of natural protein sequence clusters. PoET can be used as a retrieval-augmented language model to generate and score arbitrary modifications conditioned on any protein family of interest, and can extrapolate from short context lengths to generalize well even for small families. This is enabled by a unique Transformer layer; we model tokens sequentially within sequences while attending between sequences order invariantly, allowing PoET to scale to context lengths beyond those used during training. In extensive experiments on deep mutational scanning datasets, we show that PoET outperforms existing protein language models and evolutionary sequence models for variant function prediction across proteins of all MSA depths. We also demonstrate PoET's ability to controllably generate new protein sequences.

paragraphs: Protein generation benefits from learning across many families while remaining steerable toward a particular family. Existing approaches can struggle with that steering or require training on a large alignment from the target family. PoET addresses this tension by learning a generative model of entire protein families across tens of millions of natural sequence clusters.

It represents a family as a sequence of protein sequences. Within each protein, tokens are modeled sequentially; between proteins, attention is invariant to their order. This architecture allows the model to use contexts longer than those encountered during training. Retrieved family sequences can condition generation and scoring of modifications, including for small families.

On deep mutational scanning datasets, PoET outperforms the tested protein language models and evolutionary sequence models at predicting variant function across proteins with different alignment depths. The authors also demonstrate controlled generation of new protein sequences. The results support combining cross-family learning with family-specific context, allowing one model to use broad sequence experience while responding to the family supplied at use time.
summary.tldr: PoET learns across protein families while using retrieved family sequences to guide protein generation and variant-function prediction.

title: PoET: A generative model of protein families as sequences-of-sequences

abstract: As trained intelligent systems become increasingly pervasive, multiagent learning has emerged as a popular framework for studying complex interactions between autonomous agents. Yet, a formal understanding of how and when learners in heterogeneous environments benefit from sharing their respective experiences is far from complete. In this paper, we seek answers to these questions in the context of linear contextual bandits. We present a novel distributed learning algorithm based on the upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, which we refer to as H-LINUCB, wherein agents cooperatively minimize the group regret under the coordination of a central server. In the setting where the level of heterogeneity or dissimilarity across the environments is known to the agents, we show that H-LINUCB is provably optimal in regimes where the tasks are highly similar or highly dissimilar.

paragraphs: When several agents learn in different environments, sharing experience may help, but the usefulness of that experience depends on how similar their tasks are. This paper investigates that question for linear contextual bandits. The focus is on understanding when cooperative learning is beneficial despite differences among the environments in which agents make decisions.

The authors introduce H-LINUCB, a distributed algorithm based on the upper confidence bound approach. A central server coordinates the agents as they seek to minimize group regret, measuring the collective cost of learning through decisions. The formulation makes cooperation a group-level optimization problem while explicitly recognizing that agents need not face identical tasks.

The theoretical result assumes agents know the level of heterogeneity across environments. Under that assumption, H-LINUCB is provably optimal in regimes where tasks are highly similar or highly dissimilar. This characterizes performance at both ends of the similarity range; the stated result does not establish optimality for every intermediate level of heterogeneity or when heterogeneity is unknown.
summary.tldr: H-LINUCB coordinates heterogeneous bandit learners and is provably optimal for highly similar or highly dissimilar tasks when heterogeneity is known.

title: Multi-Agent Learning with Heterogeneous Linear Contextual Bandits

abstract: Human visual search ability enables efficient and accurate tracking of an arbitrary moving target, which is a significant research interest in cognitive neuroscience. The recently proposed Central-Peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory sheds light on how humans effectively process visual information and track moving targets in complex environments. However, existing visual object tracking algorithms still fall short of matching human performance in maintaining tracking over time, particularly in complex scenarios requiring robust visual search skills. These scenarios often involve Spatio-Temporal Discontinuities (i.e., STDChallenge), prevalent in long-term tracking and global instance tracking. To address this issue, we conduct research from a human-like modeling perspective: (1) Inspired by the CPD, we pro- pose a new tracker named CPDTrack to achieve human-like visual search ability. The central vision of CPDTrack leverages the spatio-temporal continuity of videos to introduce priors and enhance localization precision, while the peripheral vision improves global awareness and detects object movements. (2) To further evaluate and analyze STDChallenge, we create the STDChallenge Benchmark. Besides, by incorporating human subjects, we establish a human baseline, creating a high- quality environment specifically designed to assess trackers’ visual search abilities in videos across STDChallenge. (3) Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed CPDTrack not only achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in this challenge but also narrows the behavioral differences with humans. Additionally, CPDTrack exhibits strong generalizability across various challenging benchmarks. In summary, our research underscores the importance of human-like modeling and offers strategic insights for advancing intelligent visual target tracking. Code and models are available at https://github.com/ZhangDailing8/CPDTrack.
originalAbstract: Human visual search ability enables efficient and accurate tracking of an arbitrary moving target, which is a significant research interest in cognitive neuroscience. The recently proposed Central-Peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory sheds light on how humans effectively process visual information and track moving targets in complex environments. However, existing visual object tracking algorithms still fall short of matching human performance in maintaining tracking over time, particularly in complex scenarios requiring robust visual search skills. These scenarios often involve Spatio-Temporal Discontinuities (i.e., STDChallenge), prevalent in long-term tracking and global instance tracking. To address this issue, we conduct research from a human-like modeling perspective: (1) Inspired by the CPD, we pro- pose a new tracker named CPDTrack to achieve human-like visual search ability. The central vision of CPDTrack leverages the spatio-temporal continuity of videos to introduce priors and enhance localization precision, while the peripheral vision improves global awareness and detects object movements. (2) To further evaluate and analyze STDChallenge, we create the STDChallenge Benchmark. Besides, by incorporating human subjects, we establish a human baseline, creating a high- quality environment specifically designed to assess trackers’ visual search abilities in videos across STDChallenge. (3) Our extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed CPDTrack not only achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in this challenge but also narrows the behavioral differences with humans. Additionally, CPDTrack exhibits strong generalizability across various challenging benchmarks. In summary, our research underscores the importance of human-like modeling and offers strategic insights for advancing intelligent visual target tracking. Code and models are available at https://github.com/ZhangDailing8/CPDTrack.

paragraphs: Tracking a moving object becomes especially difficult when its appearance in a video breaks expected continuity across space or time. A tracker then needs effective visual search, rather than only precise localization near the last known position. This paper studies those discontinuities through a human-inspired account of central and peripheral vision.

The proposed CPDTrack gives the two forms of vision complementary roles. Its central component uses continuity across video frames to introduce prior information and improve localization precision. Its peripheral component maintains broader awareness and detects object movement. The approach connects detailed local tracking with a wider search process, addressing situations where following the immediate neighborhood alone is insufficient.

The authors also create STDChallenge, a benchmark specifically for assessing visual search across these discontinuities, and include human participants to establish a behavioral baseline. Their experiments report state-of-the-art performance on the challenge, smaller behavioral differences from humans, and strong generalization across other difficult benchmarks. The contribution therefore includes both a tracker and an evaluation setting that examines how tracking behavior compares with human search.
summary.tldr: CPDTrack combines central and peripheral visual processing to improve tracking through discontinuities and narrow measured behavioral differences from humans.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Tracking more like Human via Visual Search

abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality.In this work, we address this challenge through Sparse Activation Control. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint modules that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e. attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factualness, and bias concurrently.

paragraphs: Representation engineering seeks to influence a language model's behavior by controlling its intermediate hidden states without additional training. A difficulty arises when several requirements must be met together. Encoding qualities such as honesty and safety within a single semantic feature can make simultaneous control difficult and restrict the usefulness of the approach.

Sparse Activation Control addresses this by identifying attention heads closely associated with particular tasks. The authors find sparse characteristics in these heads that permit near-independent control of different tasks. The method therefore places control at selected internal modules, giving multiple behavioral requirements more distinct points of influence.

Experiments on open-source Llama models produce encouraging results for concurrent alignment with human preferences concerning safety, factualness, and bias. The contribution is a way to handle several trustworthiness dimensions within one activation-control approach. The reported near-independence is central to this result: it supports combining controls for different tasks without requiring all their semantic content to be represented by one feature.
summary.tldr: Sparse Activation Control targets task-associated attention heads to improve safety, factualness, and bias alignment concurrently in Llama models.

title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control

abstract: Amidst the recent strides in evaluating Large Language Models for Code (Code LLMs), existing benchmarks have mainly focused on the functional correctness of generated code, neglecting the importance of their computational efficiency. To fill the gap, we present Mercury, the first code efficiency benchmark for Code LLMs. It comprises 1,889 Python tasks, each accompanied by adequate solutions that serve as real-world efficiency baselines, enabling a comprehensive analysis of the runtime distribution. Based on the distribution, we introduce a new metric Beyond, which computes a runtime-percentile-weighted Pass score to reflect functional correctness and code efficiency simultaneously. On Mercury, leading Code LLMs can achieve 65% on Pass, while less than 50% on Beyond. Given that an ideal Beyond score would be aligned with the Pass score, it indicates that while Code LLMs exhibit impressive capabilities in generating functionally correct code, there remains a notable gap in their efficiency. Finally, our empirical experiments reveal that Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) serves as a robust baseline for enhancing code efficiency compared with Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT), which paves a promising avenue for future exploration of efficient code generation. Our code and data are available on GitHub: https://github.com/Elfsong/Mercury.

paragraphs: Generated code can produce the right answer yet take unnecessarily long to run. Mercury evaluates this distinction, addressing benchmarks that mainly reward functional correctness. It contains 1,889 Python tasks with accompanying solutions that provide efficiency baselines and allow the authors to examine distributions of execution time.

The paper introduces Beyond, a score that weights passing solutions according to their runtime percentile. This combines correctness and computational efficiency in one measurement. Ideally, Beyond would align with the ordinary Pass score; a gap between them indicates that some functionally correct outputs fall short on efficiency.

On Mercury, leading code models reach 65% on Pass but remain below 50% on Beyond, exposing an efficiency gap that correctness alone would obscure. The authors also compare training approaches and find that Direct Preference Optimization provides a robust baseline for improving efficiency relative to supervised fine-tuning in their experiments. The benchmark thus supplies both a way to measure efficient code generation and empirical evidence for a promising improvement strategy.
summary.tldr: Mercury evaluates correctness and runtime together, revealing efficiency gaps in generated Python code and promising results from preference optimization.

title: Mercury: A Code Efficiency Benchmark for Code Large Language Models

abstract: In this paper, we present a novel data-free method for merging neural networks in weight space. Our method optimizes for the permutations of network neurons while ensuring global coherence across all layers, and it outperforms recent layer-local approaches in a set of challenging scenarios. We then generalize the formulation to the $N$-models scenario to enforce cycle consistency of the permutations with guarantees, allowing circular compositions of permutations to be computed without accumulating error along the path. We qualitatively and quantitatively motivate the need for such a constraint, showing its benefits when merging homogeneous sets of models in scenarios spanning varying architectures and datasets. We finally show that, when coupled with activation renormalization, the approach yields the best results in the task.

We then generalize the formulation to the $N$-models scenario to enforce cycle consistency of the permutations with guarantees, allowing circular compositions of permutations to be computed without accumulating error along the path. paragraphs: Combining neural networks directly through their weights requires matching corresponding neurons across models. This paper presents a method that finds these matches without using data. It optimizes neuron permutations while maintaining coherence across all layers, and reports improvements over approaches that make alignment decisions locally within individual layers.

For merging more than two models, the method adds a guarantee of cycle consistency. This means that following a circular sequence of neuron mappings returns to a consistent correspondence, without accumulating mapping error along the route. The constraint makes the collection of alignments mutually compatible instead of treating every pair of networks as an independent matching problem.

The authors provide qualitative and quantitative evidence for the value of this constraint when merging homogeneous groups of models. Their experiments span different architecture and dataset settings. They also report that combining the method with activation renormalization produces the best results in the evaluated task. Together, the findings emphasize consistency across both layers and models as useful ingredients in weight-space merging.
summary.tldr: C²M³ merges networks without data by aligning neurons coherently across layers and enforcing consistent mappings among multiple models.

title: $C^2M^3$: Cycle-Consistent Multi-Model Merging

abstract: Training machine learning and statistical models often involves optimizing a data-driven risk criterion. The risk is usually computed with respect to the empirical data distribution, but this may result in poor and unstable out-of-sample performance due to distributional uncertainty. In the spirit of distributionally robust optimization, we propose a novel robust criterion by combining insights from Bayesian nonparametric (i.e., Dirichlet process) theory and a recent decision-theoretic model of smooth ambiguity-averse preferences. First, we highlight novel connections with standard regularized empirical risk minimization techniques, among which Ridge and LASSO regressions. Then, we theoretically demonstrate the existence of favorable finite-sample and asymptotic statistical guarantees on the performance of the robust optimization procedure. For practical implementation, we propose and study tractable approximations of the criterion based on well-known Dirichlet process representations. We also show that the smoothness of the criterion naturally leads to standard gradient-based numerical optimization. Finally, we provide insights into the workings of our method by applying it to a variety of tasks based on simulated and real datasets.

paragraphs: Training commonly minimizes an average loss calculated from the observed data. That calculation treats the empirical distribution as the basis for decision-making, even though the distribution encountered outside the training sample is uncertain. The paper develops a robust alternative intended to account for this uncertainty when choosing a model.

The proposed criterion combines Dirichlet process theory, a Bayesian nonparametric approach to distributions, with a decision-theoretic model of smooth ambiguity aversion. This brings uncertainty about the data distribution into the optimization objective. The authors also establish connections to familiar regularized training methods, including Ridge and LASSO regression, relating the new criterion to existing approaches for controlling fitted models.

The analysis provides favorable statistical guarantees for finite samples and in the large-sample limit. For implementation, the paper studies tractable approximations using representations of the Dirichlet process. Because the criterion is smooth, standard gradient-based optimization can be used. Applications to simulated and real datasets illustrate how the method works, linking its statistical motivation to a practical training procedure.
summary.tldr: A smooth Bayesian robustness criterion accounts for distributional uncertainty while supporting statistical guarantees and practical gradient-based training.

title: Bayesian Nonparametrics Meets Data-Driven Distributionally Robust Optimization

abstract: We aim to understand the optimal PAC sample complexity in multiclass learning. While finiteness of the Daniely-Shalev-Shwartz (DS) dimension has been shown to characterize the PAC learnability of a concept class [Brukhim, Carmon, Dinur, Moran, and Yehudayoff, 2022], there exist polylog factor gaps in the leading term of the sample complexity. In this paper, we reduce the gap in terms of the dependence on the error parameter to a single log factor and also propose two possible routes towards completely resolving the optimal sample complexity, each based on a key open question we formulate: one concerning list learning with bounded list size, the other concerning a new type of shifting for multiclass concept classes. We prove that a positive answer to either of the two questions would completely resolve the optimal sample complexity up to log factors of the DS dimension.

In this paper, we reduce the gap in terms of the dependence on the error parameter to a single log factor and also propose two possible routes towards completely resolving the optimal sample complexity, each based on a key open question we formulate: one concerning list learning with bounded list size, the other concerning a new type of shifting for multiclass concept classes. paragraphs: This paper studies how much labeled data is needed to learn a classifier with multiple possible labels under the PAC framework. A known result connects whether learning is possible to the finiteness of the Daniely-Shalev-Shwartz, or DS, dimension of the concept class. However, knowing that learning is possible still leaves a gap in the optimal sample requirement.

The authors improve the dependence of the sample-complexity bound on the target error, reducing the remaining gap to a single logarithmic factor. This narrows uncertainty about how the amount of training data must grow as the desired error becomes smaller. It is a theoretical improvement in learning guarantees.

The paper also formulates two open questions that could yield further progress. One concerns learning with bounded-size lists of candidate labels; the other concerns a new shifting operation for multiclass concept classes. The authors prove that a positive answer to either would settle optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors in DS dimension. These are conditional routes forward, not completed resolutions.
summary.tldr: The paper tightens multiclass PAC sample-complexity bounds and identifies two open questions whose positive resolution would close further gaps.

title: Improved Sample Complexity for Multiclass PAC Learning

abstract: Large language models are probabilistic models, and the process of generating content is essentially sampling from the output distribution of the language model. Existing watermarking techniques inject watermarks into the generated content without altering the output quality. On the other hand, existing acceleration techniques, specifically speculative sampling, leverage a draft model to speed up the sampling process while preserving the output distribution. However, there is no known method to simultaneously accelerate the sampling process and inject watermarks into the generated content. In this paper, we investigate this direction and find that the integration of watermarking and acceleration is non-trivial. We prove a no-go theorem, which states that it is impossible to simultaneously maintain the highest watermark strength and the highest sampling efficiency. Furthermore, we propose two methods that maintain either the sampling efficiency or the watermark strength, but not both. Our work provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for understanding the inherent trade-off between watermark strength and sampling efficiency in accelerating the generation of watermarked tokens for large language models. We also conduct numerical experiments to validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Language models generate text by sampling from probability distributions. Watermarking introduces a detectable signal into generated content, while speculative sampling uses a draft model to accelerate generation while preserving the output distribution. This paper asks how these two mechanisms can work together when the aim is both fast generation and strong watermarks.

The authors prove a no-go theorem: the highest watermark strength and the highest sampling efficiency cannot both be maintained simultaneously. The result identifies a conflict between optimizing these two properties. It establishes that combining watermarking with speculative acceleration requires a trade-off, even though each technique has useful properties when considered separately.

The paper proposes two methods reflecting the two priorities. One maintains sampling efficiency, while the other maintains watermark strength; neither maintains both maxima. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the methods’ effectiveness. The contribution is both a rigorous account of the trade-off and concrete approaches for navigating it when generating watermarked language-model outputs.
summary.tldr: A no-go theorem shows that speculative sampling cannot simultaneously retain maximum watermark strength and maximum sampling efficiency.

title: Inevitable Trade-off between Watermark Strength and Speculative Sampling Efficiency for Language Models

abstract: Cryo-EM is an increasingly popular method for determining the atomic resolution 3D structure of macromolecular complexes (eg, proteins) from noisy 2D images captured by an electron microscope. The computational task is to reconstruct the 3D density of the particle, along with 3D pose of the particle in each 2D image, for which the posterior pose distribution is highly multi-modal. Recent developments in cryo-EM have focused on deep learning for which amortized inference has been used to predict pose. Here, we address key problems with this approach, and propose a new semi-amortized method, cryoSPIN, in which reconstruction begins with amortized inference and then switches to a form of auto-decoding to refine poses locally using stochastic gradient descent. Through evaluation on synthetic datasets, we demonstrate that cryoSPIN is able to handle multi-modal pose distributions during the amortized inference stage, while the later, more flexible stage of direct pose optimization yields faster and more accurate convergence of poses compared to baselines. On experimental data, we show that cryoSPIN outperforms the state-of-the-art cryoAI in speed and reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: Cryo-EM reconstruction must recover a macromolecule’s three-dimensional density from noisy two-dimensional microscope images. It must also infer the particle’s pose in each image. This is difficult because several substantially different poses can be plausible, producing a pose distribution with multiple peaks. The paper examines how to improve deep learning approaches that predict these poses.

CryoSPIN uses two stages of pose inference. Reconstruction starts with amortized inference, where a learned predictor estimates poses across images. It then switches to direct, local optimization of the poses using stochastic gradient descent. This semi-amortized design combines an initial shared prediction mechanism with a later stage that gives individual pose estimates more freedom to improve.

On synthetic datasets, the method handles multimodal pose distributions during the prediction stage. Subsequent direct optimization produces faster and more accurate pose convergence than the evaluated baselines. On experimental data, CryoSPIN improves both speed and reconstruction quality over cryoAI. These findings support using learned inference to initialize reconstruction and more flexible optimization to refine it.
summary.tldr: CryoSPIN improves cryo-EM reconstruction by starting with learned pose predictions and then refining individual poses through direct optimization.

title: CryoSPIN: Improving Ab-Initio Cryo-EM Reconstruction with Semi-Amortized Pose Inference

abstract: With the continuous advancement of large language models (LLMs), it is essential to create new benchmarks to evaluate their expanding capabilities and identify areas for improvement. This work focuses on multi-image reasoning, an emerging capability in state-of-the-art LLMs. We introduce ReMI, a dataset designed to assess LLMs' ability to reason with multiple images. This dataset encompasses a diverse range of tasks, spanning various reasoning domains such as math, physics, logic, code, table/chart understanding, and spatial and temporal reasoning. It also covers a broad spectrum of characteristics found in multi-image reasoning scenarios. We have benchmarked several cutting-edge LLMs using ReMI and found a substantial gap between their performance and human-level proficiency. This highlights the challenges in multi-image reasoning and the need for further research. Our analysis also reveals the strengths and weaknesses of different models, shedding light on the types of reasoning that are currently attainable and areas where future models require improvement. We anticipate that ReMI will be a valuable resource for developing and evaluating more sophisticated LLMs capable of handling real-world multi-image understanding tasks.

paragraphs: ReMI evaluates whether language models can reason using multiple images. The paper treats this as an emerging capability that needs dedicated assessment as models become more capable. Its contribution is a dataset designed to reveal what models can infer from collections of images and where their reasoning still falls short.

The dataset covers mathematics, physics, logic, code, tables and charts, and spatial and temporal reasoning. It also spans varied characteristics of multi-image scenarios. This breadth allows the evaluation to examine several kinds of reasoning within the same resource, making it possible to compare models' strengths and weaknesses across different task categories.

Benchmarking several leading language models reveals a substantial gap from human-level proficiency. The accompanying analysis identifies reasoning types that current models can handle and areas where improvement is needed. ReMI therefore contributes both a common evaluation resource and evidence that multi-image reasoning remains challenging for the evaluated systems. Its proposed role in future development is to help assess progress toward more capable real-world multi-image understanding.
summary.tldr: ReMI tests reasoning across multiple images and reveals a substantial performance gap between evaluated language models and humans.

title: ReMI: A Dataset for Reasoning with Multiple Images

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown great performance in various tasks, with the core idea of learning from data labels and aggregating messages within the neighborhood of nodes. However, the common challenges in graphs are twofold: insufficient accurate (high-quality) labels and limited neighbors for nodes, resulting in weak GNNs. Existing graph augmentation methods typically address only one of these challenges, often adding training costs or relying on oversimplified or knowledge-intensive strategies, limiting their generalization.To simultaneously address both challenges faced by graphs in a generalized way, we propose an elegant method called IntraMix. Considering the incompatibility of vanilla Mixup with the complex topology of graphs, IntraMix innovatively employs Mixup among inaccurate labeled data of the same class, generating high-quality labeled data at minimal cost. Additionally, it finds data with high confidence of being clustered into the same group as the generated data to serve as their neighbors, thereby enriching the neighborhoods of graphs. IntraMix efficiently tackles both issues faced by graphs and challenges the prior notion of the limited effectiveness of Mixup in node classification. IntraMix is a theoretically grounded plug-in-play method that can be readily applied to all GNNs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of IntraMix across various GNNs and datasets. Our code is available at: [https://github.com/Zhengsh123/IntraMix](https://github.com/Zhengsh123/IntraMix).

paragraphs: IntraMix addresses two weaknesses that can limit graph neural networks: too few reliable labels and too few neighbors from which nodes can gather information. These problems affect both supervision and message aggregation. The paper proposes one augmentation method that improves both, rather than treating label quality and graph connectivity as separate tasks.

The method adapts Mixup to graph data by combining imperfectly labeled examples assigned to the same class. The authors describe this as producing higher-quality labeled examples at low cost. IntraMix then looks for data that can be confidently grouped with those generated examples and uses them as neighbors. The generated data therefore come with both supervision and connections for graph-based learning.

The paper presents theoretical grounding and describes IntraMix as a readily attachable method for graph neural networks. Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate its effectiveness. These findings challenge the view that Mixup has limited value for node classification: the contribution is to adapt the mixing and neighborhood construction together so that the augmentation fits the graph setting.
summary.tldr: IntraMix combines same-class data mixing with confident neighbor selection to improve supervision and connectivity for graph neural networks.

title: IntraMix: Intra-Class Mixup Generation for Accurate Labels and Neighbors

abstract: Relative entropy coding (REC) algorithms encode a random sample following a target distribution $Q$, using a coding distribution $P$ shared between the sender and receiver. Sadly, general REC algorithms suffer from prohibitive encoding times, at least on the order of $2^{D_{\text{KL}}[Q||P]}$, and faster algorithms are limited to very specific settings. This work addresses this issue by introducing a REC scheme utilizing space partitioning to reduce runtime in practical scenarios. We provide theoretical analyses of our method and demonstrate its effectiveness with both toy examples and practical applications. Notably, our method successfully handles REC tasks with $D_{\text{KL}}[Q||P]$ about three times greater than what previous methods can manage, and reduces the bitrate by approximately 5-15\% in VAE-based lossless compression on MNIST and INR-based lossy compression on CIFAR-10, compared to previous methods, significantly improving the practicality of REC for neural compression.

This work addresses this issue by introducing a REC scheme utilizing space partitioning to reduce runtime in practical scenarios. paragraphs: Relative entropy coding communicates a random sample drawn from a target distribution using another distribution already shared by the sender and receiver. Its practical difficulty is encoding time: general algorithms require work that grows at least exponentially with the divergence between these two distributions. A larger mismatch can therefore make an otherwise useful compression approach too slow.

The paper introduces a coding scheme that partitions the sample space to reduce runtime in practical settings. The central change is how the coding problem is organized, with space partitioning providing a way to make harder distribution pairs more manageable. The authors support the method with theoretical analysis, simple examples, and neural compression applications.

In the reported evaluations, the method handles distribution divergences roughly three times larger than previous methods could manage. It also reduces bitrate by approximately 5–15% in the tested lossless MNIST and lossy CIFAR-10 compression applications. These results support improved practical reach and compression efficiency in those settings; the abstract does not claim to eliminate the general exponential encoding difficulty.
summary.tldr: Space partitioning makes relative entropy coding practical for larger distribution mismatches and improves bitrate in the tested neural compression applications.

title: Accelerating Relative Entropy Coding with Space Partitioning

abstract: Group Recommendation (GR), which aims to recommend items to groups of users, has become a promising and practical direction for recommendation systems. This paper points out two issues of the state-of-the-art GR models. (1) The pre-defined and fixed number of user groups is inadequate for real-time industrial recommendation systems, where the group distribution can shift dynamically. (2) The training schema of existing GR methods is supervised, necessitating expensive user-group and group-item labels, leading to significant annotation costs. To this end, we present a novel unsupervised group recommendation framework named $\underline{\text{I}}$dentify $\underline{\text{T}}$hen $\underline{\text{R}}$ecommend ($\underline{\text{ITR}}$), where it first identifies the user groups in an unsupervised manner even without the pre-defined number of groups, and then two pre-text tasks are designed to conduct self-supervised group recommendation. Concretely, at the group identification stage, we first estimate the adaptive density of each user point, where areas with higher densities are more likely to be recognized as group centers. Then, a heuristic merge-and-split strategy is designed to discover the user groups and decision boundaries. Subsequently, at the self-supervised learning stage, the pull-and-repulsion pre-text task is proposed to optimize the user-group distribution. Besides, the pseudo group recommendation pre-text task is designed to assist the recommendations. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority and effectiveness of ITR on both user recommendation (e.g., 22.22\% NDCG@5 $\uparrow$) and group recommendation (e.g., 22.95\% NDCG@5 $\uparrow$). Furthermore, we deploy ITR on the industrial recommender and achieve promising results.

paragraphs: Identify Then Recommend, or ITR, addresses recommendation for groups whose structure is not known in advance. Existing approaches can assume a fixed number of groups and require labels connecting users to groups and groups to items. Those requirements are costly and can be awkward when the distribution of groups changes in an industrial recommendation system.

ITR first identifies groups without supervision or a predefined group count. It estimates an adaptive density around each user representation, treating denser regions as more likely group centers. A heuristic process then merges and splits groups to determine their membership and boundaries. After identification, two self-supervised tasks provide training signals: one adjusts the user-group distribution through attraction and repulsion, and another supplies pseudo group recommendations.

Experiments report improvements in both individual and group recommendation, with example NDCG@5 gains of 22.22% and 22.95%, respectively. The authors also report promising results after deployment in an industrial recommender. The approach links flexible group discovery with recommendation training that avoids the stated expensive group-level labels.
summary.tldr: ITR discovers user groups without a preset group count and trains recommendations through self-supervised tasks.

title: Identify Then Recommend: Towards Unsupervised Group Recommendation

abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have achieved impressive progress in diverse applications, becoming a prevalent research direction. In this paper, we build FIRE, a feedback-refinement dataset, consisting of 1.1M multi-turn conversations that are derived from 27 source datasets, empowering VLMs to spontaneously refine their responses based on user feedback across diverse tasks. To scale up the data collection, FIRE is collected in two components: FIRE-100K and FIRE-1M, where FIRE-100K is generated by GPT-4V, and FIRE-1M is freely generated via models trained on FIRE-100K. Then, we build FIRE-Bench, a benchmark to comprehensively evaluate the feedback-refining capability of VLMs, which contains 11K feedback-refinement conversations as the test data, two evaluation settings, and a model to provide feedback for VLMs. We develop the FIRE-LLaVA model by fine-tuning LLaVA on FIRE-100K and FIRE-1M, which shows remarkable feedback-refining capability on FIRE-Bench and outperforms untrained VLMs by 50%, making more efficient user-agent interactions and underscoring the significance of the FIRE dataset.

paragraphs: FIRE focuses on what happens after a vision-language model gives an answer: can it use user feedback to improve its response? The authors construct 1.1 million multi-turn conversations drawn from 27 source datasets. This makes feedback-driven revision an explicit training target across diverse tasks, rather than evaluating only the model's initial response.

The collection process has two stages. GPT-4V generates FIRE-100K, and models trained on that collection generate FIRE-1M. The larger component scales up the available refinement conversations using models trained on the initial data. The authors also build FIRE-Bench, comprising 11,000 test conversations, two evaluation settings, and a model that supplies feedback during evaluation.

Fine-tuning LLaVA on both dataset components produces FIRE-LLaVA. On FIRE-Bench, the authors report strong refinement capability and a 50% improvement over untrained vision-language models. This finding supports the value of specifically training models to incorporate feedback, with the aim of making user-agent interactions more efficient through better revisions.
summary.tldr: FIRE supplies feedback-refinement training conversations and a benchmark, with a fine-tuned LLaVA model showing improved response revision.

title: FIRE: A Dataset for Feedback Integration and Refinement Evaluation of Multimodal Models

abstract: Accurate motion forecasting for traffic agents is crucial for ensuring the safety and efficiency of autonomous driving systems in dynamically changing environments. Mainstream methods adopt a one-query-one-trajectory paradigm, where each query corresponds to a unique trajectory for predicting multi-modal trajectories. While straightforward and effective, the absence of detailed representation of future trajectories may yield suboptimal outcomes, given that the agent states dynamically evolve over time. To address this problem, we introduce DeMo, a framework that decouples multi-modal trajectory queries into two types: mode queries capturing distinct directional intentions and state queries tracking the agent's dynamic states over time. By leveraging this format, we separately optimize the multi-modality and dynamic evolutionary properties of trajectories. Subsequently, the mode and state queries are integrated to obtain a comprehensive and detailed representation of the trajectories. To achieve these operations, we additionally introduce combined Attention and Mamba techniques for global information aggregation and state sequence modeling, leveraging their respective strengths. Extensive experiments on both the Argoverse 2 and nuScenes benchmarks demonstrate that our DeMo achieves state-of-the-art performance in motion forecasting. In addition, we will make our code and models publicly available.

paragraphs: Motion forecasting for autonomous driving must represent several plausible futures while also describing how a traffic participant's state changes over time. Many approaches assign one internal query to each complete possible trajectory. DeMo addresses the concern that this representation may not capture enough detail about a trajectory's evolving states.

The framework separates trajectory queries into two groups. Mode queries describe distinct directional intentions, while state queries represent dynamic states over time. This separation lets the model optimize the diversity of possible movements and their temporal evolution individually. It then combines the two query types to construct a more detailed representation of each predicted trajectory.

DeMo uses attention for aggregating global information and Mamba techniques for modeling state sequences. These components support the two complementary parts of its trajectory representation. Experiments on Argoverse 2 and nuScenes report state-of-the-art forecasting performance. The results support the paper's central design choice: giving directional alternatives and evolving motion states explicit, separate representations before integrating them into predictions.
summary.tldr: DeMo separates directional intentions from evolving motion states to improve forecasts of multiple possible traffic trajectories.

title: DeMo: Decoupling Motion Forecasting into Directional Intentions and Dynamic States

abstract: Videos carry rich visual information including object description, action, interaction, etc., but the existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) fell short in referential understanding scenarios such as video-based referring. In this paper, we present Artemis, an MLLM that pushes video-based referential understanding to a finer level. Given a video, Artemis receives a natural-language question with a bounding box in any video frame and describes the referred target in the entire video. The key to achieving this goal lies in extracting compact, target-specific video features, where we set a solid baseline by tracking and selecting spatiotemporal features from the video. We train Artemis on the newly established ViderRef45K dataset with 45K video-QA pairs and design a computationally efficient, three-stage training procedure. Results are promising both quantitatively and qualitatively. Additionally, we show that Artemis can be integrated with video grounding and text summarization tools to understand more complex scenarios. Code and data are available at https://github.com/NeurIPS24Artemis/Artemis.

paragraphs: Understanding a video becomes more specific when a question refers to one particular target. Artemis addresses this setting by accepting a natural-language question together with a bounding box in any video frame. Its task is to describe that selected target across the entire video, connecting a localized reference to information spread over time.

The central design choice is to extract compact video features focused on the target. The authors establish a baseline that tracks the target and selects relevant features across space and time. This gives the model a representation suited to the referenced entity and its changing visual context. They train Artemis using ViderRef45K, a new dataset containing 45,000 video question-answer pairs, through a computationally efficient three-stage procedure.

The reported quantitative and qualitative results are promising for this finer-grained form of video understanding. The authors also demonstrate integration with video-grounding and text-summarization tools for more complex scenarios. The contribution combines a target-focused model, training data, and a practical way to connect referential understanding with other video tools.
summary.tldr: Artemis uses a question and a bounding box to describe a selected target throughout a video using compact, target-specific features.

title: Artemis: Towards Referential Understanding in Complex Videos

abstract: We study calibration measures in a sequential prediction setup. In addition to rewarding accurate predictions (completeness) and penalizing incorrect ones (soundness), an important desideratum of calibration measures is *truthfulness*, a minimal condition for the forecaster not to be incentivized to exploit the system. Formally, a calibration measure is truthful if the forecaster (approximately) minimizes the expected penalty by predicting the conditional expectation of the next outcome, given the prior distribution of outcomes. We conduct a taxonomy of existing calibration measures. Perhaps surprisingly, all of them are far from being truthful. We introduce a new calibration measure termed the *Subsampled Smooth Calibration Error (SSCE)*, which is complete and sound, and under which truthful prediction is optimal up to a constant multiplicative factor. In contrast, under existing calibration measures, there are simple distributions on which a polylogarithmic (or even zero) penalty is achievable, while truthful prediction leads to a polynomial penalty.

We conduct a taxonomy of existing calibration measures. Perhaps surprisingly, all of them are far from being truthful. paragraphs: A calibration measure evaluates probabilistic predictions, but its scoring rules can also create incentives. This paper asks whether a forecaster minimizes its expected penalty by honestly reporting the conditional expectation of the next outcome. It calls this property truthfulness and studies it alongside completeness and soundness, which concern rewarding accurate predictions and penalizing incorrect ones.

The authors classify existing calibration measures and find that all those examined are far from truthful. They give simple outcome distributions where a forecaster can obtain a polylogarithmic or even zero penalty, while truthful predictions incur a polynomial penalty. The issue is therefore more than imperfect scoring: a measure can substantially favor reports that differ from the forecaster's actual conditional expectations.

The proposed Subsampled Smooth Calibration Error, or SSCE, satisfies completeness and soundness while making truthful prediction optimal up to a constant multiplicative factor. This is an approximate incentive guarantee rather than exact optimality. The contribution provides a calibration criterion that better aligns low evaluation penalties with honest forecasting in the sequential setting.
summary.tldr: SSCE measures calibration while making truthful sequential forecasting optimal up to a constant factor.

title: Truthfulness of Calibration Measures

abstract: We introduce multiple physics pretraining (MPP), an autoregressive task-agnostic pretraining approach for physical surrogate modeling of spatiotemporal systems with transformers. In MPP, rather than training one model on a specific physical system, we train a backbone model to predict the dynamics of multiple heterogeneous physical systems simultaneously in order to learn features that are broadly useful across systems and facilitate transfer. In order to learn effectively in this setting, we introduce a shared embedding and normalization strategy that projects the fields of multiple systems into a shared embedding space. We validate the efficacy of our approach on both pretraining and downstream tasks over a broad fluid mechanics-oriented benchmark. We show that a single MPP-pretrained transformer is able to match or outperform task-specific baselines on all pretraining sub-tasks without the need for finetuning. For downstream tasks, we demonstrate that finetuning MPP-trained models results in more accurate predictions across multiple time-steps on systems with previously unseen physical components or higher dimensional systems compared to training from scratch or finetuning pretrained video foundation models. We open-source our code and model weights trained at multiple scales for reproducibility.

paragraphs: Physical surrogate models predict how a system changes across space and time. Multiple physics pretraining, or MPP, trains one transformer backbone on several heterogeneous physical systems together. The goal is to learn features useful across systems, providing a starting point that can transfer to new prediction tasks.

MPP uses autoregressive prediction and a shared embedding and normalization strategy. This projects the fields from different systems into a common representation, enabling them to contribute to the same training process. The approach is evaluated on a broad benchmark oriented toward fluid mechanics, covering both the systems used during pretraining and downstream tasks.

A single pretrained transformer matches or exceeds task-specific baselines on every pretraining subtask without fine-tuning. For downstream systems with previously unseen physical components or higher dimensionality, fine-tuned MPP models make more accurate multi-step predictions than models trained from scratch or adapted from video foundation models. These findings support learning across several physical systems as a useful basis for both shared prediction and later specialization.
summary.tldr: Pretraining a transformer across multiple physical systems improves shared prediction and transfer to new physical forecasting tasks.

title: Multiple Physics Pretraining for Spatiotemporal Surrogate Models

abstract: Federated reinforcement learning (RL) enables collaborative decision making of multiple distributed agents without sharing local data trajectories. In this work, we consider a multi-task setting, in which each agent has its own private reward function corresponding to different tasks, while sharing the same transition kernel of the environment. Focusing on infinite-horizon Markov decision processes, the goal is to learn a globally optimal policy that maximizes the sum of the discounted total rewards of all the agents in a decentralized manner, where each agent only communicates with its neighbors over some prescribed graph topology.We develop federated vanilla and entropy-regularized natural policy gradient (NPG) methods in the tabular setting under softmax parameterization, where gradient tracking is applied to estimate the global Q-function to mitigate the impact of imperfect information sharing. We establish non-asymptotic global convergence guarantees under exact policy evaluation, where the rates are nearly independent of the size of the state-action space and illuminate the impacts of network size and connectivity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time that global convergence is established for federated multi-task RL using policy optimization. We further go beyond the tabular setting by proposing a federated natural actor critic (NAC) method for multi-task RL with function approximation, and establish its finite-time sample complexity taking the errors of function approximation into account.

paragraphs: This paper studies distributed reinforcement learning agents that share environment dynamics but have different private reward functions. The agents seek one policy maximizing their combined discounted rewards without exchanging local trajectories. Communication is decentralized: each agent shares information only with neighbors in a prescribed network, making incomplete information exchange part of the optimization problem.

For tabular problems with softmax policies, the authors develop standard and entropy-regularized federated natural policy gradient methods. Gradient tracking helps each agent estimate the global action-value function despite limited communication. Under exact policy evaluation, the analysis establishes global convergence rates that are nearly independent of the number of states and actions, while exposing the effects of network size and connectivity.

The paper also develops a federated natural actor-critic method with function approximation, extending beyond explicit tables of states and actions. Its finite-time sample-complexity analysis accounts for approximation errors. The results thus distinguish a convergence guarantee under exact tabular evaluation from a broader learning method whose analysis explicitly incorporates imperfect function representation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops decentralized policy optimization methods with global convergence guarantees under exact evaluation and sample-complexity analysis with function approximation.

title: Federated Natural Policy Gradient and Actor Critic Methods for Multi-task Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Most jailbreak papers claim the jailbreaks they propose are highly effective, often boasting near-100% attack success rates. However, it is perhaps more common than not for jailbreak developers to substantially exaggerate the effectiveness of their jailbreaks. We suggest this problem arises because jailbreak researchers lack a standard, high-quality benchmark for evaluating jailbreak performance, leaving researchers to create their own. To create a benchmark, researchers must choose a dataset of forbidden prompts to which a victim model will respond, along with an evaluation method that scores the harmfulness of the victim model’s responses. We show that existing benchmarks suffer from significant shortcomings and introduce the StrongREJECT benchmark to address these issues. StrongREJECT's dataset contains prompts that victim models must answer with specific, harmful information, while its automated evaluator measures the extent to which a response gives useful information to forbidden prompts. In doing so, the StrongREJECT evaluator achieves state-of-the-art agreement with human judgments of jailbreak effectiveness. Notably, we find that existing evaluation methods significantly overstate jailbreak effectiveness compared to human judgments and the StrongREJECT evaluator. We describe a surprising and novel phenomenon that explains this discrepancy: jailbreaks bypassing a victim model’s safety fine-tuning tend to reduce its capabilities. Together, our findings underscore the need for researchers to use a high-quality benchmark, such as StrongREJECT, when developing new jailbreak attacks. We release the StrongREJECT code and data at https://strong-reject.readthedocs.io/.

paragraphs: A jailbreak evaluation needs to distinguish between a model appearing willing to answer and actually providing useful harmful information. This paper argues that weaknesses in existing benchmarks help explain why reported attack success can substantially exceed effectiveness as judged by people. The problem involves both the questions used to test attacks and the way responses are scored.

StrongREJECT addresses these two parts together. Its dataset uses forbidden requests that require specific harmful information, and its automated evaluator assesses how much useful information a response supplies. This makes the evaluation sensitive to the substance of an answer. The authors report leading agreement with human judgments of jailbreak effectiveness.

The study also finds that attacks bypassing safety fine-tuning tend to impair the model’s capabilities. That helps explain how an attack can produce apparent compliance without an effective answer. Existing evaluation methods substantially overestimate effectiveness relative to human judgments and StrongREJECT. The contribution is therefore both a benchmark and evidence that capability loss matters when interpreting jailbreak results.
summary.tldr: StrongREJECT evaluates whether jailbreak responses contain useful harmful information, revealing that existing measures often overstate attack effectiveness.

title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks

abstract: Recent advances in large language models have shown capabilities that are extraordinary and near-superhuman. These models operate with such complexity that reliably evaluating and aligning them proves challenging for humans. This leads to the natural question: can guidance from weak models (like humans) adequately direct the capabilities of strong models? In a recent and somewhat surprising work, Burns et al. (2023) empirically demonstrated that when strong models (like GPT-4) are finetuned using labels generated by weak supervisors (like GPT-2), the strong models outperform their weaker counterparts---a phenomenon they term *weak-to-strong generalization*.In this work, we present a theoretical framework for understanding weak-to-strong generalization. Specifically, we show that the improvement in performance achieved by strong models over their weaker counterparts is quantified by the *misfit error* incurred by the strong model on labels generated by the weaker model. Our theory reveals several curious algorithmic insights. For instance, we can predict the amount by which the strong model will improve over the weak model, and also choose among different weak models to train the strong model, based on its misfit error. We validate our theoretical findings through various empirical assessments.

paragraphs: Weak-to-strong generalization occurs when a stronger model learns from a weaker supervisor's labels yet performs better than that supervisor. This raises a central question for supervising highly capable systems: how can guidance from a less capable source support better performance? The paper develops a theoretical framework to explain and quantify that improvement.

Its central quantity is misfit error, the error the strong model incurs on labels produced by the weak model. Within the proposed theory, this quantity characterizes the performance gain over the weaker supervisor. The framework therefore gives a predictive role to how the stronger model fits its supervisor's labels when explaining the benefit of training.

The authors draw algorithmic implications from this relationship, including predicting the size of the improvement and choosing among weak supervisors using misfit error. Empirical assessments support the theoretical findings. The contribution turns the observed phenomenon into a quantitative framework that can inform supervision choices, connecting a measurable training relationship with the gain achieved by the stronger model.
summary.tldr: A theoretical framework uses misfit error on weak-supervisor labels to quantify weak-to-strong gains and inform supervisor selection.

title: Quantifying the Gain in Weak-to-Strong Generalization

abstract: As with many other problems, real-world regression is plagued by the presence of noisy labels, an inevitable issue that demands our attention. Fortunately, much real-world data often exhibits an intrinsic property of continuously ordered correlations between labels and features, where data points with similar labels are also represented with closely related features.In response, we propose a novel approach named ConFrag, where we collectively model the regression data by transforming them into disjoint yet contrasting fragmentation pairs. This enables the training of more distinctive representations, enhancing the ability to select clean samples.Our ConFrag framework leverages a mixture of neighboring fragments to discern noisy labels through neighborhood agreement among expert feature extractors.We extensively perform experiments on four newly curated benchmark datasets of diverse domains, including age prediction, price prediction, and music production year estimation.We also introduce a metric called Error Residual Ratio (ERR) to better account for varying degrees of label noise.Our approach consistently outperforms fourteen state-of-the-art baselines, being robust against symmetric and random Gaussian label noise.

Fortunately, much real-world data often exhibits an intrinsic property of continuously ordered correlations between labels and features, where data points with similar labels are also represented with closely related features.In response, we propose a novel approach named ConFrag, where we collectively model the regression data by transforming them into disjoint yet contrasting fragmentation pairs. paragraphs: Regression learns numerical targets, but incorrect labels can distort that learning. ConFrag builds on a pattern found in much real-world data: nearby target values often correspond to related features. This ordered relationship provides evidence for deciding whether a sample’s label agrees with the surrounding data.

The method reorganizes regression data into disjoint, contrasting pairs of fragments. Learning to distinguish these fragments produces more distinctive representations, supporting the selection of clean samples. It then combines neighboring fragments and checks agreement among expert feature extractors to identify labels that do not fit their neighborhood.

The authors evaluate ConFrag on four newly assembled benchmarks spanning domains including age, price, and music production year prediction. They also introduce Error Residual Ratio, a metric intended to account better for different degrees of label noise. ConFrag consistently outperforms fourteen leading baselines in the reported experiments and is robust to symmetric and random Gaussian label noise. The findings support using ordered feature–label relationships as a practical signal for sample selection in noisy regression.
summary.tldr: ConFrag identifies cleaner regression samples by learning contrasting data fragments and checking agreement among neighboring feature experts.

title: Sample Selection via Contrastive Fragmentation for Noisy Label Regression

abstract: We consider the problem of selecting all the minimal-size subsets of multivariate time-series (TS) variables whose past leads to an optimal predictive model for the future (forecasting) of a given target variable (multiple feature selection problem for times-series). Identifying these subsets leads to gaining insights, domain intuition,and a better understanding of the data-generating mechanism; it is often the first step in causal modeling. While identifying a single solution to the feature selection problem suffices for forecasting purposes, identifying all such minimal-size, optimally predictive subsets is necessary for knowledge discovery and important to avoid misleading a practitioner. We develop the theory of multiple feature selection for time-series data, propose the ChronoEpilogi algorithm, and prove its soundness and completeness under two mild, broad, non-parametric distributional assumptions, namely Compositionality of the distribution and Interchangeability of time-series variables in solutions. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the scalability of ChronoEpilogi to hundreds of TS variables and its efficacy in identifying multiple solutions. In the real datasets, ChronoEpilogi is shown to reduce the number of TS variables by 96% (on average) by conserving or even improving forecasting performance. Furthermore, it is on par with GroupLasso performance, with the added benefit of providing multiple solutions.

Its forecasting performance is comparable to GroupLasso, with the additional ability to return alternative minimal predictive subsets rather than a single selection.
summary.tldr: ChronoEpilogi finds multiple minimal predictive variable sets for time series, with guarantees under two distributional assumptions.

title: ChronoEpilogi: Scalable Time Series Selection with Multiple Solutions

abstract: Fairness metrics are a core tool in the fair machine learning literature (FairML),used to determine that ML models are, in some sense, “fair.” Real-world data,however, are typically plagued by various measurement biases and other violatedassumptions, which can render fairness assessments meaningless. We adapt toolsfrom causal sensitivity analysis to the FairML context, providing a general frame-work which (1) accommodates effectively any combination of fairness metric andbias that can be posed in the “oblivious setting”; (2) allows researchers to inves-tigate combinations of biases, resulting in non-linear sensitivity; and (3) enablesflexible encoding of domain-specific constraints and assumptions. Employing thisframework, we analyze the sensitivity of the most common parity metrics under 3varieties of classifier across 14 canonical fairness datasets. Our analysis reveals thestriking fragility of fairness assessments to even minor dataset biases. We show thatcausal sensitivity analysis provides a powerful and necessary toolkit for gaugingthe informativeness of parity metric evaluations. Our repository is \href{https://github.com/Jakefawkes/fragile_fair}{available here}.

Measurement biases or other assumption violations can undermine what a fairness score means. This paper adapts causal sensitivity analysis to examine how robust fairness assessments are to such problems.

The framework accommodates effectively any combination of fairness metric and bias that can be expressed in the oblivious setting. It also examines multiple biases together, allowing their combined effect to be nonlinear. Researchers can encode domain-specific assumptions and constraints, making the analysis responsive to the kinds of data problems considered plausible in a particular application.

The authors study common parity metrics using three classifier varieties across fourteen fairness datasets. They find that even small dataset biases can make fairness assessments strikingly fragile. The contribution is a way to evaluate how informative a reported parity result remains when its underlying assumptions are questioned, providing context for interpreting the metric itself.
summary.tldr: Causal sensitivity analysis reveals that common fairness assessments can be highly fragile to small dataset biases.

title: The Fragility of Fairness: Causal Sensitivity Analysis for Fair Machine Learning

abstract: Human safety awareness gaps often prevent the timely recognition of everyday risks.In solving this problem, a proactive safety artificial intelligence (AI) system would work better than a reactive one. Instead of just reacting to users' questions, it would actively watch people’s behavior and their environment to detect potential dangers in advance.Our Proactive Safety Bench (PaSBench) evaluates this capability through 416 multimodal scenarios (128 image sequences, 288 text logs) spanning 5 safety-critical domains.Evaluation of 36 advanced models reveals fundamental limitations: Top performers like Gemini-2.5-pro achieve 71\% image and 64\% text accuracy, but miss 45-55\% risks in repeated trials. Through failure analysis, we identify unstable proactive reasoning rather than knowledge deficits as the primary limitation.This work establishes (1) a proactive safety benchmark, (2) systematic evidence of model limitations, and (3) critical directions for developing reliable protective AI. We believe our dataset and findings can promote the development of safer AI assistants that actively prevent harm rather than merely respond to requests.
