Nonlinear versions broaden what can be discovered, yet can be prohibitively expensive at large scales. This paper uses randomized feature construction to develop scalable nonlinear variants of both methods.

The motivation comes from random-feature approaches that reveal nonlinear patterns while reducing computational demands. Earlier results for tasks such as regression and classification showed little or no performance loss alongside large savings. The authors bring this strategy to component analysis, using randomness to make nonlinear relationships accessible to scalable multivariate analysis methods.

The proposed ideas also extend to tools such as spectral clustering and linear discriminant analysis. The authors evaluate their algorithms on real-world data against state-of-the-art methods and provide an R implementation. The contribution is a route to computationally manageable nonlinear analysis, together with empirical comparisons and usable software, rather than a claim that nonlinear analysis is cost-free or universally superior.
summary.tldr: Randomized feature construction yields scalable nonlinear PCA and CCA methods, with extensions to other multivariate analysis tools.

title: Randomized Nonlinear Component Analysis

abstract: Kernel density estimation (KDE) is a popular nonparametric density estimation method. We (1) derive finite-sample high-probability density estimation bounds for multivariate KDE under mild density assumptions which hold uniformly in $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and bandwidth matrices. We apply these results to (2) mode, (3) density level set, and (4) class probability estimation and attain optimal rates up to logarithmic factors. We then (5) provide an extension of our results under the manifold hypothesis. Finally, we (6) give uniform convergence results for local intrinsic dimension estimation.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation builds a density estimate from observed data without requiring a fixed parametric form. This paper derives finite-sample bounds on its estimation error for multivariate data under mild assumptions on the density. The bounds hold with high probability and uniformly across locations and bandwidth matrices.

Uniformity makes the results relevant to more than the density estimate at a single chosen point. The authors apply their analysis to finding modes, estimating regions above a density threshold, and estimating class probabilities. For these applications, they obtain optimal convergence rates up to logarithmic factors, connecting a general estimation result to several downstream statistical tasks.

The paper also extends its results under the manifold hypothesis and establishes uniform convergence for estimating local intrinsic dimension. These additions bring the analysis to settings where the geometry of the data is itself relevant to estimation. The overall contribution is a collection of linked statistical guarantees: finite-sample control for KDE supports precise rates for derived quantities and extends to questions about underlying dimensional structure.
summary.tldr: Uniform finite-sample KDE bounds yield near-optimal rates for several estimation tasks, with extensions to manifolds and local intrinsic dimension.

title: Uniform Convergence Rates for Kernel Density Estimation

abstract: While machine learning is going through an era of celebrated success, concerns have been raised about the vulnerability of its backbone: stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Recent approaches have been proposed to ensure the robustness of distributed SGD against adversarial (Byzantine) workers sending poisoned gradients during the training phase. Some of these approaches have been proven Byzantine–resilient : they ensure the convergence of SGD despite the presence of a minority of adversarial workers. We show in this paper that convergence is not enough . In high dimension $d \gg 1$, an adver\-sary can build on the loss function’s non–convexity to make SGD converge to ineffective models. More precisely, we bring to light that existing Byzantine–resilient schemes leave a margin of poisoning of $\bigOmega\left(f(d)\right)$, where $f(d)$ increases at least like $\sqrt[p]{d }$. Based on this leeway , we build a simple attack, and experimentally show its strong to utmost effectivity on CIFAR–10 and MNIST. We introduce Bulyan , and prove it significantly reduces the attackers leeway to a narrow $\bigO\,( \sfrac{1}{\sqrt{d }})$ bound. We empirically show that Bulyan does not suffer the fragility of existing aggregation rules and, at a reasonable cost in terms of required batch size, achieves convergence as if only non–Byzantine gradients had been used to update the model.

This paper shows why that guarantee alone is insufficient: in high-dimensional, nonconvex learning problems, an attacker can still steer convergence toward an ineffective model.

The work connects a dimension-dependent theoretical vulnerability with an attack and a method designed to sharply restrict it.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that Byzantine-resilient convergence can still yield ineffective models and introduces Bulyan to sharply reduce poisoning freedom.

title: The Hidden Vulnerability of Distributed Learning in Byzantium

abstract: Meta-learning agents excel at rapidly learning new tasks from open-ended task distributions; yet, they forget what they learn about each task as soon as the next begins. When tasks reoccur {–} as they do in natural environments {–} meta-learning agents must explore again instead of immediately exploiting previously discovered solutions. We propose a formalism for generating open-ended yet repetitious environments, then develop a meta-learning architecture for solving these environments. This architecture melds the standard LSTM working memory with a differentiable neural episodic memory. We explore the capabilities of agents with this episodic LSTM in five meta-learning environments with reoccurring tasks, ranging from bandits to navigation and stochastic sequential decision problems.

paragraphs: An agent can become good at learning new tasks quickly yet still forget the solution to a particular task when it moves on. If that task returns, the agent has to explore again. This paper studies that mismatch between rapid adaptation and retaining useful experience across recurring tasks.

The authors first introduce a formal way to construct environments that keep presenting new tasks while also repeating earlier ones. They then develop an architecture that combines an LSTM's working memory with a differentiable episodic memory. The combination is designed to support both learning during the current task and recalling information from earlier encounters.

The resulting episodic LSTM is explored in five meta-learning environments, covering bandits, navigation, and stochastic sequential decisions. These settings make task recurrence an explicit part of the evaluation. The paper's contribution is a framework and memory architecture for studying how agents can reuse particular experiences alongside their general ability to adapt to unfamiliar problems.
summary.tldr: An episodic LSTM combines working memory with recall of past tasks to study meta-learning in environments where tasks recur.

title: Been There, Done That: Meta-Learning with Episodic Recall

abstract: Submodular functions have become a ubiquitous tool in machine learning. They are learnable from data, and can be optimized efficiently and with guarantees. Nonetheless, recent negative results show that optimizing learned surrogates of submodular functions can result in arbitrarily bad approximations of the true optimum. Our goal in this paper is to highlight the source of this hardness, and propose an alternative criterion for optimizing general combinatorial functions from sampled data. We prove a tight equivalence showing that a class of functions is optimizable if and only if it can be learned. We provide efficient and scalable optimization algorithms for several function classes of interest, and demonstrate their utility on the task of optimally choosing trending social media items.
originalAbstract: Submodular functions have become a ubiquitous tool in machine learning. They are learnable from data, and can be optimized efficiently and with guarantees. Nonetheless, recent negative results show that optimizing learned surrogates of submodular functions can result in arbitrarily bad approximations of the true optimum. Our goal in this paper is to highlight the source of this hardness, and propose an alternative criterion for optimizing general combinatorial functions from sampled data. We prove a tight equivalence showing that a class of functions is optimizable if and only if it can be learned. We provide efficient and scalable optimization algorithms for several function classes of interest, and demonstrate their utility on the task of optimally choosing trending social media items.

paragraphs: A function can be learnable from data and efficiently optimizable, yet optimizing its learned approximation can still produce a very poor answer for the true function. This paper examines that problem for combinatorial optimization, motivated by negative results for submodular functions. The gap concerns using learned predictions to choose a good solution.

The authors investigate the source of this difficulty and propose an alternative criterion for optimization from sampled data. Under that criterion, they prove a tight equivalence: a function class is optimizable if and only if it is learnable. The criterion is central to interpreting the result; the equivalence does not erase the earlier failures of surrogate optimization.

The paper also supplies efficient, scalable optimization algorithms for several function classes and demonstrates their utility in selecting trending social media items. The work therefore combines a theoretical reframing with algorithms and an application. Its main message is that the definition of successful optimization from data determines how learning guarantees can support decision-making.
summary.tldr: An alternative criterion for combinatorial optimization from samples yields a tight equivalence between learnability and optimizability.

title: Learning to Optimize Combinatorial Functions

abstract: Recently similarity graphs became the leading paradigm for efficient nearest neighbor search, outperforming traditional tree-based and LSH-based methods. Similarity graphs perform the search via greedy routing: a query traverses the graph and in each vertex moves to the adjacent vertex that is the closest to this query. In practice, similarity graphs are often susceptible to local minima, when queries do not reach its nearest neighbors, getting stuck in suboptimal vertices. In this paper we propose to learn the routing function that overcomes local minima via incorporating information about the graph global structure. In particular, we augment the vertices of a given graph with additional representations that are learned to provide the optimal routing from the start vertex to the query nearest neighbor. By thorough experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed learnable routing successfully diminishes the local minima problem and significantly improves the overall search performance.

paragraphs: Similarity graphs support nearest neighbor search by moving through connected data points. A conventional greedy search chooses the adjacent point closest to the query at each step. That local rule can become trapped at a suboptimal vertex, preventing the search from reaching the actual nearest neighbor even when the graph contains it.

The paper proposes learning how to route queries using information about the graph’s global structure. It augments the vertices of an existing graph with learned representations intended to support optimal routes from starting vertices to query neighbors. The routing decision can therefore draw on information beyond the immediate closeness comparison used by the greedy rule.

The authors report that extensive experiments show fewer problems with local minima and significant improvements in overall search performance. The result supports learning navigation as a way to improve similarity graph search. Its empirical claim is a reduction in the local-minimum problem, rather than a guarantee that every query always follows an optimal route.
summary.tldr: Learned vertex representations incorporate global graph structure into nearest neighbor routing, reducing local-minimum failures and improving empirical search performance.

title: Learning to Route in Similarity Graphs

abstract: We study the exploration problem in episodic MDPs with rich observations generated from a small number of latent states. Under certain identifiability assumptions, we demonstrate how to estimate a mapping from the observations to latent states inductively through a sequence of regression and clustering steps—where previously decoded latent states provide labels for later regression problems—and use it to construct good exploration policies. We provide finite-sample guarantees on the quality of the learned state decoding function and exploration policies, and complement our theory with an empirical evaluation on a class of hard exploration problems. Our method exponentially improves over $Q$-learning with naïve exploration, even when $Q$-learning has cheating access to latent states.

Our method exponentially improves over $Q$-learning with naïve exploration, even when $Q$-learning has cheating access to latent states.

paragraphs: An agent may receive complicated observations even when its environment has only a small number of underlying states. This paper studies exploration in episodic decision processes with that structure. The goal is to learn how observations correspond to hidden states and use the resulting representation to guide exploration effectively.

Under specified identifiability assumptions, the method builds a decoding function through successive regression and clustering steps. States decoded earlier supply labels for later regression problems, allowing the representation to develop inductively. The learned mapping is then used to construct exploration policies, directly connecting state identification with the agent’s ability to gather useful experience.

The authors provide finite-sample guarantees for both the decoding function and the exploration policies, alongside experiments on hard exploration problems. They report an exponential improvement over Q-learning with naive exploration, even when that comparator is given access to the true latent states. This comparison highlights the importance of exploration strategy alongside representation learning, within the structured setting and assumptions studied.
summary.tldr: Under identifiability assumptions, successive regression and clustering recover latent states and enable exploration with finite-sample guarantees.

title: Provably efficient RL with Rich Observations via Latent State Decoding

abstract: We introduce Compositional Imitation Learning and Execution (CompILE): a framework for learning reusable, variable-length segments of hierarchically-structured behavior from demonstration data. CompILE uses a novel unsupervised, fully-differentiable sequence segmentation module to learn latent encodings of sequential data that can be re-composed and executed to perform new tasks. Once trained, our model generalizes to sequences of longer length and from environment instances not seen during training. We evaluate CompILE in a challenging 2D multi-task environment and a continuous control task, and show that it can find correct task boundaries and event encodings in an unsupervised manner. Latent codes and associated behavior policies discovered by CompILE can be used by a hierarchical agent, where the high-level policy selects actions in the latent code space, and the low-level, task-specific policies are simply the learned decoders. We found that our CompILE-based agent could learn given only sparse rewards, where agents without task-specific policies struggle.

paragraphs: Demonstrated behavior can contain reusable pieces of different lengths, but their boundaries may not be labeled. CompILE learns these pieces from demonstration sequences using an unsupervised, fully differentiable segmentation module. It produces latent encodings that describe segments of hierarchically structured behavior and can be recombined to carry out new tasks.

The learned segments also provide a way to organize a hierarchical agent. A high-level policy chooses latent codes, while learned decoders act as the corresponding low-level behavior policies. This connects identifying structure in demonstrations with executing that structure: the discovered representations serve as selectable behaviors rather than only descriptions of recorded sequences.

In a challenging two-dimensional multitask environment and a continuous-control task, the authors report recovery of correct task boundaries and event encodings without supervision. They also report generalization to longer sequences and previously unseen environment instances. A CompILE-based agent learns with sparse rewards in settings where agents lacking task-specific policies struggle. These findings suggest that reusable behaviors extracted from demonstrations can provide useful building blocks for subsequent learning and execution.
summary.tldr: CompILE discovers reusable behavior segments in demonstrations and turns them into policies that can be recombined for new tasks.

title: CompILE: Compositional Imitation Learning and Execution

abstract: Predicting delayed outcomes is an important problem in recommender systems (e.g., if customers will finish reading an ebook). We formalize the problem as an adversarial, delayed online learning problem and consider how a proxy for the delayed outcome (e.g., if customers read a third of the book in 24 hours) can help minimize regret, even though the proxy is not available when making a prediction. Motivated by our regret analysis, we propose two neural network architectures: Factored Forecaster (FF) which is ideal if the proxy is informative of the outcome in hindsight, and Residual Factored Forecaster (RFF) that is robust to a non-informative proxy. Experiments on two real-world datasets for predicting human behavior show that RFF outperforms both FF and a direct forecaster that does not make use of the proxy. Our results suggest that exploiting proxies by factorization is a promising way to mitigate the impact of long delays in human-behavior prediction tasks.

paragraphs: A recommender may need to predict an outcome long before it becomes observable, such as whether someone will finish an ebook. Earlier behavior can provide a proxy for that eventual outcome. The paper asks how such proxies can help learning even when they are themselves unavailable at the moment a prediction is made.

The authors formalize the problem as adversarial online learning with delayed feedback and analyze regret. That analysis motivates two neural architectures. Factored Forecaster is suited to a proxy that proves informative about the outcome in hindsight. Residual Factored Forecaster is designed to remain robust when the proxy carries little useful information.

On two real-world datasets involving human-behavior prediction, Residual Factored Forecaster outperforms both Factored Forecaster and a direct predictor that does not use the proxy. The results suggest that factoring prediction through proxy information can help mitigate long outcome delays. They also highlight the value of an architecture that accommodates variation in how informative the available proxy actually is.
summary.tldr: Proxy-aware forecasting architectures help learn from delayed outcomes, with a residual variant outperforming both a factored and a direct predictor on two datasets.

title: Learning from Delayed Outcomes via Proxies with Applications to Recommender Systems

abstract: Constraining linear layers in neural networks to respect symmetry transformations from a group $G$ is a common design principle for invariant networks that has found many applications in machine learning. In this paper, we consider a fundamental question that has received very little attention to date: Can these networks approximate any (continuous) invariant function? We tackle the rather general case where $G\leq S_n$ (an arbitrary subgroup of the symmetric group) that acts on $\R^n$ by permuting coordinates. This setting includes several recent popular invariant networks. We present two main results: First, $G$-invariant networks are universal if high-order tensors are allowed. Second, there are groups $G$ for which higher-order tensors are unavoidable for obtaining universality. $G$-invariant networks consisting of only first-order tensors are of special interest due to their practical value. We conclude the paper by proving a necessary condition for the universality of $G$-invariant networks that incorporate only first-order tensors. Lastly, we propose a conjecture stating that this condition is also sufficient.

paragraphs: Invariant networks are designed to give the same output when an input undergoes specified symmetry transformations. This paper asks whether networks built from symmetry-respecting linear layers can approximate every continuous invariant function. It considers groups that act by permuting input coordinates, covering an arbitrary subgroup of the symmetric group.

The first main result establishes universality when the network is allowed to use higher-order tensors. The second shows that these richer representations are essential for some groups: restricting the network to first-order tensors can prevent universality. Thus, enforcing the desired symmetry alone does not settle whether an architecture has enough expressive power.

Because first-order representations are practically attractive, the authors also prove a necessary condition for universality in that restricted setting. They conjecture that the condition is sufficient as well, but do not present that sufficiency as a theorem. The paper therefore establishes both a general route to universality and a sharper boundary around what simpler invariant architectures can express.
summary.tldr: Permutation-invariant networks are universal with higher-order tensors, and some symmetry groups require those tensors to achieve universality.

title: On the Universality of Invariant Networks

abstract: Human decision-making underlies all economic behavior. For the past four decades, human decision-making under uncertainty has continued to be explained by theoretical models based on prospect theory, a framework that was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences. However, theoretical models of this kind have developed slowly, and robust, high-precision predictive models of human decisions remain a challenge. While machine learning is a natural candidate for solving these problems, it is currently unclear to what extent it can improve predictions obtained by current theories. We argue that this is mainly due to data scarcity, since noisy human behavior requires massive sample sizes to be accurately captured by off-the-shelf machine learning methods. To solve this problem, what is needed are machine learning models with appropriate inductive biases for capturing human behavior, and larger datasets. We offer two contributions towards this end: first, we construct “cognitive model priors” by pretraining neural networks with synthetic data generated by cognitive models (i.e., theoretical models developed by cognitive psychologists). We find that fine-tuning these networks on small datasets of real human decisions results in unprecedented state-of-the-art improvements on two benchmark datasets. Second, we present the first large-scale dataset for human decision-making, containing over 240,000 human judgments across over 13,000 decision problems. This dataset reveals the circumstances where cognitive model priors are useful, and provides a new standard for benchmarking prediction of human decisions under uncertainty.

paragraphs: Predicting human choices under uncertainty is difficult because behavior is noisy and datasets can be small. The authors argue that this scarcity helps explain why ordinary machine learning has struggled to establish clear gains over theories of decision-making. title: Cognitive model priors for predicting human decisions

abstract: We consider estimating a high-dimensional vector from non-linear measurements where the unknown vector is represented by a generative model $G:\mathbb{R}^k\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^d$ with $k\ll d$. Such a model poses structural priors on the unknown vector without having a dedicated basis, and in particular allows new and efficient approaches solving recovery problems with number of measurements far less than the ambient dimension of the vector. While progresses have been made recently regarding theoretical understandings on the linear Gaussian measurements, much less is known when the model is possibly misspecified and the measurements are non-Gaussian. In this paper, we make a step towards such a direction by considering the scenario where the measurements are non-Gaussian, subject to possibly unknown nonlinear transformations and the responses are heavy-tailed. We then propose new estimators via score functions based on the first and second order Stein’s identity, and prove the sample size bound of $m=\mathcal{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2}\log(L/\varepsilon))$ achieving an $\varepsilon$ error in the form of exponential concentration inequalities. Furthermore, for the special case of multi-layer ReLU generative model, we improve the sample bound by a logarithm factor to $m=\mathcal{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d))$, matching the state-of-art statistical rate in compressed sensing for estimating $k$-sparse vectors. On the technical side, we develop new chaining methods bounding heavy-tailed processes, which could be of independent interest.

The challenge is to recover the vector when measurements are non-Gaussian, may undergo unknown nonlinear transformations, and produce heavy-tailed responses.

The authors construct estimators using score functions and first- and second-order Stein identities. This matches the stated statistical rate for recovering k-sparse vectors in compressed sensing. The analysis also develops chaining methods for bounding heavy-tailed processes, contributing theoretical tools alongside the recovery estimators.
summary.tldr: Score-based estimators provide recovery guarantees for generative signal models with nonlinear, non-Gaussian measurements and heavy-tailed responses.

title: On the statistical rate of nonlinear recovery in generative models with heavy-tailed data

abstract: Distance metric learning (DML) is to learn a representation space equipped with a metric, such that similar examples are closer than dissimilar examples concerning the metric. The recent success of DNNs motivates many DML losses that encourage the intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. The trade-off between inter-class compactness and inter-class separability shapes the DML representation space by determining how much information of the original inputs to retain. In this paper, we propose a Distance Metric Learning with Joint Representation Diversification (JRD) that allows a better balancing point between intra-class compactness and inter-class separability. Specifically, we propose a Joint Representation Similarity regularizer that captures different abstract levels of invariant features and diversifies the joint distributions of representations across multiple layers. Experiments on three deep DML benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Distance metric learning builds a representation in which similar examples lie closer together than dissimilar ones. Neural approaches often encourage examples from the same class to cluster tightly while separating different classes. These objectives shape how much information from the original inputs survives in the learned space, making their balance a central design issue.

The paper proposes Joint Representation Diversification to obtain a better balance between within-class compactness and between-class separation. Its main mechanism is a Joint Representation Similarity regularizer. This regularizer works across multiple network layers, capturing invariant features at different levels of abstraction and diversifying the joint distributions of those representations.

Considering multiple layers gives the method access to different levels of learned information when shaping the final distance space. Experiments on three deep metric learning benchmarks support the effectiveness of the approach. The stated finding is that this form of representation diversification improves the balance pursued by metric learning in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: A regularizer spanning multiple network layers improves the balance between keeping similar examples close and separating different classes in the evaluated metric learning tasks.

title: Distance Metric Learning with Joint Representation Diversification

abstract: This paper presents a recursive reasoning formalism of Bayesian optimization (BO) to model the reasoning process in the interactions between boundedly rational, self-interested agents with unknown, complex, and costly-to-evaluate payoff functions in repeated games, which we call Recursive Reasoning-Based BO (R2-B2). Our R2-B2 algorithm is general in that it does not constrain the relationship among the payoff functions of different agents and can thus be applied to various types of games such as constant-sum, general-sum, and common-payoff games. We prove that by reasoning at level 2 or more and at one level higher than the other agents, our R2-B2 agent can achieve faster asymptotic convergence to no regret than that without utilizing recursive reasoning. We also propose a computationally cheaper variant of R2-B2 called R2-B2-Lite at the expense of a weaker convergence guarantee. The performance and generality of our R2-B2 algorithm are empirically demonstrated using synthetic games, adversarial machine learning, and multi-agent reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: R2-B2 combines Bayesian optimization with recursive reasoning in repeated games. It addresses agents whose payoff functions are unknown, complex, and expensive to evaluate. Recursive reasoning models how an agent accounts for other agents' reasoning while making its own decisions, with the agents treated as boundedly rational and self-interested.

The framework does not impose a particular relationship between different agents' payoffs. It can therefore cover constant-sum, general-sum, and common-payoff games. The authors prove faster asymptotic convergence to no regret than without recursive reasoning when an agent reasons at level two or higher and exactly one level above the other agents. The improvement is conditional on that reasoning relationship.

A cheaper variant, R2-B2-Lite, reduces computation at the cost of a weaker convergence guarantee. Experiments involving synthetic games, adversarial machine learning, and multi-agent reinforcement learning demonstrate the method's performance and breadth. The paper thus connects strategic reasoning depth with learning efficiency, while making the tradeoff between computational cost and theoretical guarantees explicit.
summary.tldr: R2-B2 combines recursive reasoning and Bayesian optimization, proving faster no-regret convergence under a specific advantage in reasoning depth.

title: R2-B2: Recursive Reasoning-Based Bayesian Optimization for No-Regret Learning in Games

abstract: We study local SGD (also known as parallel SGD and federated SGD), a natural and frequently used distributed optimization method. Its theoretical foundations are currently lacking and we highlight how all existing error guarantees in the convex setting are dominated by a simple baseline, minibatch SGD. (1) For quadratic objectives we prove that local SGD strictly dominates minibatch SGD and that accelerated local SGD is minmax optimal for quadratics; (2) For general convex objectives we provide the first guarantee that at least \emph{sometimes} improves over minibatch SGD, but our guarantee does not always improve over, nor even match, minibatch SGD; (3) We show that indeed local SGD does \emph{not} dominate minibatch SGD by presenting a lower bound on the performance of local SGD that is worse than the minibatch SGD guarantee.

paragraphs: Local SGD is a widely used distributed optimization method, also called parallel or federated SGD. This paper asks whether its theoretical performance improves on the simpler minibatch SGD baseline. It begins by observing that existing convex-setting guarantees for local SGD were dominated by guarantees for that baseline.

The answer depends on the objective being optimized. For quadratic objectives, the authors prove that local SGD strictly dominates minibatch SGD. They also show that an accelerated local version is minimax optimal for quadratics, establishing a best-possible worst-case result within that setting. These conclusions provide a strong positive case for local updates on this class of problems.

For general convex objectives, the picture is mixed. A new guarantee sometimes improves on minibatch SGD, but does not always improve on or even match it. A lower bound further establishes that local SGD cannot universally dominate the baseline. The contribution therefore distinguishes a setting with a clear advantage from a broader setting where that advantage cannot be assumed.
summary.tldr: Local SGD provably outperforms minibatch SGD for quadratic objectives, but does not dominate it across general convex problems.

title: Is Local SGD Better than Minibatch SGD?

abstract: We propose a transductive Laplacian-regularized inference for few-shot tasks. Given any feature embedding learned from the base classes, we minimize a quadratic binary-assignment function containing two terms: (1) a unary term assigning query samples to the nearest class prototype, and (2) a pairwise Laplacian term encouraging nearby query samples to have consistent label assignments. Our transductive inference does not re-train the base model, and can be viewed as a graph clustering of the query set, subject to supervision constraints from the support set. We derive a computationally efficient bound optimizer of a relaxation of our function, which computes independent (parallel) updates for each query sample, while guaranteeing convergence. Following a simple cross-entropy training on the base classes, and without complex meta-learning strategies, we conducted comprehensive experiments over five few-shot learning benchmarks. Our LaplacianShot consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significant margins across different models, settings, and data sets. Furthermore, our transductive inference is very fast, with computational times that are close to inductive inference, and can be used for large-scale few-shot tasks.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification uses a small labeled support set to classify new query samples. LaplacianShot treats the queries jointly through transductive inference, using relationships among them as well as their proximity to known classes. It operates on a feature embedding learned from base classes and does not retrain that base model during inference.

The assignment objective has two parts. One favors assigning each query to its nearest class prototype; the other encourages nearby queries to receive consistent labels. Together, they form a graph-clustering view of the query set, guided by the labeled support examples. The authors relax the assignment problem and derive an efficient bound optimizer with independent, parallel query updates and a convergence guarantee.

Using ordinary cross-entropy training on base classes, the method is evaluated across five few-shot benchmarks. The reported results consistently exceed state-of-the-art methods across models, settings, and datasets. Inference times are close to those of inductive inference, supporting use on large-scale few-shot tasks. The findings highlight the value of organizing query predictions jointly without requiring complex meta-learning procedures.
summary.tldr: LaplacianShot improves few-shot classification by jointly assigning query labels using class prototypes and neighborhood consistency.

title: Laplacian Regularized Few-Shot Learning

abstract: There has been a recent surge of interest in non-parametric bandit algorithms based on subsampling. One drawback however of these approaches is the additional complexity required by random subsampling and the storage of the full history of rewards. Our first contribution is to show that a simple deterministic subsampling rule, proposed in the recent work of \citet{baudry2020sub} under the name of “last-block subsampling”, is asymptotically optimal in one-parameter exponential families. In addition, we prove that these guarantees also hold when limiting the algorithm memory to a polylogarithmic function of the time horizon. These findings open up new perspectives, in particular for non-stationary scenarios in which the arm distributions evolve over time. We propose a variant of the algorithm in which only the most recent observations are used for subsampling, achieving optimal regret guarantees under the assumption of a known number of abrupt changes. Extensive numerical simulations highlight the merits of this approach, particularly when the changes are not only affecting the means of the rewards.

paragraphs: Subsampling-based bandit algorithms can avoid specifying a full parametric reward model, but random subsampling and storing all past rewards add complexity. This paper studies a simpler deterministic rule called last-block subsampling. It asks whether this approach can retain strong learning guarantees while reducing the amount of history that must be kept.

The authors prove asymptotic optimality for one-parameter exponential families. They also show that the guarantees survive when memory grows only as a polylogarithmic function of the time horizon. This establishes that, in the analyzed setting, keeping the complete reward history is unnecessary for the stated long-run performance.

The paper then considers changing reward distributions and proposes a variant that subsamples only recent observations. Under the assumption that the number of abrupt changes is known, it achieves optimal regret guarantees. Numerical simulations highlight the approach’s strengths, particularly when changes affect aspects of reward distributions beyond their means. The stationary and changing-environment results each retain their stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Deterministic last-block subsampling retains optimal bandit guarantees with limited memory and supports a variant for abruptly changing rewards.

title: On Limited-Memory Subsampling Strategies for Bandits

abstract: Hierarchical topic models such as the gamma belief network (GBN) have delivered promising results in mining multi-layer document representations and discovering interpretable topic taxonomies. However, they often assume in the prior that the topics at each layer are independently drawn from the Dirichlet distribution, ignoring the dependencies between the topics both at the same layer and across different layers. To relax this assumption, we propose sawtooth factorial topic embedding guided GBN, a deep generative model of documents that captures the dependencies and semantic similarities between the topics in the embedding space. Specifically, both the words and topics are represented as embedding vectors of the same dimension. The topic matrix at a layer is factorized into the product of a factor loading matrix and a topic embedding matrix, the transpose of which is set as the factor loading matrix of the layer above. Repeating this particular type of factorization, which shares components between adjacent layers, leads to a structure referred to as sawtooth factorization. An auto-encoding variational inference network is constructed to optimize the model parameter via stochastic gradient descent. Experiments on big corpora show that our models outperform other neural topic models on extracting deeper interpretable topics and deriving better document representations.

This paper introduces a gamma belief network guided by topic embeddings to capture those dependencies and the semantic similarities among topics.

The contribution makes relationships among hierarchical topics part of the model’s parameterization, with empirical benefits for both interpreting the hierarchy and representing documents.
summary.tldr: Shared word and topic embeddings connect adjacent layers of a gamma belief network, improving hierarchical topics and document representations.

title: Sawtooth Factorial Topic Embeddings Guided Gamma Belief Network

abstract: We study off-policy evaluation (OPE) from multiple logging policies, each generating a dataset of fixed size, i.e., stratified sampling. Previous work noted that in this setting the ordering of the variances of different importance sampling estimators is instance-dependent, which brings up a dilemma as to which importance sampling weights to use. In this paper, we resolve this dilemma by finding the OPE estimator for multiple loggers with minimum variance for any instance, i.e., the efficient one. In particular, we establish the efficiency bound under stratified sampling and propose an estimator achieving this bound when given consistent $q$-estimates. To guard against misspecification of $q$-functions, we also provide a way to choose the control variate in a hypothesis class to minimize variance. Extensive experiments demonstrate the benefits of our methods’ efficiently leveraging of the stratified sampling of off-policy data from multiple loggers.

paragraphs: The paper studies policy evaluation when several logging policies each contribute a dataset of fixed size. This is stratified sampling, and its structure affects estimator variance. Previous work found that the relative performance of importance sampling estimators depends on the instance, leaving no simple universal choice among their weighting schemes.

The authors establish an efficiency bound for this sampling setup and propose an estimator that achieves it when supplied with consistent q-estimates. This identifies the minimum-variance target and gives a conditional route to reaching it. The consistency requirement matters because the efficiency claim depends on the quality of these estimates.

The paper also addresses possible q-function misspecification by providing a way to select a control variate from a hypothesis class to minimize variance. Extensive experiments demonstrate benefits from explicitly exploiting the fixed-size contributions of multiple loggers. The broader lesson is that how logged data were collected is part of the estimation problem: respecting the stratified structure can improve statistical efficiency.
summary.tldr: An estimator exploits stratified data from multiple logging policies to attain the efficiency bound when given consistent q-estimates.

title: Optimal Off-Policy Evaluation from Multiple Logging Policies

abstract: In the deep learning era, the vast majority of methods to predict pose from a single image are trained to classify or regress to a single given ground truth pose per image. Such methods have two main shortcomings, i) they cannot represent uncertainty about the predictions, and ii) they cannot handle symmetric objects, where multiple (potentially infinite) poses may be correct. Only recently these shortcomings have been addressed, but current approaches as limited in that they cannot express the full rich space of distributions on the rotation manifold. To this end, we introduce a method to estimate arbitrary, non-parametric distributions on SO(3). Our key idea is to represent the distributions implicitly, with a neural network that estimates the probability density, given the input image and a candidate pose. At inference time, grid sampling or gradient ascent can be used to find the most likely pose, but it is also possible to evaluate the density at any pose, enabling reasoning about symmetries and uncertainty. This is the most general way of representing distributions on manifolds, and to demonstrate its expressive power we introduce a new dataset containing symmetric and nearly-symmetric objects. Our method also shows advantages on the popular object pose estimation benchmarks ModelNet10-SO(3) and T-LESS. Code, data, and visualizations may be found at implicit-pdf.github.io.

paragraphs: Predicting one pose from an image can hide uncertainty and mishandle symmetry. A symmetric object may have several, or even infinitely many, valid orientations. This paper represents a probability distribution over three-dimensional rotations so that the output can express the range of plausible poses instead of committing all of its information to one estimate.

The method uses a neural network that accepts an image and a candidate rotation, then estimates the probability density at that rotation. This implicit representation is designed to express arbitrary non-parametric distributions on SO(3), the space of rotations. Grid sampling or gradient ascent can identify a most likely pose, while density queries retain information about alternative poses.

The authors introduce a dataset of symmetric and nearly symmetric objects to demonstrate this expressiveness. They also report advantages on ModelNet10-SO(3) and T-LESS. The approach matters because pose selection and uncertainty representation share one model: a system can seek a likely orientation while also examining how symmetry or ambiguity distributes probability across other orientations.
summary.tldr: Implicit-PDF learns flexible probability densities over rotations, enabling image-based pose estimation that represents symmetry and uncertainty.

title: Implicit-PDF: Non-Parametric Representation of Probability Distributions on the Rotation Manifold

abstract: The design of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to accurately process sequential inputs with long-time dependencies is very challenging on account of the exploding and vanishing gradient problem. To overcome this, we propose a novel RNN architecture which is based on a structure preserving discretization of a Hamiltonian system of second-order ordinary differential equations that models networks of oscillators. The resulting RNN is fast, invertible (in time), memory efficient and we derive rigorous bounds on the hidden state gradients to prove the mitigation of the exploding and vanishing gradient problem. A suite of experiments are presented to demonstrate that the proposed RNN provides state of the art performance on a variety of learning tasks with (very) long-time dependencies.

To overcome this, we propose a novel RNN architecture which is based on a structure preserving discretization of a Hamiltonian system of second-order ordinary differential equations that models networks of oscillators. The resulting RNN is fast, invertible (in time), memory efficient and we derive rigorous bounds on the hidden state gradients to prove the mitigation of the exploding and vanishing gradient problem. A suite of experiments are presented to demonstrate that the proposed RNN provides state of the art performance on a variety of learning tasks with (very) long-time dependencies.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks struggle with long sequences when gradients either shrink away or grow excessively. This makes it difficult to learn relationships between inputs separated by many time steps. UnICORNN addresses the problem through an architecture derived from a Hamiltonian system of second-order differential equations modeling a network of oscillators.

The authors convert that continuous-time system into recurrent updates using a structure-preserving discretization. The resulting network is fast, memory efficient, and invertible in time. They also derive rigorous bounds on hidden-state gradients, using those bounds to prove mitigation of the exploding and vanishing gradient problem. The architecture therefore comes with an analysis tied directly to the difficulty it is designed to address.

A suite of experiments demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on several learning tasks with very long dependencies. These findings support the usefulness of the oscillator-based construction for the evaluated sequence problems. The contribution combines a physically motivated recurrent design, gradient control, and computational properties that matter when processing extended sequences.
summary.tldr: UnICORNN uses structure-preserving oscillator dynamics to mitigate gradient problems and learn very long sequence dependencies.

title: UnICORNN: A recurrent model for learning very long time dependencies

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is rapidly closing the gap with supervised methods on large computer vision benchmarks. A successful approach to SSL is to learn embeddings which are invariant to distortions of the input sample. However, a recurring issue with this approach is the existence of trivial constant solutions. Most current methods avoid such solutions by careful implementation details. We propose an objective function that naturally avoids collapse by measuring the cross-correlation matrix between the outputs of two identical networks fed with distorted versions of a sample, and making it as close to the identity matrix as possible. This causes the embedding vectors of distorted versions of a sample to be similar, while minimizing the redundancy between the components of these vectors. The method is called Barlow Twins, owing to neuroscientist H. Barlow’s redundancy-reduction principle applied to a pair of identical networks. Barlow Twins does not require large batches nor asymmetry between the network twins such as a predictor network, gradient stopping, or a moving average on the weight updates. Intriguingly it benefits from very high-dimensional output vectors. Barlow Twins outperforms previous methods on ImageNet for semi-supervised classification in the low-data regime, and is on par with current state of the art for ImageNet classification with a linear classifier head, and for transfer tasks of classification and object detection.

The challenge is to make their representations agree without letting the network produce the same constant output for every image. Such a constant solution would satisfy agreement while discarding the information that makes the representation useful.

The method measures cross-correlations between the outputs of two identical networks and pushes the resulting matrix toward the identity matrix. This encourages corresponding representation components to agree across views while reducing overlap in the information carried by different components. The objective therefore combines consistency under image distortion with reduced redundancy inside the representation.

It improves on previous methods for ImageNet semi-supervised classification with little labeled data, while matching leading performance for linear classification and transfer to classification and object detection.
summary.tldr: Barlow Twins learns useful image representations by making distorted views agree while reducing redundancy between representation components.

title: Barlow Twins: Self-Supervised Learning via Redundancy Reduction

abstract: We introduce two new no-regret algorithms for the stochastic shortest path (SSP) problem with a linear MDP that significantly improve over the only existing results of (Vial et al., 2021). Our first algorithm is computationally efficient and achieves a regret bound $O(\sqrt{d^3B_{\star}^2T_{\star} K})$, where $d$ is the dimension of the feature space, $B_{\star}$ and $T_{\star}$ are upper bounds of the expected costs and hitting time of the optimal policy respectively, and $K$ is the number of episodes. The same algorithm with a slight modification also achieves logarithmic regret of order $O(\frac{d^3B_{\star}^4}{c_{\min}^2\text{\rm gap}_{\min} }\ln^5\frac{dB_{\star} K}{c_{\min}})$, where $\text{\rm gap}_{\min}$ is the minimum sub-optimality gap and $c_{\min}$ is the minimum cost over all state-action pairs. Our result is obtained by developing a simpler and improved analysis for the finite-horizon approximation of (Cohen et al., 2021) with a smaller approximation error, which might be of independent interest. On the other hand, using variance-aware confidence sets in a global optimization problem, our second algorithm is computationally inefficient but achieves the first “horizon-free” regret bound $O(d^{3.5}B_{\star}\sqrt{K})$ with no polynomial dependency on $T_{\star}$ or $1/c_{\min}$, almost matching the $\Omega(dB_{\star}\sqrt{K})$ lower bound from (Min et al., 2021).

Its regret grows with the square root of the number of episodes, with additional dependence on feature dimension, optimal expected cost, and optimal expected time to reach the goal. A modification gives a logarithmic-type bound involving the minimum suboptimality gap and minimum state-action cost. The analysis improves the accuracy of a finite-horizon approximation used to handle the original problem.

The second algorithm uses confidence sets that account for variance within a global optimization problem. It is computationally inefficient, but its regret bound has no polynomial dependence on optimal hitting time or inverse minimum cost. This separates two achievements: an efficient method with stronger guarantees than earlier results, and a horizon-free theoretical bound that approaches the stated lower bound while retaining a gap in its dependence on feature dimension.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms improve regret guarantees for linear stochastic shortest path problems, including a computationally inefficient method with a horizon-free bound.

title: Improved No-Regret Algorithms for Stochastic Shortest Path with Linear MDP

abstract: Given a new dataset D and a low compute budget, how should we choose a pre-trained model to fine-tune to D, and set the fine-tuning hyperparameters without risking overfitting, particularly if D is small? Here, we extend automated machine learning (AutoML) to best make these choices. Our domain-independent meta-learning approach learns a zero-shot surrogate model which, at test time, allows to select the right deep learning (DL) pipeline (including the pre-trained model and fine-tuning hyperparameters) for a new dataset D given only trivial meta-features describing D such as image resolution or the number of classes. To train this zero-shot model, we collect performance data for many DL pipelines on a large collection of datasets and meta-train on this data to minimize a pairwise ranking objective. We evaluate our approach under the strict time limit of the vision track of the ChaLearn AutoDL challenge benchmark, clearly outperforming all challenge contenders.

paragraphs: Choosing a pretrained model and fine-tuning settings can be expensive when a new dataset comes with a small compute budget. Repeated experimentation is also a concern for small datasets. This paper proposes learning how to make those choices from experience collected across many previous datasets.

The method trains a surrogate model using performance measurements from many deep-learning pipelines. Each pipeline includes a pretrained model and fine-tuning hyperparameters. A pairwise ranking objective teaches the surrogate which pipelines are preferable. For a new dataset, selection requires only simple descriptive features, such as image resolution or the number of classes.

The zero-shot aspect concerns selecting the pipeline from those dataset descriptions; the selected pipeline still includes fine-tuning. Under the strict time budget of the ChaLearn AutoDL vision benchmark, the approach clearly outperforms all challenge contenders. The result supports transferring knowledge about pipeline performance across datasets as a practical way to make model-selection decisions when extensive new experimentation is costly.
summary.tldr: A meta-learned ranking model selects pretrained models and fine-tuning settings using only simple descriptions of a new dataset.

title: Zero-shot AutoML with Pretrained Models

abstract: The communication bottleneck has been a critical problem in large-scale distributed deep learning. In this work, we study distributed SGD with random block-wise sparsification as the gradient compressor, which is ring-allreduce compatible and highly computation-efficient but leads to inferior performance. To tackle this important issue, we improve the communication-efficient distributed SGD from a novel aspect, that is, the trade-off between the variance and second moment of the gradient. With this motivation, we propose a new detached error feedback (DEF) algorithm, which shows better convergence bound than error feedback for non-convex problems. We also propose DEF-A to accelerate the generalization of DEF at the early stages of the training, which shows better generalization bounds than DEF. Furthermore, we establish the connection between communication-efficient distributed SGD and SGD with iterate averaging (SGD-IA) for the first time. Extensive deep learning experiments show significant empirical improvement of the proposed methods under various settings. Our reproducible codes and scripts for all experiments in this work will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial effort communicating gradients between workers. Random block-wise sparsification reduces that traffic and fits ring-allreduce communication, but its computational convenience comes with poorer learning performance. This paper examines how to improve distributed SGD using this compressor by reconsidering the balance between gradient variance and the gradient’s second moment.

The resulting algorithm, detached error feedback, or DEF, has a better convergence bound than error feedback for non-convex problems. The authors also introduce DEF-A to improve generalization early in training. Their analysis gives DEF-A better generalization bounds than DEF, distinguishing the basic method’s convergence contribution from the accelerated variant’s generalization contribution.

The paper further establishes a connection between communication-efficient distributed SGD and SGD with iterate averaging. This relates compressed distributed training to another way of organizing the optimization process. Extensive deep learning experiments show substantial empirical improvements across multiple settings. The contribution therefore combines improved theoretical bounds, a conceptual connection to averaging, and practical evidence that the proposed corrections help training under gradient compression.
summary.tldr: Detached error feedback improves theoretical and empirical behavior of distributed SGD with random block sparsification, with a variant targeting early generalization.

title: Detached Error Feedback for Distributed SGD with Random Sparsification

abstract: While leveraging additional training data is well established to improve adversarial robustness, it incurs the unavoidable cost of data collection and the heavy computation to train models. To mitigate the costs, we propose *Guided Adversarial Training * (GAT), a novel adversarial training technique that exploits auxiliary tasks under a limited set of training data. Our approach extends single-task models into multi-task models during the min-max optimization of adversarial training, and drives the loss optimization with a regularization of the gradient curvature across multiple tasks. GAT leverages two types of auxiliary tasks: self-supervised tasks, where the labels are generated automatically, and domain-knowledge tasks, where human experts provide additional labels. Experimentally, under limited data, GAT increases the robust accuracy on CIFAR-10 up to four times (from 11% to 42% robust accuracy) and the robust AUC of CheXpert medical imaging dataset from 50% to 83%. On the full CIFAR-10 dataset, GAT outperforms eight state-of-the-art adversarial training strategies. Our large study across five datasets and six tasks demonstrates that task augmentation is an efficient alternative to data augmentation, and can be key to achieving both clean and robust performances.

paragraphs: Adversarial training seeks models that remain accurate under adversarial perturbations, but improving robustness with additional data can be expensive. Guided Adversarial Training, or GAT, instead adds learning tasks to a limited training dataset. The idea is to obtain more useful supervision from available examples while reducing reliance on collecting additional examples.

GAT turns a single-task model into a multitask model during adversarial training's min-max optimization. It guides optimization through a regularizer involving gradient curvature across tasks. Auxiliary tasks come from two sources: self-supervised tasks with automatically generated labels, and tasks based on domain knowledge with labels supplied by human experts.

Under limited data, the reported CIFAR-10 robust accuracy rises from 11% to 42%, while CheXpert robust AUC rises from 50% to 83%. On full CIFAR-10, GAT outperforms eight state-of-the-art adversarial training strategies. Across five datasets and six tasks, the results support task augmentation as an efficient alternative to data augmentation and as a possible way to improve both ordinary and adversarial performance.
summary.tldr: GAT uses auxiliary tasks to improve adversarial robustness, with substantial reported gains when training data is limited.

title: GAT: Guided Adversarial Training with Pareto-optimal Auxiliary Tasks

abstract: Understanding the gradient variance of black-box variational inference (BBVI) is a crucial step for establishing its convergence and developing algorithmic improvements. However, existing studies have yet to show that the gradient variance of BBVI satisfies the conditions used to study the convergence of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), the workhorse of BBVI. In this work, we show that BBVI satisfies a matching bound corresponding to the ABC condition used in the SGD literature when applied to smooth and quadratically-growing log-likelihoods. Our results generalize to nonlinear covariance parameterizations widely used in the practice of BBVI. Furthermore, we show that the variance of the mean-field parameterization has provably superior dimensional dependence.

paragraphs: Black-box variational inference uses stochastic gradient descent to fit an approximate Bayesian distribution. Understanding how much its gradient estimates fluctuate is important for proving convergence and improving algorithms. This paper addresses a gap between existing analyses of those fluctuations and the conditions used in stochastic-gradient convergence theory.

The authors establish a matching bound corresponding to the ABC condition from the stochastic-gradient literature. The result applies when log-likelihoods are smooth and grow quadratically. These are substantive conditions on the inference problem: they define the setting in which the paper connects gradient variance to the convergence-analysis framework. The contribution supplies a theoretical bridge between BBVI and the optimization method commonly used to train it.

The analysis also extends to nonlinear ways of parameterizing covariance, which are widely used in practical BBVI. In addition, the authors prove that a mean-field parameterization has better dimensional dependence in its variance. This identifies a theoretical advantage in how gradient noise scales with dimension, alongside the broader result connecting practical variational parameterizations to established optimization conditions.
summary.tldr: For smooth, quadratically growing log-likelihoods, BBVI satisfies a matching gradient-variance bound tied to SGD theory, with favorable dimensional scaling for mean-field parameterizations.

title: Practical and Matching Gradient Variance Bounds for Black-Box Variational Bayesian Inference

abstract: Neural architectures that learn potential energy surfaces from molecular data have undergone fast improvement in recent years. A key driver of this success is the Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) paradigm. Its favorable scaling with system size partly relies upon a spatial distance limit on messages. While this focus on locality is a useful inductive bias, it also impedes the learning of long-range interactions such as electrostatics and van der Waals forces. To address this drawback, we propose Ewald message passing: a nonlocal Fourier space scheme which limits interactions via a cutoff on frequency instead of distance, and is theoretically well-founded in the Ewald summation method. It can serve as an augmentation on top of existing MPNN architectures as it is computationally inexpensive and agnostic to architectural details. We test the approach with four baseline models and two datasets containing diverse periodic (OC20) and aperiodic structures (OE62). Across all models and datasets, we observe robust improvements in energy mean absolute errors, averaging 10% on OC20 and 16% on OE62. Our analysis shows an outsize impact of these improvements on structures with high long-range contributions to the ground-truth energy.

That local focus can make it harder to learn interactions acting over longer distances, including electrostatic and van der Waals effects. This paper adds a way for molecular models to represent those distant influences when predicting energy.

Ewald message passing operates in Fourier space and limits interactions by frequency rather than by physical distance. The construction draws theoretical support from Ewald summation. It is designed as an inexpensive addition to existing message-passing networks without depending on their architectural details, so the proposed long-range component can complement established local modeling.

summary.tldr: Ewald message passing adds inexpensive long-range interactions to molecular networks, reducing energy errors across the tested models and datasets.

title: Ewald-based Long-Range Message Passing for Molecular Graphs

abstract: There are strong incentives to build classification systems that show outstanding performance on various datasets and benchmarks. This can encourage a narrow focus on models and the performance metrics used to evaluate and compare them—resulting in a growing body of literature to evaluate and compare metrics . This paper strives for a more balanced perspective on binary classifier performance metrics by showing how uncertainty in these metrics can easily eclipse differences in empirical performance. We emphasise the discrete nature of confusion matrices and show how they can be well represented in a 3D lattice whose cross-sections form the space of receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. We develop novel interactive visualisations of performance metric contours within (and beyond) ROC space, showing the discrete probability mass functions of true and false positive rates and how these relate to performance metric distributions. We aim to raise awareness of the substantial uncertainty in performance metric estimates that can arise when classifiers are evaluated on empirical datasets and benchmarks, and that performance claims should be tempered by this understanding.

paragraphs: A small difference between two measured classification scores can look meaningful even when uncertainty in those scores is much larger. This paper develops visual tools for understanding that problem in binary classification. Its focus is how performance estimates vary when they are calculated from empirical datasets and benchmarks.

The authors emphasize that confusion matrices consist of discrete counts. They represent these matrices on a three-dimensional lattice, with cross-sections corresponding to receiver operating characteristic space. This geometric view connects the possible count combinations to familiar ways of displaying classifier performance, while keeping the underlying discreteness visible.

These are connected to distributions of performance metrics themselves. The purpose is to put observed score differences in perspective: uncertainty can eclipse those differences, so a higher measured value does not by itself establish a convincing performance advantage. The paper encourages claims calibrated to that uncertainty rather than attention to metric values alone.
summary.tldr: Interactive confusion-matrix visualizations show how uncertainty in classification metrics can outweigh observed performance differences.

title: Never mind the metrics---what about the uncertainty? Visualising binary confusion matrix metric distributions to put performance in perspective

abstract: Generative Flow Networks or GFlowNets are related to Monte-Carlo Markov chain methods (as they sample from a distribution specified by an energy function), reinforcement learning (as they learn a policy to sample composed objects through a sequence of steps), generative models (as they learn to represent and sample from a distribution) and amortized variational methods (as they can be used to learn to approximate and sample from an otherwise intractable posterior, given a prior and a likelihood). They are trained to generate an object $x$ through a sequence of steps with probability proportional to some reward function $R(x)$ (or $\exp(-\mathcal{E}(x))$ with $\mathcal{E}(x)$ denoting the energy function), given at the end of the generative trajectory. Like for other RL settings where the reward is only given at the end, the efficiency of training and credit assignment may suffer when those trajectories are longer. With previous GFlowNet work, no learning was possible from incomplete trajectories (lacking a terminal state and the computation of the associated reward). In this paper, we consider the case where the energy function can be applied not just to terminal states but also to intermediate states. This is for example achieved when the energy function is additive, with terms available along the trajectory. We show how to reparameterize the GFlowNet state flow function to take advantage of the partial reward already accrued at each state. This enables a training objective that can be applied to update parameters even with incomplete trajectories. Even when complete trajectories are available, being able to obtain more localized credit and gradients is found to speed up training convergence, as demonstrated across many simulations.

paragraphs: GFlowNets build objects through sequences of decisions and learn to sample completed objects in proportion to their rewards. When a reward appears only at the end, training must work out which earlier decisions deserve credit. Longer sequences make this harder, and previous GFlowNet methods could not learn from sequences that stopped before a terminal reward was available.

This paper considers a specific opportunity: the energy function can also be evaluated at intermediate states. An additive energy, whose terms become available as construction proceeds, is one example. The authors change the parameterization of the state flow function so it incorporates the partial reward already accumulated. The central advance is therefore a way to use available partial reward information both to expand which trajectories support learning and to make learning from finished trajectories more efficient.
summary.tldr: When intermediate energies are available, GFlowNets can learn from unfinished trajectories and converge faster through more local credit assignment.

title: Better Training of GFlowNets with Local Credit and Incomplete Trajectories

abstract: Diffusion models have found widespread adoption in various areas. However, their sampling process is slow because it requires hundreds to thousands of network evaluations to emulate a continuous process defined by differential equations. In this work, we use neural operators, an efficient method to solve the probability flow differential equations, to accelerate the sampling process of diffusion models. Compared to other fast sampling methods that have a sequential nature, we are the first to propose a parallel decoding method that generates images with only one model forward pass. We propose diffusion model sampling with neural operator (DSNO) that maps the initial condition, i.e., Gaussian distribution, to the continuous-time solution trajectory of the reverse diffusion process. To model the temporal correlations along the trajectory, we introduce temporal convolution layers that are parameterized in the Fourier space into the given diffusion model backbone. We show our method achieves state-of-the-art FID of 3.78 for CIFAR-10 and 7.83 for ImageNet-64 in the one-model-evaluation setting.

Compared to other fast sampling methods that have a sequential nature, we are the first to propose a parallel decoding method that generates images with only one model forward pass. paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples through a process described by differential equations, but emulating that process can require hundreds or thousands of network evaluations. This paper targets that sampling cost by learning the relationship between an initial noise sample and the reverse diffusion trajectory. The aim is to produce images with a single model evaluation.

The proposed method, diffusion model sampling with neural operator, or DSNO, uses a neural operator to map a Gaussian initial condition to a continuous-time solution trajectory. It adds temporal convolution layers to a diffusion backbone, with those layers parameterized in Fourier space. Their role is to represent relationships across time along the trajectory.

Learning the trajectory in this form enables parallel decoding, whereas other fast sampling approaches discussed in the abstract remain sequential. In the one-model-evaluation setting, the authors report state-of-the-art FID values of 3.78 on CIFAR-10 and 7.83 on ImageNet-64. The result demonstrates that trajectory-level learning can deliver competitive image generation under an especially tight sampling budget, with the reported quality claims specifically tied to that single-evaluation setting.
summary.tldr: DSNO learns reverse diffusion trajectories with a neural operator, enabling parallel image generation in one model forward pass.

title: Fast Sampling of Diffusion Models via Operator Learning

abstract: This paper focuses on over-parameterized deep neural networks (DNNs) with ReLU activation functions and proves that when the data distribution is well-separated, DNNs can achieve Bayes-optimal test error for classification while obtaining (nearly) zero-training error under the lazy training regime. For this purpose, we unify three interrelated concepts of overparameterization, benign overfitting, and the Lipschitz constant of DNNs. Our results indicate that interpolating with smoother functions leads to better generalization. Furthermore, we investigate the special case where interpolating smooth ground-truth functions is performed by DNNs under the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime for generalization. Our result demonstrates that the generalization error converges to a constant order that only depends on label noise and initialization noise, which theoretically verifies benign overfitting. Our analysis provides a tight lower bound on the normalized margin under non-smooth activation functions, as well as the minimum eigenvalue of NTK under high-dimensional settings, which has its own interest in learning theory.
originalAbstract: This paper focuses on over-parameterized deep neural networks (DNNs) with ReLU activation functions and proves that when the data distribution is well-separated, DNNs can achieve Bayes-optimal test error for classification while obtaining (nearly) zero-training error under the lazy training regime. For this purpose, we unify three interrelated concepts of overparameterization, benign overfitting, and the Lipschitz constant of DNNs. Our results indicate that interpolating with smoother functions leads to better generalization. Furthermore, we investigate the special case where interpolating smooth ground-truth functions is performed by DNNs under the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime for generalization. Our result demonstrates that the generalization error converges to a constant order that only depends on label noise and initialization noise, which theoretically verifies benign overfitting. Our analysis provides a tight lower bound on the normalized margin under non-smooth activation functions, as well as the minimum eigenvalue of NTK under high-dimensional settings, which has its own interest in learning theory.

paragraphs: Fitting training examples almost perfectly does not always prevent a neural network from predicting well on new data. This paper studies that possibility in overparameterized deep networks with ReLU activations. Under a well-separated data distribution and the lazy training regime, it proves that networks can reach Bayes-optimal classification error while achieving nearly zero training error.

The analysis connects overparameterization, benign overfitting, and the network’s Lipschitz constant, a measure related to how sharply its output can change. The results indicate that smoother functions that interpolate the training data generalize better. This gives a way to discuss the quality of an exact fit beyond simply asking whether the network has memorized its training examples.

For smooth ground-truth functions in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime, the authors show that generalization error approaches a constant order determined only by label noise and initialization noise. They also establish lower bounds concerning normalized margins and the smallest kernel eigenvalue. These are theoretical results within the stated distributional and training settings.
summary.tldr: Under specified data and lazy-training conditions, overparameterized ReLU networks can nearly interpolate training data while achieving optimal classification error.

title: Benign Overfitting in Deep Neural Networks under Lazy Training

abstract: We introduce the Differentiable Weightless Neural Network (DWN), a model based on interconnected lookup tables. Training of DWNs is enabled by a novel Extended Finite Difference technique for approximate differentiation of binary values. We propose Learnable Mapping, Learnable Reduction, and Spectral Regularization to further improve the accuracy and efficiency of these models. We evaluate DWNs in three edge computing contexts: (1) an FPGA-based hardware accelerator, where they demonstrate superior latency, throughput, energy efficiency, and model area compared to state-of-the-art solutions, (2) a low-power microcontroller, where they achieve preferable accuracy to XGBoost while subject to stringent memory constraints, and (3) ultra-low-cost chips, where they consistently outperform small models in both accuracy and projected hardware area. DWNs also compare favorably against leading approaches for tabular datasets, with higher average rank. Overall, our work positions DWNs as a pioneering solution for edge-compatible high-throughput neural networks.
