paragraphs: Differentiable Weightless Neural Networks, or DWNs, use interconnected lookup tables as their model structure. The training challenge is how to optimize a system involving binary values. The paper introduces Extended Finite Difference, an approximate differentiation technique that enables these models to be trained.

The authors also introduce Learnable Mapping, Learnable Reduction, and Spectral Regularization to improve accuracy and efficiency. They evaluate the resulting models in three edge-computing settings: an FPGA accelerator, a low-power microcontroller, and ultra-low-cost chips. These settings test whether the approach remains useful when hardware resources and memory are central constraints.

On the FPGA accelerator, DWNs outperform the compared state-of-the-art solutions in latency, throughput, energy efficiency, and model area. Together, these results support lookup-table networks as a practical option for efficient edge inference, with the chip-area result explicitly based on projections.
summary.tldr: Approximate differentiation enables trainable lookup-table networks with favorable accuracy and hardware efficiency in evaluated edge-computing settings.

title: Differentiable Weightless Neural Networks

abstract: As synthetic data becomes higher quality and proliferates on the internet, machine learning models are increasingly trained on a mix of human- and machine-generated data. Despite the successful stories of using synthetic data for representation learning, using synthetic data for generative model training creates “self-consuming loops” which may lead to training instability or even collapse, unless certain conditions are met. Our paper aims to stabilize self-consuming generative model training. Our theoretical results demonstrate that by introducing an idealized correction function, which maps a data point to be more likely under the true data distribution, self-consuming loops can be made exponentially more stable. We then propose self-correction functions, which rely on expert knowledge (e.g. the laws of physics programmed in a simulator), and aim to approximate the idealized corrector automatically and at scale. We empirically validate the effectiveness of self-correcting self-consuming loops on the challenging human motion synthesis task, and observe that it successfully avoids model collapse, even when the ratio of synthetic data to real data is as high as 100%.

paragraphs: When a generative model trains on machine-generated data, its outputs can feed back into later training. Such self-consuming loops may become unstable or collapse unless suitable conditions hold. This paper investigates whether correcting generated examples can make that feedback process more stable.

The theoretical analysis introduces an idealized correction function that moves a data point toward greater likelihood under the true data distribution. With this correction, the authors show that self-consuming loops can become exponentially more stable. They then propose practical approximations using expert knowledge, such as physical laws encoded in a simulator, to automate correction at scale.

Experiments on human motion synthesis show that the proposed self-correction avoids model collapse, including when the synthetic-to-real data ratio reaches 100%. This ratio describes equal amounts of synthetic and real data. The theoretical guarantee concerns the idealized corrector, while the motion experiments provide evidence for an expert-informed approximation. Together, they support correction as a way to improve the reliability of repeated training with generated examples.
summary.tldr: Expert-informed correction stabilizes synthetic-data feedback loops in human motion experiments, supported by theory for an idealized corrector.

title: Self-Correcting Self-Consuming Loops for Generative Model Training

abstract: We study the sample complexity of reinforcement learning (RL) in Mean-Field Games (MFGs) with model-based function approximation that requires strategic exploration to find a Nash Equilibrium policy. We introduce the Partial Model-Based Eluder Dimension (P-MBED), a more effective notion to characterize the model class complexity. Notably, P-MBED measures the complexity of the single-agent model class converted from the given mean-field model class, and potentially, can be exponentially lower than the MBED proposed by Huang et al. (2024). We contribute a model elimination algorithm featuring a novel exploration strategy and establish sample complexity results polynomial w.r.t. P-MBED. Crucially, our results reveal that, under the basic realizability and Lipschitz continuity assumptions, learning Nash Equilibrium in MFGs is no more statistically challenging than solving a logarithmic number of single-agent RL problems. We further extend our results to Multi-Type MFGs, generalizing from conventional MFGs and involving multiple types of agents. This extension implies statistical tractability of a broader class of Markov Games through the efficacy of mean-field approximation. Finally, inspired by our theoretical algorithm, we present a heuristic approach with improved computational efficiency and empirically demonstrate its effectiveness.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much data model-based reinforcement learning needs to find a Nash equilibrium in mean-field games. The setting requires strategic exploration and function approximation for the model. The central question is whether learning equilibrium behavior in this multi-agent setting necessarily demands much more experience than single-agent reinforcement learning.

The authors introduce Partial Model-Based Eluder Dimension, or P-MBED, to measure model-class complexity through an associated single-agent model class. This measure can potentially be exponentially smaller than the earlier MBED measure. They then develop a model-elimination algorithm with a new exploration strategy and prove sample-complexity bounds that are polynomial in P-MBED.

Under realizability and Lipschitz continuity assumptions, the resulting statistical difficulty is no greater than solving a logarithmic number of single-agent reinforcement-learning problems. The theory also extends to mean-field games with multiple agent types. Separately, the authors develop and empirically evaluate a more computationally efficient heuristic inspired by the theoretical algorithm. This distinction matters: the main equivalence concerns data requirements, while computational efficiency receives additional treatment.
summary.tldr: Under realizability and Lipschitz assumptions, learning mean-field-game equilibria needs no more data than a logarithmic number of single-agent RL problems.

title: Model-Based RL for Mean-Field Games is not Statistically Harder than Single-Agent RL

abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) heavily rely on a variety of well-designed benchmarks, which provide environmental platforms and consistent criteria to evaluate existing and novel algorithms. Specifically, in multi-agent RL (MARL), a plethora of benchmarks based on cooperative games have spurred the development of algorithms that improve the scalability of cooperative multi-agent systems. However, for the competitive setting, a lightweight and open-sourced benchmark with challenging gaming dynamics and visual inputs has not yet been established. In this work, we present FightLadder, a real-time fighting game platform, to empower competitive MARL research. Along with the platform, we provide implementations of state-of-the-art MARL algorithms for competitive games, as well as a set of evaluation metrics to characterize the performance and exploitability of agents. We demonstrate the feasibility of this platform by training a general agent that consistently defeats 12 built-in characters in single-player mode, and expose the difficulty of training a non-exploitable agent without human knowledge and demonstrations in two-player mode. FightLadder provides meticulously designed environments to address critical challenges in competitive MARL research, aiming to catalyze a new era of discovery and advancement in the field. Videos and code at https://sites.google.com/view/fightladder/home.

paragraphs: FightLadder provides a real-time fighting-game platform for studying competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning. The paper addresses a gap in lightweight, open-source benchmarks combining challenging competitive dynamics with visual inputs. Its purpose is to give researchers shared environments and evaluation criteria for learning agents that must succeed against opponents.

The platform includes implementations of leading competitive multi-agent algorithms and metrics covering both performance and exploitability. These evaluate related but distinct qualities: winning games and avoiding weaknesses that opponents can exploit. Providing both perspectives makes the benchmark useful for examining whether a successful agent also withstands competitive pressure.

The authors demonstrate feasibility by training a general agent that consistently defeats all 12 built-in characters in single-player mode. Their two-player results also expose the difficulty of learning a non-exploitable agent without human knowledge or demonstrations. These findings show that the platform supports meaningful progress while preserving a harder research challenge: competitive robustness beyond success against the built-in opponents used in the single-player evaluation.
summary.tldr: FightLadder benchmarks visual competitive reinforcement learning through fighting games, measuring both agent performance and exploitability.

title: FightLadder: A Benchmark for Competitive Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Mean-field variational inference (MFVI) methods provide computationally cheap approximations to the posterior of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) when compared to alternatives like MCMC. However, applying MFVI to BNNs encounters limitations due to the Monte Carlo sampling problem. This problem stems from two main issues. First, most samples do not accurately represent the most probable weights. Second, random sampling from variational distributions introduces high variance in gradient estimates, which can hinder the optimization process, leading to slow convergence or even failure. In this paper, we introduce a novel sampling method called Reparameterized Importance Sampling (RIS) to estimate the first moment in neural networks, reducing variance during feed-forward propagation. We begin by analyzing the generalized form of the optimal proposal distribution and presenting an inexpensive approximation. Next, we describe the sampling process from the proposal distribution as a transformation that combines exogenous randomness with the variational parameters. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RIS method in three critical aspects: improved convergence, enhanced predictive performance, and successful uncertainty estimation for out-of-distribution data.

paragraphs: Mean-field variational inference offers a relatively inexpensive way to approximate uncertainty over Bayesian neural-network weights. Its sampling process can nevertheless make training difficult: samples may poorly represent the most probable weights, and noisy gradient estimates can slow or disrupt optimization. This paper addresses those sampling difficulties through Reparameterized Importance Sampling, or RIS.

RIS estimates the first moment in neural networks while reducing variance during feed-forward propagation. The authors first analyze a generalized optimal proposal distribution and develop a computationally inexpensive approximation. They then express sampling from that proposal as a transformation combining external randomness with the variational parameters, making the sampling construction central to the learning method.

Experiments report better convergence, improved predictive performance, and successful uncertainty estimation for out-of-distribution data. These findings address both the optimization difficulties motivating the work and the quality of the resulting predictions and uncertainty estimates. The contribution is a targeted modification to sampling within variational Bayesian networks, supported by analysis of the proposal distribution and empirical evidence across those three outcomes.
summary.tldr: RIS improves sampling in variational Bayesian neural networks, with reported gains in convergence, prediction, and out-of-distribution uncertainty estimation.

title: Reparameterized Importance Sampling for Robust Variational Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: Block coordinate descent is a powerful algorithmic template suitable for big data optimization. This template admits a lot of variants including block gradient descent (BGD), which performs gradient descent on a selected block of variables, while keeping other variables fixed. For a very long time, the stepsize for each block has tacitly been set to one divided by the block-wise Lipschitz smoothness constant, imitating the vanilla stepsize rule for gradient descent (GD). However, such a choice for BGD has not yet been able to theoretically justify its empirical superiority over GD, as existing convergence rates for BGD have worse constants than GD in the deterministic cases. To discover such theoretical justification, we set up a simple environment where we consider BGD applied to least-squares with two blocks of variables. Assuming the data matrix corresponding to each block is orthogonal, we find optimal stepsizes of BGD in closed form, which provably lead to asymptotic convergence rates twice as fast as GD with Polyak’s momentum; this means, under that orthogonality assumption, one can accelerate BGD by just tuning stepsizes and without adding any momentum. An application that satisfies this assumption is generalized alternating projection between two subspaces, and applying our stepsizes to it improves the prior convergence rate that was once claimed, slightly inaccurately, to be optimal. The main proof idea is to minimize, in stepsize variables, the spectral radius of a matrix that controls convergence rates.

paragraphs: Block gradient descent updates one group of variables while holding the others fixed. Although it can work well empirically, conventional choices of step size have not explained its advantage over ordinary gradient descent in deterministic convergence analyses. This paper asks whether choosing better step sizes can reveal an acceleration mechanism within the block updates themselves.

The authors examine least-squares problems with two variable blocks, assuming that the data matrix associated with each block is orthogonal. Within this setting, they derive optimal step sizes in closed form. Their proof minimizes the spectral radius of a matrix governing convergence, thereby choosing steps according to the behavior of the overall iteration.

Under the orthogonality assumption, the resulting asymptotic convergence rates are twice as fast as those of gradient descent with Polyak momentum, despite adding no momentum to the block method. The step sizes also improve a previous convergence rate for generalized alternating projection between two subspaces. The acceleration claim is therefore tied to a specific, explicitly analyzed structure.
summary.tldr: For two-block least-squares problems with orthogonal block matrices, optimized step sizes accelerate block gradient descent without momentum.

title: Block Acceleration Without Momentum: On Optimal Stepsizes of Block Gradient Descent for Least-Squares

abstract: Cutting plane methods are a fundamental approach for solving integer linear programs (ILPs). In each iteration of such methods, additional linear constraints (cuts) are introduced to the constraint set with the aim of excluding the previous fractional optimal solution while not affecting the optimal integer solution. In this work, we explore a novel approach within cutting plane methods: instead of only adding new cuts, we also consider the removal of previous cuts introduced at any of the preceding iterations of the method under a learnable parametric criteria. We demonstrate that in fundamental combinatorial optimization settings such cut removal policies can lead to significant improvements over both human-based and machine learning-guided cut addition policies even when implemented with simple models.

In each iteration of such methods, additional linear constraints (cuts) are introduced to the constraint set with the aim of excluding the previous fractional optimal solution while not affecting the optimal integer solution. In this work, we explore a novel approach within cutting plane methods: instead of only adding new cuts, we also consider the removal of previous cuts introduced at any of the preceding iterations of the method under a learnable parametric criteria. We demonstrate that in fundamental combinatorial optimization settings such cut removal policies can lead to significant improvements over both human-based and machine learning-guided cut addition policies even when implemented with simple models.

paragraphs: Cutting-plane methods solve integer linear programs by repeatedly adding linear constraints called cuts. A cut excludes a fractional solution encountered during optimization while preserving the optimal integer solution. The usual decision is which new constraints to add as the method progresses.

This paper expands that decision to include removing cuts added in previous iterations. A learnable, parameterized criterion determines which earlier cuts to discard. The resulting policy can revise the collection of accumulated constraints throughout the procedure. This makes the retained set of cuts an object of learning, alongside the more familiar choice of new cuts.

In fundamental combinatorial optimization settings, the authors demonstrate significant improvements over both human-designed and machine-learning-guided cut-addition policies. These gains appear even when removal decisions use simple models. The findings indicate that revisiting earlier constraint choices can be a valuable part of a cutting-plane method, and that improving such methods need not depend solely on selecting more effective new constraints.
summary.tldr: Learned policies for removing earlier cuts improve cutting-plane performance in studied combinatorial optimization settings.

title: Learning to Remove Cuts in Integer Linear Programming

abstract: Partial monitoring is a generic framework of online decision-making problems with limited feedback. To make decisions from such limited feedback, it is necessary to find an appropriate distribution for exploration. Recently, a powerful approach for this purpose, exploration by optimization (ExO), was proposed, which achieves optimal bounds in adversarial environments with follow-the-regularized-leader for a wide range of online decision-making problems. However, a naive application of ExO in stochastic environments significantly degrades regret bounds. To resolve this issue in locally observable games, we first establish a new framework and analysis for ExO with a hybrid regularizer. This development allows us to significantly improve existing regret bounds of best-of-both-worlds (BOBW) algorithms, which achieves nearly optimal bounds both in stochastic and adversarial environments. In particular, we derive a stochastic regret bound of $O(\sum_{a \neq a^*} k^2 m^2 \log T / \Delta_a)$, where $k$, $m$, and $T$ are the numbers of actions, observations and rounds, $a^*$ is an optimal action, and $\Delta_a$ is the suboptimality gap for action $a$. This bound is roughly $\Theta(k^2 \log T)$ times smaller than existing BOBW bounds. In addition, for globally observable games, we provide a new BOBW algorithm with the first $O(\log T)$ stochastic bound.

paragraphs: Partial monitoring studies repeated decisions made with limited feedback. A learner must choose how to explore even when observations do not directly reveal everything needed to judge its actions. Exploration by optimization provides strong guarantees against adversarial environments, but applying it naively in stochastic environments leads to substantially weaker regret bounds.

This paper introduces an exploration-by-optimization framework with a hybrid regularizer for locally observable games. It improves best-of-both-worlds guarantees, which aim to perform nearly optimally in both stochastic and adversarial settings. The stochastic regret bound sums k²m² log(T)/Delta_a over suboptimal actions, where k counts actions, m counts observations, T counts rounds, and Delta_a measures each action's disadvantage relative to an optimum.

The authors describe this bound as roughly a factor of k² log(T) smaller than existing best-of-both-worlds bounds. They also give a new algorithm for globally observable games with the first logarithmic-in-T stochastic bound of this kind. The results strengthen performance in stochastic environments while preserving adversarial robustness within the game classes studied.
summary.tldr: Hybrid regularization improves stochastic regret guarantees for partial monitoring while retaining best-of-both-worlds adversarial robustness.

title: Exploration by Optimization with Hybrid Regularizers: Logarithmic Regret with Adversarial Robustness in Partial Monitoring

abstract: Achieving sample efficiency in Reinforcement Learning (RL) is primarily hinged on the efficient exploration of the underlying environment, but it is still unknown what are the best exploration strategies in different settings. We consider the reward-free RL problem, which operates in two phases: an exploration phase, where the agent gathers exploration trajectories over episodes irrespective of any predetermined reward function, and a subsequent planning phase, where a reward function is introduced. The agent then utilizes the episodes from the exploration phase to calculate a near-optimal policy. Existing algorithms and sample complexities for reward-free RL are limited to tabular, linear or very smooth function approximations, leaving the problem largely open for more general cases. We consider a broad range of kernel-based function approximations, including non-smooth kernels, and propose an algorithm based on adaptive domain partitioning. We show that our algorithm achieves order-optimal sample complexity for a large class of common kernels, which includes Matérn and Neural Tangent kernels.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates discovering an environment from deciding what to accomplish in it. First, an agent gathers trajectories without a predetermined reward function. Later, a reward is supplied, and the agent uses those earlier experiences to calculate a near-optimal policy. The challenge is to collect sufficiently useful information before knowing the eventual objective.

Previous algorithms and sample complexity guarantees cover tabular models, linear approximations, or very smooth function approximations. This paper expands the setting to a broad range of kernel-based approximations, including non-smooth kernels. Its proposed exploration algorithm uses adaptive domain partitioning, allowing the analysis to address function classes beyond those previously handled by the more restrictive approaches.

The authors prove order-optimal sample complexity for a large class of common kernels, including Matérn and Neural Tangent kernels. This describes how efficiently exploration data can support the subsequent planning stage within the covered classes. The contribution broadens the theoretical basis for reward-free exploration while retaining a strong guarantee on the amount of experience required.
summary.tldr: Adaptive domain partitioning enables reward-free reinforcement learning with order-optimal sample complexity for a broad class of kernels.

title: Reward-Free Kernel-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we prove that Distributional Reinforcement Learning (DistRL), which learns the return distribution, can obtain second-order bounds in both online and offline RL in general settings with function approximation. Second-order bounds are instance-dependent bounds that scale with the variance of return, which we prove are tighter than the previously known small-loss bounds of distributional RL. To the best of our knowledge, our results are the first second-order bounds for low-rank MDPs and for offline RL. When specializing to contextual bandits (one-step RL problem), we show that a distributional learning based optimism algorithm achieves a second-order worst-case regret bound, and a second-order gap dependent bound, simultaneously. We also empirically demonstrate the benefit of DistRL in contextual bandits on real-world datasets. We highlight that our analysis with DistRL is relatively simple, follows the general framework of optimism in the face of uncertainty and does not require weighted regression. Our results suggest that DistRL is a promising framework for obtaining second-order bounds in general RL settings, thus further reinforcing the benefits of DistRL.

These guarantees depend on return variance, making them sensitive to the particular problem instance. The authors show they are tighter than previously known small-loss bounds for distributional reinforcement learning.

The results include second-order bounds for low-rank decision processes and offline reinforcement learning, which the authors identify as the first such results to their knowledge. For contextual bandits, the one-step setting, a distributional optimism algorithm simultaneously achieves a second-order worst-case regret bound and a second-order bound that depends on reward gaps.

The analysis follows optimism in the face of uncertainty and avoids weighted regression. Real-world contextual-bandit experiments also demonstrate benefits from distributional learning. Together, the theory and experiments strengthen the case that learning return distributions can improve guarantees as well as empirical behavior, with the theoretical advantage explicitly reflecting variation in returns.
summary.tldr: Distributional reinforcement learning can achieve tighter, variance-sensitive guarantees across online RL, offline RL, and contextual bandits.

title: More Benefits of Being Distributional: Second-Order Bounds for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper presents an in-depth examination of the evolution and interplay of cognitive and expressive capabilities in large language models (LLMs), with a specific focus on Baichuan-7B and Baichuan-33B, an advanced bilingual (Chinese and English) LLM series. We define and explore the model’s cognitive and expressive capabilities through linear representations across three critical phases: Pretraining, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Cognitive capability is defined as the quantity and quality of information conveyed by the neuron output vectors within the network, similar to the neural signal processing in human cognition. Expressive capability is defined as the model’s capability to produce word-level output. Our findings unveil a sequential development pattern, where cognitive abilities are largely established during Pretraining, whereas expressive abilities predominantly advance during SFT and RLHF. Statistical analyses confirm a significant correlation between the two capabilities, suggesting that cognitive capacity may limit expressive potential. The paper also explores the theoretical underpinnings of these divergent developmental trajectories and their connection to the LLMs’ architectural design. Moreover, we evaluate various optimization-independent strategies, such as few-shot learning and repeated sampling, which bridge the gap between cognitive and expressive capabilities. This research reveals the potential connection between the hidden space and the output space, contributing valuable insights into the interpretability and controllability of their training processes.

title: Exploring the LLM Journey from Cognition to Expression with Linear Representations

abstract: In this paper, we study offline-to-online Imitation Learning (IL) that pretrains an imitation policy from static demonstration data, followed by fast finetuning with minimal environmental interaction. We find the naive combination of existing offline IL and online IL methods tends to behave poorly in this context, because the initial discriminator (often used in online IL) operates randomly and discordantly against the policy initialization, leading to misguided policy optimization and unlearning of pretraining knowledge. To overcome this challenge, we propose a principled offline-to-online IL method, named OLLIE, that simultaneously learns a near-expert policy initialization along with an aligned discriminator initialization, which can be seamlessly integrated into online IL, achieving smooth and fast finetuning. Empirically, OLLIE consistently and significantly outperforms the baseline methods in 20 challenging tasks, from continuous control to vision-based domains, in terms of performance, demonstration efficiency, and convergence speed. This work may serve as a foundation for further exploration of pretraining and finetuning in the context of IL.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online imitation learning first learns behavior from a fixed demonstration dataset and then improves it through limited environmental interaction. Simply joining existing offline and online methods can go wrong at this transition. The paper identifies a mismatch between the pretrained policy and the discriminator used to guide online learning.

When that discriminator starts with random, incompatible behavior, it can give misleading training signals and cause the policy to lose knowledge gained during pretraining. OLLIE addresses the mismatch by learning both a near-expert initial policy and an aligned initial discriminator. Preparing them together is intended to make the move into online imitation learning smooth and fast.

Across 20 challenging tasks spanning continuous control and vision-based domains, OLLIE consistently and significantly outperforms the tested baselines in performance, demonstration efficiency, and convergence speed. The findings emphasize that successful pretraining transfer depends on the initialization of the learning signal as well as the policy. In these experiments, aligning both components helps preserve useful behavior while enabling further improvement through interaction.
summary.tldr: OLLIE jointly initializes an imitation policy and its discriminator to prevent disruptive offline-to-online transfer and accelerate finetuning.

title: OLLIE: Imitation Learning from Offline Pretraining to Online Finetuning

abstract: In this paper, we consider the metric $k$-center problem in the fully dynamic setting, where we are given a metric space $(V,d)$ evolving via a sequence of point insertions and deletions and our task is to maintain a subset $S \subseteq V$ of at most $k$ points that minimizes the objective $\max_{x \in V} \min_{y \in S}d(x, y)$. We want to design our algorithm so that we minimize its approximation ratio, recourse (the number of changes it makes to the solution $S$) and update time (the time it takes to handle an update). We give a simple algorithm for dynamic $k$-center that maintains a $O(1)$-approximate solution with $O(1)$ amortized recourse and $\tilde O(k)$ amortized update time, obtaining near-optimal approximation, recourse and update time simultaneously. We obtain our result by combining a variant of the dynamic $k$-center algorithm of Bateni et al. [SODA’23] with the dynamic sparsifier of Bhattacharya et al. [NeurIPS’23].

paragraphs: The k-center problem chooses at most k representative points so that every point is reasonably close to a representative. Its objective is to minimize the largest distance to the nearest chosen center. This paper studies the fully dynamic version, where points can both arrive and disappear, requiring the chosen centers to be maintained as the dataset changes.

Three goals compete in this setting: keeping the clustering close to optimal, making few changes to the selected centers, and processing updates quickly. The number of center changes is called recourse. The proposed algorithm combines a variant of an existing dynamic k-center method with a dynamic sparsifier to address all three goals together.

The resulting guarantees are a constant approximation factor, constant amortized recourse, and amortized update time that is roughly linear in k, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Amortized guarantees describe costs averaged across a sequence of updates, rather than a bound on every individual update. The stated contribution is achieving near-optimal quality, stability, and update efficiency simultaneously.
summary.tldr: A dynamic k-center algorithm simultaneously achieves near-optimal clustering quality, few center changes, and efficient amortized updates.

title: Almost Optimal Fully Dynamic $k$-Center Clustering with Recourse

abstract: Recent work on inference-time alignment has established benefits of increasing inference-time computation in language models, but naively scaling compute through techniques like Best-of-N sampling can cause performance to degrade due to reward hacking. Toward a theoretical understanding of how to best leverage additional computation, we formalize inference-time alignment as improving a pre-trained policy’s responses for a prompt of interest, given access to an imperfect reward model. We analyze the performance of inference-time alignment algorithms in terms of (i) response quality, and (ii) compute, and provide new results that highlight the importance of the pre-trained policy’s coverage over high-quality responses for performance and compute scaling: (1) We show that Best-of-N alignment with an ideal N can achieve optimal performance under stringent notions of coverage, but provably suffers from reward hacking when N is large, and fails to achieve tight guarantees under more realistic coverage conditions; (2) We introduce InferenceTimePessimism, a new algorithm which mitigates reward hacking through deliberate use of inference-time compute, implementing pessimism in the face of uncertainty; we prove that its performance is optimal and scaling-monotonic, i.e., does ot degrade as N increases. We complement our theoretical results with experiments that demonstrate the practicality of our algorithm across a variety of tasks and models.

paragraphs: Generating more candidate responses and choosing the highest-scoring one can improve language-model output, but an imperfect reward model can make this strategy backfire. This paper studies inference-time alignment through both response quality and computational cost. A central factor is coverage: how well the pretrained policy’s response distribution includes high-quality answers.

The analysis shows that Best-of-N can achieve optimal performance with a suitably chosen N under stringent coverage conditions. However, increasing N too far provably leads to reward hacking, and the method lacks tight guarantees under more realistic coverage conditions. Extra computation can therefore amplify the consequences of an unreliable reward signal rather than steadily improve responses.

The authors introduce InferenceTimePessimism, which uses additional computation to act conservatively when facing uncertainty. Within their theoretical framework, they prove optimal performance and scaling monotonicity, meaning that performance does not deteriorate as N grows. Experiments across several tasks and models demonstrate practical applicability. The contribution links useful compute scaling to both the policy’s coverage and how the selection algorithm handles uncertainty.
summary.tldr: InferenceTimePessimism addresses reward hacking in inference-time alignment, with theoretical guarantees that performance does not worsen as computation increases.

title: Is Best-of-N the Best of Them? Coverage, Scaling, and Optimality in Inference-Time Alignment

abstract: Language models exhibit complex, diverse behaviors when prompted with free-form text, making it hard to characterize the space of possible outputs. We study the problem of behavioral elicitation, where the goal is to search for prompts that induce specific target behaviors (e.g., hallucinations, harmful responses) from a target language model. To navigate the exponentially large space of possible prompts, we train amortized investigator models to emulate the posterior distribution over the prompts, conditioned on the target behavior. Specifically, we first fit a reverse model and then use reinforcement learning to optimize likelihood of generating the target behavior. To improve the diversity of the prompt distribution, we further propose a novel iterative training objective based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm that encourages each iteration to discover different sets of prompts not captured by previous iterations. Our investigator models produce prompts that exhibit a variety of effective and human-interpretable strategies for behavior elicitation, obtaining a 100% attack success rate on AdvBench (Harmful Behaviors) and an 85% hallucination rate.

paragraphs: A language model’s behavior can change substantially with its prompt, making it difficult to discover which inputs trigger a particular response. This paper studies behavioral elicitation: searching for prompts that induce a chosen behavior, including hallucinations or harmful responses. The challenge is the enormous number of possible prompts.

The authors train investigator models to generate prompts conditioned on a target behavior. Training begins with a reverse model and then uses reinforcement learning to increase the likelihood of eliciting that behavior. Because a successful investigator could repeatedly produce similar prompts, the paper adds an iterative objective based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm that encourages discovery of prompt sets missed by earlier iterations.

The resulting prompts use varied strategies that the authors describe as effective and understandable to humans. They report a 100% attack success rate on AdvBench’s Harmful Behaviors benchmark and an 85% hallucination rate. These experimental results show that learned investigators can expose targeted behaviors while the diversity objective broadens the range of prompts discovered.
summary.tldr: Trained investigator models discover diverse prompts that effectively elicit targeted language-model behaviors, including harmful responses and hallucinations.

title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

abstract: Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) is a powerful framework for enhancing statistical estimates by combining limited gold-standard data with machine learning (ML) predictions. While prior work has demonstrated PPI’s benefits for individual statistical problems, modern applications require answering numerous parallel statistical questions. We introduce Prediction-Powered Adaptive Shrinkage ($\texttt{PAS}$), a method that bridges PPI with empirical Bayes shrinkage to improve estimation of multiple means. $\texttt{PAS}$ debiases noisy ML predictions $\textit{within}$ each task and then borrows strength $\textit{across}$ tasks by using those same predictions as a reference point for shrinkage. The amount of shrinkage is determined by minimizing an unbiased estimate of risk, and we prove that this tuning strategy is asymptotically optimal. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that $\texttt{PAS}$ adapts to the reliability of the ML predictions and outperforms traditional and modern baselines in large-scale applications.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference improves statistical estimation by combining limited gold-standard observations with machine-learning predictions. This paper extends that idea to applications asking many statistical questions simultaneously. Its method, Prediction-Powered Adaptive Shrinkage, estimates multiple means by combining prediction-powered inference with empirical Bayes shrinkage, allowing related estimation tasks to inform one another.

The method gives predictions two roles. Within each task, it corrects bias in noisy machine-learning predictions. Across tasks, it uses those same predictions as reference points for shrinkage. The amount of shrinkage is selected by minimizing an unbiased estimate of risk, giving the method a data-driven way to determine how strongly to use these reference points.

The authors prove that this tuning strategy is asymptotically optimal. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the method adapts to prediction reliability and outperforms traditional and modern baselines in large-scale applications. The contribution is a unified approach to correcting prediction errors within individual tasks while borrowing statistical strength across a collection of tasks.
summary.tldr: Prediction-Powered Adaptive Shrinkage combines within-task prediction debiasing with cross-task shrinkage and an asymptotically optimal tuning strategy.

title: Prediction-Powered Adaptive Shrinkage Estimation

abstract: We tackle the problem of identifying whether a variable is the cause of a specified target using observational data. State-of-the-art causal learning algorithms that handle latent variables typically rely on identifying the global causal structure, often represented as a partial ancestral graph (PAG), to infer causal relationships. Although effective, these approaches are often redundant and computationally expensive when the focus is limited to a specific causal relationship. In this work, we introduce novel local characterizations that are necessary and sufficient for various types of causal relationships between two variables, enabling us to bypass the need for global structure learning. Leveraging these local insights, we develop efficient and fully localized algorithms that accurately identify causal relationships from observational data. We theoretically demonstrate the soundness and completeness of our approach. Extensive experiments on benchmark networks and real-world datasets further validate the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to determine whether one variable causes a particular target using observational data when some variables are unobserved. Existing methods that handle these latent variables commonly reconstruct a global causal structure before answering the question. That work can be computationally expensive and redundant when the interest concerns only a specific pair of variables.

The authors introduce local characterizations for several types of causal relationships. These characterizations are necessary and sufficient within the paper’s formulation, allowing the relevant relationship to be identified without first learning the entire global structure. They use these results to construct fully localized algorithms that focus computation on answering the relationship question.

The theoretical contribution establishes soundness and completeness of the proposed approach. Experiments on benchmark networks and real datasets also support its effectiveness and efficiency. The practical significance is that a narrowly targeted causal question can be addressed through local reasoning, avoiding the overhead of global structure learning in the setting studied.
summary.tldr: Local causal characterizations enable sound and complete relationship identification without learning a global causal structure in the studied latent-variable setting.

title: Local Identifying Causal Relations in the Presence of Latent Variables

abstract: Instruction-based image editing, which aims to modify the image faithfully towards instruction while preserving irrelevant content unchanged, has made advanced progresses. However, there still lacks a comprehensive metric for assessing the editing quality. Existing metrics either require high costs concerning human evaluation, which hinders large-scale evaluation, or adapt from other tasks and lose specified concerns, failing to comprehensively evaluate the modification of instruction and the preservation of irrelevant regions, resulting in biased evaluation. To tackle it, we introduce a new metric Balancing Preservation Modification (BPM), that tailored for instruction-based image editing by explicitly disentangling the image into editing-relevant and irrelevant regions for specific consideration. We first identify and locate editing-relevant regions, followed by a two-tier process to assess editing quality: Region-Aware Judge evaluates whether the position and size of the edited region align with instruction, and Semantic-Aware Judge further assesses the instruction content compliance within editing-relevant regions as well as content preservation within irrelevant regions, yielding comprehensive and interpretable quality assessment. Moreover, the editing-relevant region localization in BPM can be integrated into image editing approaches to improve the editing quality, manifesting its wild application. We verify the effectiveness of BPM metric on comprehensive instruction-editing data, and the re- sults show that we yield the highest alignment with human evaluation compared to existing metrics, indicating efficacy. The code is available at https://joyli-x.github.io/BPM/.

paragraphs: An image edit can follow an instruction in one area while accidentally changing unrelated content elsewhere. Assessing editing quality therefore requires checking both the requested modification and the preservation of everything outside its scope. The paper introduces Balancing Preservation Modification, or BPM, to evaluate these two responsibilities explicitly.

BPM first locates the regions relevant to the instruction. Its Region-Aware Judge checks whether the location and size of the edited area fit the request. Its Semantic-Aware Judge then evaluates whether the relevant region contains the requested change and whether unrelated regions retain their content. Separating these judgments makes the assessment more interpretable than a score that combines all image changes indiscriminately.

Across the evaluated instruction-editing data, BPM achieves the strongest agreement with human evaluation among the compared metrics. The authors also show that its region-localization component can be incorporated into editing methods to improve their outputs. The contribution thus includes both a way to assess edits and a component that can help guide where changes should occur.
summary.tldr: BPM evaluates image edits by separately checking where changes occur, whether they follow instructions, and whether unrelated content is preserved.

title: Balancing Preservation and Modification: A Region and Semantic Aware Metric for Instruction-Based Image Editing

abstract: Federated learning provides an efficient privacy-preserving distributed training framework for large language models, addressing the growing scarcity of publicly available training data while enabling the utilization of private datasets. While integrating large language model fine-tuning with federated learning emerges as a promising research direction, researchers pay limited attention to non-IID instruction-following scenarios. Our key insight is decomposing client updates into consensus and divergence components, enabling the model to maintain core capabilities while adapting to domain-specific knowledge. We propose a novel federated learning framework called FedICU (Splitting with ImportanCe-aware Updating for Heterogeneous Federated Learning with Large Language Models), which introduces an aggregation mechanism that dynamically balances these components based on their contribution to global model performance, while implementing an importance-aware parameter updating strategy to prevent catastrophic forgetting and domain overfitting. Extensive experiments across diverse domains demonstrate that FedICU significantly outperforms existing federated learning approaches in terms of both generalization performance and domain adaptation. Our code is available at https://github.com/liaosunny123/FedICU.

paragraphs: Federated fine-tuning lets language models learn from private datasets held by distributed clients. When instruction-following data differ across clients, updates must accommodate specialized knowledge while preserving general capabilities. FedICU addresses this heterogeneous setting by separating client updates into components that express consensus and components that express divergence.

Its aggregation mechanism dynamically balances those components according to their contribution to global model performance. This gives shared learning and domain-specific adaptation distinct roles in the update process. An importance-aware parameter update strategy further aims to prevent catastrophic forgetting and excessive adaptation to individual domains, keeping the model’s existing abilities relevant during specialization.

Experiments across diverse domains report significantly better generalization and domain adaptation than existing federated learning approaches. The findings support treating disagreement among client updates as something to evaluate and balance, rather than collapsing all updates into an undifferentiated signal. The framework’s main contribution is coordinating that component-level aggregation with parameter-level importance during federated language-model fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: FedICU balances shared and divergent client updates to improve language-model generalization and domain adaptation in heterogeneous federated learning.

title: Splitting with Importance-aware Updating for Heterogeneous Federated Learning with Large Language Models

abstract: In Amazon robotic warehouses, the destination-to-chute mapping problem is crucial for efficient package sorting. Often, however, this problem is complicated by uncertain and dynamic package induction rates, which can lead to increased package recirculation. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a Distributionally Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (DRMARL) framework that learns a destination-to-chute mapping policy that is resilient to adversarial variations in induction rates. Specifically, DRMARL relies on group distributionally robust optimization (DRO) to learn a policy that performs well not only on average but also on each individual subpopulation of induction rates within the group that capture, for example, different seasonality or operation modes of the system. This approach is then combined with a novel contextual bandit-based estimator of the worst-case induction distribution for each state-action pair, significantly reducing the cost of exploration and thereby increasing the learning efficiency and scalability of our framework. Extensive simulations demonstrate that DRMARL achieves robust chute mapping in the presence of varying induction distributions, reducing package recirculation by an average of 80% in the simulation scenario.

paragraphs: In robotic package sorting, destinations must be assigned to chutes while the rate of incoming packages changes. Poor mappings can increase package recirculation. This paper develops a distributionally robust multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to learn mappings that remain effective under adversarial variations in those incoming rates.

The framework uses group distributionally robust optimization to consider distinct subpopulations of arrival conditions. These groups can represent seasonal patterns or different operating modes. The objective emphasizes performance within each group as well as overall performance, addressing the possibility that a policy with a good average result behaves poorly under particular conditions.

A contextual bandit estimator identifies a worst-case induction distribution for each state-action pair. The authors report that this reduces exploration cost and improves learning efficiency and scalability. In extensive simulations, the resulting mappings remain robust as induction distributions vary, with package recirculation reduced by an average of 80% in the simulation scenario. The result supports robust optimization as a way to handle changing sorting demand within the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: DRMARL learns chute mappings robust to changing package arrival patterns, reducing recirculation by an average of 80% in the simulation scenario.

title: Distributionally Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Chute Mapping

abstract: With the rise of AIGC technologies, particularly diffusion models, highly realistic fake images that can deceive human visual perception has become feasible. Consequently, various forgery detection methods have emerged. However, existing methods treat the generation process of fake images as either a black-box or an auxiliary tool, offering limited insights into its underlying mechanisms. In this paper, we propose Spatio-Temporal Distribution Fitting Deviation (STD-FD) for AIGC forgery detection, which explores the generative process in detail. By decomposing and reconstructing data within generative diffusion models, initial experiments reveal temporal distribution fitting deviations during the image reconstruction process. These deviations are captured through reconstruction noise maps for each spatial semantic unit, derived via a super-resolution algorithm. Extensive experiments show that STD-FD effectively captures distribution patterns in AIGC-generated data, demonstrating strong robustness and generalizability while outperforming state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods on major datasets. The source code is available at this link.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning abilities, but they still struggle with faithful reasoning due to knowledge gaps and hallucinations. To address these issues, knowledge graphs (KGs) have been utilized to enhance LLM reasoning through their structured knowledge. However, existing KG-enhanced methods, either retrieval-based or agent-based, encounter difficulties in accurately retrieving knowledge and efficiently traversing KGs at scale. In this work, we introduce graph-constrained reasoning (GCR), a novel framework that bridges structured knowledge in KGs with unstructured reasoning in LLMs. To eliminate hallucinations, GCR ensures faithful KG-grounded reasoning by integrating KG structure into the LLM decoding process through KG-Trie, a trie-based index that encodes KG reasoning paths. KG-Trie constrains the decoding process, allowing LLMs to directly reason on graphs and generate faithful reasoning paths grounded in KGs. Additionally, GCR leverages a lightweight KG-specialized LLM for graph-constrained reasoning alongside a powerful general LLM for inductive reasoning over multiple reasoning paths, resulting in accurate reasoning with zero reasoning hallucination. Extensive experiments on several KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that GCR achieves state-of-the-art performance and exhibits strong zero-shot generalizability to unseen KGs without additional training.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can supply structured facts that language models lack, but using them effectively requires accurate retrieval and efficient traversal. The framework also divides work between a lightweight model specialized for graph-constrained reasoning and a more powerful general model that performs inductive reasoning over multiple paths.

The authors report zero reasoning hallucination in this graph-grounded framework, alongside state-of-the-art results on several knowledge-graph question-answering benchmarks. They also report strong zero-shot generalization to unseen graphs without additional training. The grounding claim concerns faithfulness to the knowledge graph: the contribution is a mechanism for keeping generated reasoning tied to structured paths while still combining information across them.
summary.tldr: Graph-constrained reasoning restricts decoding to knowledge-graph paths and combines specialist and general models for faithful graph-based question answering.

title: Graph-constrained Reasoning: Faithful Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs with Large Language Models

abstract: Hallucinations in LLMs pose a significant concern to their safe deployment in real-world applications. Recent approaches have leveraged the latent space of LLMs for hallucination detection, but their embeddings, optimized for linguistic coherence rather than factual accuracy, often fail to clearly separate truthful and hallucinated content. To this end, we propose the Truthfulness Separator Vector (TSV), a lightweight and flexible steering vector that reshapes the LLM’s representation space during inference to enhance the separation between truthful and hallucinated outputs, without altering model parameters. Our two-stage framework first trains TSV on a small set of labeled exemplars to form compact and well-separated clusters. It then augments the exemplar set with unlabeled LLM generations, employing an optimal transport-based algorithm for pseudo-labeling combined with a confidence-based filtering process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TSV achieves state-of-the-art performance with minimal labeled data, exhibiting strong generalization across datasets and providing a practical solution for real-world LLM applications.

paragraphs: A language model’s internal representations are trained for coherent language, so truthful and hallucinated content may not separate clearly within them. This paper proposes the Truthfulness Separator Vector, or TSV, to make that distinction easier to detect. The vector steers representations during inference without changing the language model’s parameters.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, a small labeled set teaches TSV to form compact, separated clusters for truthful and hallucinated content. The method then expands the exemplars using unlabeled model generations. An optimal-transport algorithm assigns provisional labels, and a confidence filter selects examples for this augmentation process.

The authors report state-of-the-art detection performance with little labeled data and strong generalization across datasets. The contribution is a lightweight way to reshape the information used by a hallucination detector while leaving the underlying model parameters intact. The findings support improved separation and detection of hallucinated content; the method’s stated role is to identify that content through steered representations.
summary.tldr: TSV steers language-model representations to improve hallucination detection using a small labeled set and filtered pseudo-labels.

title: Steer LLM Latents for Hallucination Detection

abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are impressive at visual question answering and image captioning. But they underperform on multi-step visual reasoning—even compared to LLMs on the same tasks presented in text form—giving rise to perceptions of modality imbalance or brittleness. Towards a systematic study of such issues, we introduce a synthetic framework for assessing the ability of VLMs to perform algorithmic visual reasoning, comprising three tasks: Table Readout, Grid Navigation, and Visual Analogy. Each has two levels of difficulty, SIMPLE and HARD, and even the SIMPLE versions are difficult for frontier VLMs. We propose strategies for training on the SIMPLE version of tasks that improve performance on the corresponding HARD task, i.e., simple-to-hard (S2H) generalization. This controlled setup, where each task also has an equivalent text-only version, allows a quantification of the modality imbalance and how it is impacted by training strategy. We show that 1) explicit image-to-text conversion is important in promoting S2H generalization on images, by transferring reasoning from text; 2) conversion can be internalized at test time. We also report results of mechanistic study of this phenomenon. We identify measures of gradient alignment that can identify training strategies that promote better S2H generalization. Ablations highlight the importance of chain-of-thought.

summary.tldr: Controlled visual reasoning tasks show how image-to-text conversion can help models generalize from simple training problems to harder ones.

title: Generalizing from SIMPLE to HARD Visual Reasoning: Can We Mitigate Modality Imbalance in VLMs?

abstract: The long-standing dominance of gradient-boosted decision trees on tabular data is currently challenged by tabular foundation models using In-Context Learning (ICL): setting the training data as context for the test data and predicting in a single forward pass without parameter updates. While TabPFNv2 foundation model excels on tables with up to 10K samples, its alternating column- and row-wise attentions make handling large training sets computationally prohibitive. So, can ICL be effectively scaled and deliver a benefit for larger tables? We introduce TabICL, a tabular foundation model for classification, pretrained on synthetic datasets with up to 60K samples and capable of handling 500K samples on affordable resources. This is enabled by a novel two-stage architecture: a column-then-row attention mechanism to build fixed-dimensional embeddings of rows, followed by a transformer for efficient ICL. Across 200 classification datasets from the TALENT benchmark, TabICL is on par with TabPFNv2 while being systematically faster (up to 10 times), and significantly outperforms all other approaches. On 53 datasets with over 10K samples, TabICL surpasses both TabPFNv2 and CatBoost, demonstrating the potential of ICL for large data. Pretraining code, inference code, and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/soda-inria/tabicl.

paragraphs: Tabular in-context learning predicts from a table by placing labeled training examples in context, without updating model parameters for the new dataset. This approach can be computationally demanding on large tables. TabICL addresses that scaling problem for classification, targeting settings beyond the roughly 10,000-sample range where the abstract describes TabPFNv2 as particularly effective.

Its architecture separates representation building from in-context prediction. Column-then-row attention first converts rows into fixed-dimensional embeddings. A subsequent transformer performs in-context learning on those representations. TabICL is pretrained on synthetic datasets containing up to 60,000 samples, and the authors report that it can handle 500,000 samples using affordable resources.

On 53 datasets exceeding 10,000 samples, it surpasses both TabPFNv2 and CatBoost. The results support the architectural separation as a way to extend in-context classification to larger tables while retaining competitive predictive performance.
summary.tldr: TabICL scales in-context tabular classification through a two-stage architecture, delivering competitive accuracy and faster inference on large datasets.

title: TabICL: A Tabular Foundation Model for In-Context Learning on Large Data

abstract: Many generative applications, such as synthesis-based 3D molecular design, involve constructing compositional objects with continuous features. Here, we introduce Compositional Generative Flows (CGFlow), a novel framework that extends flow matching to generate objects in compositional steps while modeling continuous states. Our key insight is that modeling compositional state transitions can be formulated as a straightforward extension of the flow matching interpolation process. We further build upon the theoretical foundations of generative flow networks (GFlowNets), enabling reward-guided sampling of compositional structures. We apply CGFlow to synthesizable drug design by jointly designing the molecule’s synthetic pathway with its 3D binding pose. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art binding affinity and synthesizability on all 15 targets from the LIT-PCBA benchmark, and 4.2x improvement in sampling efficiency compared to 2D synthesis-based baseline. To our best knowledge, our method is also the first to achieve state of-art-performance in both Vina Dock (-9.42) and AiZynth success rate (36.1%) on the CrossDocked2020 benchmark.

paragraphs: Designing a molecule involves both discrete construction choices and continuous geometry. This paper introduces Compositional Generative Flows, or CGFlow, to handle objects built in stages while also modeling their continuous features. In its drug-design application, the system jointly proposes a synthetic pathway and the molecule’s three-dimensional binding pose.

The key technical idea extends the interpolation process used in flow matching to transitions between compositional states. The framework also draws on generative flow networks to guide sampling with rewards. These ingredients connect stepwise construction with continuous modeling, allowing synthesis decisions and spatial arrangement to be considered within one generative approach.

On all 15 LIT-PCBA targets, the authors report state-of-the-art binding affinity and synthesizability, together with 4.2 times better sampling efficiency than a two-dimensional synthesis-based baseline. They also report strong results on CrossDocked2020 for both Vina Dock and AiZynth success rate. These benchmark findings support joint optimization of molecular geometry and synthetic construction, rather than treating the generation of a molecule and its pathway as unrelated objectives.
summary.tldr: CGFlow jointly generates molecular synthesis pathways and three-dimensional binding poses through reward-guided compositional flow modeling.

title: Compositional Flows for 3D Molecule and Synthesis Pathway Co-design

abstract: Many variants of Optimal Transport (OT) have been developed to address its heavy computation. Among them, notably, Sliced Wasserstein (SW) is widely used for application domains by projecting the OT problem onto one-dimensional lines, and leveraging the closed-form expression of the univariate OT to reduce the computational burden. However, projecting measures onto low-dimensional spaces can lead to a loss of topological information. To mitigate this issue, in this work, we propose to replace one-dimensional lines with a more intricate structure, called tree systems. This structure is metrizable by a tree metric, which yields a closed-form expression for OT problems on tree systems. We provide an extensive theoretical analysis to formally define tree systems with their topological properties, introduce the concept of splitting maps, which operate as the projection mechanism onto these structures, then finally propose a novel variant of Radon transform for tree systems and verify its injectivity. This framework leads to an efficient metric between measures, termed Tree-Sliced Wasserstein distance on Systems of Lines (TSW-SL). By conducting a variety of experiments on gradient flows, image style transfer, and generative models, we illustrate that our proposed approach performs favorably compared to SW and its variants.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides a way to compare distributions, but its computation can be expensive. Sliced Wasserstein methods reduce that burden by projecting distributions onto lines, where transport has a closed-form expression. This paper addresses the loss of topological information that can occur when richer data geometry is reduced to one-dimensional projections.

The authors replace individual lines with tree systems. These structures admit a tree metric and retain a closed-form transport calculation. The theoretical development defines their topology, introduces splitting maps for projecting distributions onto them, and constructs a corresponding Radon transform. The authors prove that this transform is injective, supporting its ability to distinguish measures.

These pieces produce Tree-Sliced Wasserstein distance on Systems of Lines, an efficient metric between distributions. Experiments on gradient flows, image style transfer, and generative models show favorable performance compared with Sliced Wasserstein and its variants. The approach combines richer projection geometry with tractable transport computation, addressing the representational cost of simplifying every comparison to a line.
summary.tldr: Tree systems provide richer projection geometry for an efficient Wasserstein metric, with theoretical guarantees and favorable experimental results.

title: Tree-Sliced Wasserstein Distance: A Geometric Perspective

abstract: While contrastive multi-view clustering has achieved remarkable success, it implicitly assumes balanced class distribution. However, real-world multi-view data primarily exhibits class imbalance distribution. Consequently, existing methods suffer performance degradation due to their inability to perceive and model such imbalance. To address this challenge, we present the first systematic study of imbalanced multi-view clustering, focusing on two fundamental problems: i. perceiving class imbalance distribution, and ii. mitigating representation degradation of minority samples. We propose PROTOCOL, a novel PaRtial Optimal TranspOrt-enhanced COntrastive Learning framework for imbalanced multi-view clustering. First, for class imbalance perception, we map multi-view features into a consensus space and reformulate the imbalanced clustering as a partial optimal transport (POT) problem, augmented with progressive mass constraints and weighted KL divergence for class distributions. Second, we develop a POT-enhanced class-rebalanced contrastive learning at both feature and class levels, incorporating logit adjustment and class-sensitive learning to enhance minority sample representations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PROTOCOL significantly improves clustering performance on imbalanced multi-view data, filling a critical research gap in this field.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering groups examples using several views of the same data. The paper argues that contrastive approaches implicitly assume balanced classes, which creates problems when some groups are much smaller than others. It separates the challenge into recognizing the unequal class distribution and preventing minority examples from receiving weaker representations.

PROTOCOL first maps features from different views into a consensus space. It formulates imbalanced clustering as a partial optimal transport problem, adding progressive mass constraints and a weighted KL divergence for class distributions. These components allow the clustering formulation to account for imbalance. The method then uses transport-enhanced contrastive learning at both feature and class levels.

Logit adjustment and class-sensitive learning rebalance the contrastive process to improve minority representations. The approach therefore connects estimating unequal group structure with changing how representations are learned. Extensive experiments report significant clustering improvements on imbalanced multi-view data, supporting the value of addressing imbalance in both the assignment process and the feature learning objective.
summary.tldr: PROTOCOL combines partial optimal transport with rebalanced contrastive learning to improve clustering when multi-view data has unequal class sizes.

title: PROTOCOL: Partial Optimal Transport-enhanced Contrastive Learning for Imbalanced Multi-view Clustering

abstract: Symmetry in the parameter space of deep neural networks (DNNs) has proven beneficial for various deep learning applications. A well-known example is the permutation symmetry in Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), where permuting the rows of weight matrices in one layer and applying the inverse permutation to adjacent layers yields a functionally equivalent model. While permutation symmetry fully characterizes the equivalence set for MLPs, its discrete nature limits its utility for transformers. In this paper, we introduce rotation symmetry, a novel form of parameter space symmetry for transformers that generalizes permutation symmetry by rotating parameter matrices in self-attention layers. Unlike permutation symmetry, rotation symmetry operates in a continuous domain, thereby significantly expanding the equivalence set for transformers. Based on this property, we propose a theoretically optimal parameter matching algorithm as a plug-and-play module to enhance model fusion. We evaluate our approach using pre-trained transformers across diverse natural language and vision tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our rotation symmetry-based matching algorithm substantially improves model fusion, highlighting the potential of parameter space symmetry to facilitate model fusion. Our code is available on https://github.com/zhengzaiyi/RotationSymmetry

paragraphs: Two neural networks can implement the same function even when their parameters look different. This matters for model fusion: combining parameters is easier when equivalent internal representations are aligned. The paper studies how to obtain that alignment in transformers by exploiting transformations that preserve a model’s function.

The authors introduce rotation symmetry in self-attention layers. Permutation symmetry rearranges parameter coordinates, whereas rotation symmetry allows continuous transformations of parameter matrices. This expands the set of equivalent transformer representations available for matching. The practical significance is that alignment can search beyond discrete rearrangements when bringing separately trained models into correspondence.

Using this symmetry, the authors develop a parameter matching algorithm described as theoretically optimal, packaged as a module for model fusion. Experiments with pretrained transformers on language and vision tasks report substantial improvements in fusion. These findings support continuous symmetry as a useful resource for matching models; the optimality claim concerns parameter matching, while the benefits to fusion are established experimentally.
summary.tldr: Rotation symmetry expands the ways transformer parameters can be aligned, enabling a matching algorithm that improves model fusion in language and vision experiments.

title: Beyond the Permutation Symmetry of Transformers: The Role of Rotation for Model Fusion

abstract: Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) have recently demonstrated impressive generative capabilities. There is emerging evidence that their sample reconstruction ability can yield meaningful representations for recognition tasks. In this paper, we demonstrate that the objectives underlying generation and representation learning are not perfectly aligned. Through a spectral analysis, we find that minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between the original graph and its reconstructed counterpart does not necessarily optimize representations for downstream tasks. Instead, focusing on reconstructing a small subset of features, specifically those capturing global information, proves to be more effective for learning powerful representations. Motivated by these insights, we propose a novel framework, the Smooth Diffusion Model for Graphs (SDMG), which introduces a multi-scale smoothing loss and low-frequency information encoders to promote the recovery of global, low-frequency details, while suppressing irrelevant high-frequency noise. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our method, suggesting a promising direction for advancing diffusion models in graph representation learning.

paragraphs: A diffusion model that reconstructs a graph accurately does not necessarily learn the most useful representation for recognizing its properties. This paper examines that mismatch between generation and representation learning. Its spectral analysis shows that minimizing reconstruction mean squared error need not optimize the information used by downstream tasks.

The authors find that emphasizing a smaller set of features carrying global information can produce stronger representations. Their Smooth Diffusion Model for Graphs, or SDMG, uses a multi-scale smoothing loss and low-frequency information encoders. These components encourage reconstruction of global, low-frequency structure while suppressing high-frequency variation treated as irrelevant noise.

The approach changes which reconstruction errors the learning process emphasizes, connecting the training objective more closely to the desired representation. Extensive experiments support its effectiveness for graph representation learning. The findings suggest that diffusion models’ reconstruction ability can be more useful for recognition when the objective prioritizes relevant structure; they do not establish that minimizing ordinary reconstruction error always produces poor representations.
summary.tldr: SDMG improves graph representations by directing diffusion reconstruction toward global, low-frequency information.

title: SDMG: Smoothing Your Diffusion Models for Powerful Graph Representation Learning

abstract: We analyze algorithms for solving stochastic variational inequalities (VI) without the bounded variance or bounded domain assumptions, where our main focus is min-max optimization with possibly unbounded constraint sets. We focus on two classes of problems: monotone VIs; and structured nonmonotone VIs that admit a solution to the weak Minty VI. The latter assumption allows us to solve structured nonconvex-nonconcave min-max problems. For both classes of VIs, to make the expected residual norm less than $\varepsilon$, we show an oracle complexity of $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$, which is the best-known for constrained VIs. In our setting, this complexity had been obtained with the bounded variance assumption in the literature, which is not even satisfied for bilinear min-max problems with an unbounded domain. We obtain this complexity for stochastic oracles whose variance can grow as fast as the squared norm of the optimization variable.
originalAbstract: We analyze algorithms for solving stochastic variational inequalities (VI) without the bounded variance or bounded domain assumptions, where our main focus is min-max optimization with possibly unbounded constraint sets. We focus on two classes of problems: monotone VIs; and structured nonmonotone VIs that admit a solution to the weak Minty VI. The latter assumption allows us to solve structured nonconvex-nonconcave min-max problems. For both classes of VIs, to make the expected residual norm less than $\varepsilon$, we show an oracle complexity of $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$, which is the best-known for constrained VIs. In our setting, this complexity had been obtained with the bounded variance assumption in the literature, which is not even satisfied for bilinear min-max problems with an unbounded domain. We obtain this complexity for stochastic oracles whose variance can grow as fast as the squared norm of the optimization variable.

The authors note that bounded variance can fail even for bilinear min-max problems when the domain is unbounded.
