title: Solving Stochastic Variational Inequalities without the Bounded Variance Assumption

abstract: Text-to-3D generation has advanced rapidly, yet state-of-the-art models, encompassing both optimization-based and feed-forward architectures, still face two fundamental limitations. First, they struggle with coarse semantic alignment, often failing to capture fine-grained prompt details. Second, they lack robust 3D spatial understanding, leading to geometric inconsistencies and catastrophic failures in part assembly and spatial relationships. To address these challenges, we propose VLM3D, a general framework that repurposes large vision-language models (VLMs) as powerful, differentiable semantic and spatial critics. Our core contribution is a dual-query critic signal derived from the VLM’s "Yes/No" log-odds, which assesses both semantic fidelity and geometric coherence. We demonstrate the generality of this guidance signal across two distinct paradigms: (1) As a reward objective for optimization-based pipelines, VLM3D significantly outperforms existing methods on standard benchmarks. (2) As a test-time guidance module for feed-forward pipelines, it actively steers the iterative sampling process of SOTA native 3D models to correct severe spatial errors. VLM3D establishes a principled and generalizable path to inject the VLM’s rich, language-grounded understanding of both semantics and space into diverse 3D generative pipelines.

title: Let Language Constrain Geometry: Vision–Language Models as Semantic and Spatial Critics for 3D Generation

abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable generative capability, yet adapting these large pretrained text-to-video (T2V) models to video super-resolution (VSR) typically encounters challenges, such as artifacts introduced by complex degradations in real-world scenarios and compromised fidelity due to the strong generative capacity of the powerful T2V models. We present WEVSR, a novel approach that adapts a pretrained flow-matching video diffusion transformer to VSR. First, we design a task-oriented adaptation strategy that leverages timestep sampling and noise augmentation to enhance detail restoration while preserving structural stability. Second, we propose a lightweight multi-level discrete wavelet transform (DWT) front-end for the VAE encoder, injecting explicit frequency priors into the latent space without modifying the pretrained decoder. Extensive experiments across multiple VSR benchmarks demonstrate that WEVSR achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing approaches. Code and models will be released here.

paragraphs: Powerful video generators can supply detail for video super-resolution, but adapting them introduces a tension between visual richness and fidelity to the input. Real-world degradations can create artifacts, while strong generative behavior can compromise structural accuracy. WEVSR adapts a pretrained flow-matching video diffusion transformer to address these issues.

The method has two main components. A task-specific adaptation strategy uses timestep sampling and noise augmentation to improve detail restoration while maintaining structural stability. A lightweight front-end applies a multilevel discrete wavelet transform before the variational autoencoder’s encoder. This supplies explicit frequency information to the latent representation while keeping the pretrained decoder unchanged.

The combination targets both the restoration process and the representation of the degraded input. Wavelet-based guidance provides frequency structure, while the adaptation strategy controls how the pretrained generator is used for restoration. Experiments across multiple video super-resolution benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance against existing approaches. The findings support adapting large video generators through targeted training choices and a compact encoder addition to improve restoration quality.
summary.tldr: WEVSR combines task-specific diffusion adaptation with a wavelet-enhanced encoder to achieve reported state-of-the-art video super-resolution performance.

title: WEVSR: Video Diffusion Generators for Real-World Video Super-Resolution with Wavelet-Enhanced VAE Encoder

abstract: Fine-tuning large models on edge devices is severely hindered by the memory-intensive backpropagation (BP) in standard frameworks like federated learning and split learning. While substituting BP with zeroth-order optimization can significantly reduce memory footprints, it typically suffers from prohibitively degraded convergence speed. To resolve this dilemma, we propose Hybrid-Order Split Federated Learning (HO-SFL). By reformulating the split learning process within a Lagrangian framework, HO-SFL decouples the optimization landscape: The server performs precise first-order updates (i.e., BP), whereas clients conduct memory-efficient zeroth-order optimization. This hybrid design not only eliminates the need for client-side BP but also enables dimension-free model aggregation, drastically lowering communication costs. Crucially, we provide a theoretical convergence analysis, demonstrating that HO-SFL mitigates the dimension-dependent convergence slowdown of zeroth-order optimization, achieving a convergence rate comparable to first-order methods. Extensive experiments on tasks across vision and language modalities validate that HO-SFL achieves convergence speeds comparable to first-order baselines while significantly reducing communication costs and client memory footprints.

paragraphs: HO-SFL tackles the memory demands of fine-tuning large models on edge devices. Backpropagation makes conventional federated and split learning expensive for these clients. Zeroth-order optimization can reduce memory needs, but its slow convergence creates a competing cost. The paper seeks to retain its memory advantage without accepting the usual convergence penalty.

The method reformulates split learning within a Lagrangian framework and assigns different optimization methods to the server and clients. The server uses first-order updates through backpropagation, while clients use zeroth-order optimization. This removes client-side backpropagation and enables dimension-free model aggregation, substantially lowering communication costs as well as client memory requirements.

The theoretical analysis shows that HO-SFL mitigates the dimension-dependent slowdown associated with zeroth-order optimization and achieves a convergence rate comparable to first-order methods. Experiments across vision and language tasks likewise report comparable convergence speeds alongside significant memory and communication reductions. The findings support dividing optimization responsibilities according to the different capabilities of the server and edge devices.
summary.tldr: HO-SFL pairs server backpropagation with client zeroth-order updates to reduce memory and communication while retaining comparable convergence speed.

title: HO-SFL: Hybrid-Order Split Federated Learning with Backprop-Free Clients and Dimension-Free Aggregation

abstract: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely-used test-time inference technique for improving performance in chain-of-thought reasoning. It consists of generating multiple responses, or "samples," from a large language model (LLM) and selecting the most frequent answer. This procedure can naturally be viewed as a majority vote or empirical mode estimation. Despite its effectiveness, self-consistency is prohibitively expensive at scale when naively applied to datasets, and it lacks a unified theoretical treatment of sample efficiency and scaling behavior. In this paper, we provide the first comprehensive analysis of SC’s scaling behavior and its variants, drawing on mode estimation and voting theory. We derive and empirically validate power law scaling for self-consistency across datasets, and analyze the sample efficiency for fixed-allocation and dynamic-allocation sampling schemes. From these insights, we introduce Blend-ASC, a novel variant of self-consistency that dynamically allocates samples to questions during inference, achieving state-of-the-art sample efficiency. Our approach uses $4.8\times$ fewer samples than vanilla SC on average, outperforming both fixed- and dynamic-allocation SC baselines, thereby demonstrating the superiority of our approach in terms of efficiency. In contrast to existing variants, we note that Blend-ASC is hyperparameter-free and can fit any budget of samples, ensuring it can be easily applied to any self-consistency application.

paragraphs: Self-consistency improves language-model reasoning by generating multiple responses and choosing the answer that appears most often. Its cost can become substantial when applied across many questions. This paper treats that procedure as a problem of estimating the most common answer, using mode estimation and voting theory to study how efficiently samples can be used.

The authors derive and empirically validate power-law scaling behavior across datasets. They also analyze approaches that assign a fixed number of samples to questions and approaches that adjust allocations dynamically. summary.tldr: Blend-ASC dynamically allocates reasoning samples across questions, using 4.8 times fewer samples than vanilla self-consistency on average.

title: Optimal Self-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning with Large Language Models

abstract: We identify a security–fidelity tradeoff in defending LLMs against indirect prompt injection: defenses resist injected instructions largely by suppressing untrusted text, which corrupts tasks that must preserve it, such as translation and document editing. Attack-success metrics cannot see this, because a model that ignores an injection and one that faithfully processes it as data score identically. We introduce SecFid, a benchmark built so that executing an injection, processing it as data, and ignoring it produce distinguishable outputs. This makes fidelity measurable, and exposes a frontier: across 1,168 examples and 48 configurations, no model or defense achieves both objectives. The highest-fidelity model reaches 96.5% fidelity at 47.8% security, while the most secure defenses invert this, at 99.3% security but only 71.0%–73.9% fidelity. Even defenses with identical security differ in how they earn it: some repair hijacks into faithful processing, others simply suppress benign content. A decision-theoretic analysis shows why no fixed choice can be right everywhere: the correct behavior is not a property of the defense but of the deployment, set by its relative cost of a hijack versus a dropped span. Security alone therefore measures only half of robustness, and reporting it without fidelity hides the price at which it was bought.

paragraphs: A prompt-injection defense can appear successful by discarding suspicious text, even when the task requires preserving that text through translation or editing. Standard attack-success metrics cannot distinguish this omission from correctly processing the text as data. The paper introduces SecFid to measure security alongside fidelity to the requested transformation.

A decision-theoretic analysis explains why the appropriate tradeoff depends on deployment-specific costs of hijacking versus dropping text. The findings make fidelity an essential companion to security reporting, because a strong security number alone can conceal substantial damage to the intended task.
summary.tldr: SecFid shows that prompt-injection defenses can gain security by dropping required content, exposing a deployment-dependent tradeoff with fidelity.

title: Security–Fidelity Tradeoffs: The Hidden Cost of Prompt Injection Defense

abstract: While diffusion models have advanced anomaly detection, their reliance on multi-step noise schedules introduces significant computational complexity. In this paper, we demonstrate that the generative capability of diffusion is not required for tabular anomaly detection. We revisit core principles of denoising without targeting data generation and present a deep-learning approach that streamlines these objectives into a fixed-noise formulation. Unlike denoising autoencoders that rely on reconstruction error, our method utilizes a preconditioning with an explicit linear reference channel. We train a self-supervised fixed-noise denoising predictor and derive an anomaly score from the expected deviation under repeated perturbations, yielding a stability proxy rather than merely measuring distance to the data manifold. On the well-established ADBench benchmark, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with improvements over existing baselines of 1.22% in AUCROC and 1.13% in AUCPR, the most informative and threshold-independent metrics. Our approach emphasizes structural simplicity and efficiency, demonstrating that a single-step, stability-based objective outperforms complex generative schedules.

This paper asks whether tabular anomaly detection needs that generative machinery. It develops a simpler method that learns to denoise at a fixed noise level, without targeting the generation of new data.

The method trains a self-supervised denoising predictor and uses preconditioning with an explicit linear reference channel. Its anomaly score comes from expected deviations under repeated perturbations. These findings support the usefulness of a single-step denoising objective for this benchmark. The computational simplification concerns the denoising formulation: scoring still involves repeated perturbations. The broader contribution is showing that effective anomaly detection can draw on denoising without requiring a full generative diffusion schedule.
summary.tldr: A fixed-noise denoiser detects tabular anomalies through perturbation stability and outperforms existing baselines on ADBench.

title: Denoising without Diffusion: Fixed-Noise Denoiser Anomaly Detection in Tabular Data

abstract: Aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with specific personas typically relies on Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) or Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF); however, these methods are resource-intensive, requiring expensive data collection and distinct model training for each target personality. In this work, we propose a parameter-efficient framework for continuous, multi-dimensional personality control via inference-time activation steering. Our approach addresses the challenge of combining multiple interventions by iteratively retraining probes on the residual stream modified by prior traits, ensuring compatibility. Once established, these steering vectors function as modular, reusable primitives; users can instantly synthesize novel, complex personality profiles by simply adjusting steering coefficients ($\alpha$) without any additional training. To support this, we introduce an automated pipeline that identifies optimal intervention layers via activation separation analysis and calibrates coefficients via hyperparameter optimization to maximize alignment while constraining perplexity. Empirical evaluations validate individual trait shifts using an LLM-as-a-judge framework and demonstrate, via the Big Five inventory, that our method effectively modulates the model’s holistic personality profile without updating base model parameters.

paragraphs: This paper develops continuous control over an LLM’s expressed personality by steering its internal activations during inference. Conventional persona alignment can require costly data collection and separate training for different personalities. Here, the base model’s parameters stay fixed, and reusable steering vectors provide adjustable controls over multiple traits.

Combining those controls requires accounting for their interactions. The method repeatedly retrains probes on the residual stream after earlier trait interventions have modified it, making subsequent interventions compatible with previous ones. An automated pipeline chooses intervention layers by examining activation separation. It also calibrates steering strengths through hyperparameter optimization, seeking stronger personality alignment while constraining perplexity.

Evaluations use an LLM judge to assess individual trait changes and the Big Five inventory to assess the broader personality profile. The findings support modular inference-time control over both specific traits and their combined expression, with preparation concentrated in constructing and calibrating the reusable interventions.
summary.tldr: Reusable activation-steering vectors let users adjust and combine LLM personality traits at inference time without changing base model parameters.

title: Controllable and Explainable Personality Sliders for LLMs at Inference Time

abstract: Recent advances in large image editing models have shifted the paradigm from text-driven instructions to vision-prompt editing, where user intent is inferred directly from visual inputs such as marks, arrows, and visual–text prompts. While this paradigm greatly expands usability, it also introduces a critical and underexplored safety risk: the attack surface itself becomes visual. In this work, we propose Vision-Centric Jailbreak Attack (VJA), the first visual-to-visual jailbreak attack that conveys malicious instructions purely through visual inputs. To systematically study this emerging threat, we introduce IESBench, a safety-oriented benchmark for image editing models. Extensive experiments on IESBench demonstrate that VJA effectively compromises state-of-the-art commercial models, achieving attack success rates of up to 80.9% on Nano Banana Pro and 70.1% on GPT-Image-1.5. To mitigate this vulnerability, we propose a training-free defense based on introspective multimodal reasoning, which substantially improves the safety of poorly aligned models to a level comparable with commercial systems, without auxiliary guard models and with negligible computational overhead. Our findings expose new vulnerabilities, provide both a benchmark and practical defense to advance safe and trustworthy modern image editing systems.

abstract: Recent years have witnessed significant progress in developing effective diffusion models. Parallel sampling is a promising recent approach that reformulates the sequential denoising process as solving a system of nonlinear equations, and it can be combined with other acceleration techniques. However, current progress is limited by the trade-off between high fidelity and computational efficiency. This paper addresses the challenge of scaling to high-dimensional, multi-modal generation. Specifically, we present ROPA (Robust Parallel Diffusion Sampling), which takes into account the properties of the denoising process and solves the linear system using adaptive local sparsity to achieve stable parallel sampling. Extensive experiments demonstrate ROPA’s effectiveness: it significantly accelerates sampling across diverse image and video diffusion models, achieving up to $2.9\times$ speedup with eight core, an improvement of 20.8% over baselines without sacrificing sample quality. ROPA enables parallel sampling methods to provide a solid foundation for real-time, high-fidelity diffusion generation.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation usually proceeds through sequential denoising steps. Parallel sampling instead expresses that process as a system of nonlinear equations, creating opportunities to perform work concurrently. The challenge is to gain speed while keeping generated samples faithful, especially for high-dimensional image and video generation.

ROPA, or Robust Parallel Diffusion Sampling, uses properties of the denoising process to choose adaptive local sparsity when solving the associated linear system. This changes how much local dependency information the solver retains as it works. The approach is designed to support stable parallel sampling while managing the computation required by those dependencies.

Experiments across image and video diffusion models report sampling speedups of up to 2.9 times with eight cores, representing a 20.8% improvement over baselines without sacrificing sample quality. These are reported experimental outcomes across the tested models. The work strengthens the case for parallel sampling as a component of fast, high-fidelity generation, and the abstract notes that this general sampling strategy can be combined with other acceleration techniques.
summary.tldr: ROPA adapts local sparsity in parallel diffusion sampling, reporting up to 2.9× speedup without sacrificing sample quality.

title: Robust Parallel Diffusion Sampling via Dynamic Jacobian Bandwidth

abstract: Evaluation of socially unsafe content in spoken dialogues remains text-centric, missing prosody and transcription failures. We present LALM-as-a-Judge, which includes an open benchmark of 24,000 multi-turn spoken dialogues with one localized unsafe turn, generated out of 8 socially unsafe categories and 5 severity levels. We evaluate 6 large audio-language models (LALMs) as judges, open and closed-source, in text-only, audio-only, and multimodal setups by their sensitivity, severity-order specificity, and turn-position bias for socially harmful content in the dialogue. Results show that audio contributes non-lexical evidence beyond transcript semantics and that multimodal gains are not universal but can be text-anchored, balanced, conservative, and interfering, which we link to the audio pathway bottlenecks and fusion limits. We position the benchmark as diagnostic and derive practitioner guidance for model, modality, and prompts choices.
originalAbstract: Evaluation of socially unsafe content in spoken dialogues remains text-centric, missing prosody and transcription failures. We present LALM-as-a-Judge, which includes an open benchmark of 24,000 multi-turn spoken dialogues with one localized unsafe turn, generated out of 8 socially unsafe categories and 5 severity levels. We evaluate 6 large audio-language models (LALMs) as judges, open and closed-source, in text-only, audio-only, and multimodal setups by their sensitivity, severity-order specificity, and turn-position bias for socially harmful content in the dialogue. Results show that audio contributes non-lexical evidence beyond transcript semantics and that multimodal gains are not universal but can be text-anchored, balanced, conservative, and interfering, which we link to the audio pathway bottlenecks and fusion limits. We position the benchmark as diagnostic and derive practitioner guidance for model, modality, and prompts choices.

paragraphs: Safety evaluation of spoken conversations often relies on transcripts, which can lose vocal information and contain transcription errors. This paper introduces a benchmark for testing whether large audio-language models can judge socially unsafe content in multi-turn speech. It contains 24,000 generated dialogues, each with one localized unsafe turn, spanning eight categories and five severity levels.

The authors evaluate six open- and closed-source models using text alone, audio alone, and both modalities together. They examine sensitivity to harmful content, distinctions among severity levels, and whether a harmful turn’s position changes the judgment. These measures make the benchmark useful for diagnosing different kinds of evaluation behavior.

The findings show that audio supplies evidence beyond the words captured by a transcript. However, combining audio and text does not always improve judgments: models can remain anchored to text, balance the modalities, become conservative, or experience interference. The authors connect these patterns to limitations in audio processing and modality fusion, and derive guidance for choosing models, input modalities, and prompts.
summary.tldr: A spoken-dialogue safety benchmark shows that audio adds useful evidence, but combining it with text does not consistently improve judgments.

title: LALM-as-a-Judge: Benchmarking Large Audio-Language Models for Safety Evaluation in Multi-Turn Spoken Dialogues

abstract: End-to-end prediction of high-order crystal tensor properties from atomic structures remains challenging: while spherical-harmonic equivariant models are expressive, their Clebsch-Gordan tensor products incur substantial compute and memory costs for higher-order targets. We propose the Cartesian Environment Interaction Tensor Network (CEITNet), an approach that constructs a multi-channel Cartesian local environment tensor for each atom and performs flexible many-body mixing via learnable channel-space interactions. By performing learning in channel space and using Cartesian tensor bases to assemble equivariant outputs, CEITNet enables efficient construction of high-order tensor. Across benchmark datasets for order-2 dielectric, order-3 piezoelectric, and order-4 elastic tensor prediction, CEITNet surpasses prior high-order prediction methods on key accuracy criteria while offering high computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Predicting crystal properties from atomic structure becomes demanding when the output is a high-order tensor, a quantity with several directional components. The prediction must transform consistently when the structure is rotated. Existing spherical-harmonic models can provide this equivariance, but their tensor-product operations become costly in computation and memory for higher-order outputs.

CEITNet changes how these interactions are represented and learned. For each atom, it builds a multichannel Cartesian tensor describing the local environment. Learnable interactions between channels provide flexible many-body mixing. Cartesian tensor bases then assemble the final equivariant outputs, allowing much of the learning to take place in channel space.

The authors evaluate second-order dielectric, third-order piezoelectric, and fourth-order elastic tensor prediction. CEITNet exceeds prior high-order prediction methods on key accuracy criteria while retaining high computational efficiency. The reported results support this separation between learned channel interactions and geometric output construction as an effective route to accurate, efficient crystal tensor prediction.
summary.tldr: CEITNet uses Cartesian environment tensors and learned channel interactions to predict high-order crystal properties accurately and efficiently.

title: Efficient Equivariant High-Order Crystal Tensor Prediction via Cartesian Local-Environment Many-Body Coupling

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in stateless systems, such as autonomous driving and robotics. This paper investigates a novel threat: Semantic-Aware Hijacking. We explore the feasibility of hijacking multiple stateless decisions simultaneously using a single universal perturbation. We introduce the Semantic-Aware Universal Perturbation (SAUP), which acts as a semantic router, "actively" perceiving input semantics and routing them to distinct, attacker-defined targets. To achieve this, we conduct a theoretical and empirical analysis on the geometric properties in the latent space. Guided by these insights, we propose the Semantic-Oriented (SORT) optimization strategy and annotate a new dataset with fine-grained semantics to evaluate performance. Extensive experiments on three representative MLLMs demonstrate the fundamental feasibility of this attack, achieving a 66% attack success rate over five targets using a single frame against Qwen.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a single universal adversarial perturbation can redirect multiple independent decisions by a multimodal language model. The targeted behavior depends on the meaning of the input: different semantic cases are steered toward different attacker-selected outputs. The question is especially relevant to stateless systems, where the decisions do not rely on retained conversational state.

The proposed Semantic-Aware Universal Perturbation acts as a semantic router. The authors analyze geometric properties of the model’s latent space theoretically and empirically, then use those findings to develop the Semantic-Oriented optimization strategy. They also annotate a dataset with fine-grained semantic labels to evaluate this form of input-dependent redirection.

Experiments across three representative multimodal models establish the attack’s feasibility. The reported Qwen result reaches a 66% attack success rate over five targets using a single frame. This demonstrates the studied possibility of one perturbation supporting multiple semantic destinations; the result is a measured success rate in the evaluated setting, rather than evidence of reliable control over every decision.
summary.tldr: The paper demonstrates that one adversarial perturbation can steer a multimodal model toward different attacker-selected outputs depending on input semantics.

title: Semantic Router: On the Feasibility of Hijacking MLLMs via a Single Adversarial Perturbation

abstract: Despite the rapid progress of vision-language-action (VLA) models, the prevailing practice of predicting action chunks as discrete waypoints remains structurally misaligned with the intrinsic continuity of physical motion. This discretization arises naturally from fixed-rate robot data collection and the token-by-token prediction paradigm of large language models, but ties actions to rigid sampling rates, does not naturally support analytically consistent higher-order derivatives, and introduces quantization artifacts that hinder precise, compliant interaction. We propose Neural Implicit Action Fields (NIAF), which reformulates chunk-level action representation from discrete waypoints to continuous action functions. Using a vision-language model as a hierarchical spectral modulator over a learnable motion prior, NIAF synthesizes continuous-time action manifolds with arbitrary temporal resolution. This formulation enables analytical differentiation, allowing explicit supervision of velocity and regularization of higher-order derivative signals to promote mathematical consistency, physical plausibility, and control smoothness. Our approach achieves strong results on CALVIN and LIBERO across diverse backbones. Real-world experiments further confirm that NIAF supports stable impedance control, bridging policy-side action generation and execution-side smooth control.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models commonly predict robot movements as chunks of discrete waypoints. The paper argues that this representation fits fixed-rate data collection but poorly matches continuous physical motion. It ties actions to particular sampling rates, introduces quantization artifacts, and does not naturally provide analytically consistent derivatives for smooth, precise control.

Neural Implicit Action Fields represents each action chunk as a continuous function of time. A vision-language model acts as a hierarchical spectral modulator over a learned motion prior to generate these functions. The resulting actions can be evaluated at arbitrary temporal resolution and differentiated analytically, connecting the predicted motion directly to its velocity and higher-order derivatives.

This allows explicit velocity supervision and regularization of higher-order derivative signals to encourage consistent, physically plausible, smooth movement. The authors report strong results on CALVIN and LIBERO across multiple backbones. Real-world experiments also demonstrate support for stable impedance control. Together, the results connect a continuous policy representation with the smooth execution needed for compliant physical interaction.
summary.tldr: NIAF represents robot action chunks as continuous functions, enabling flexible sampling and derivative-based supervision for smoother control.

title: Neural Implicit Action Fields: From Discrete Waypoints to Continuous Functions for Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) aims to reconcile model generalization in the presence of distribution shifts. Current TTA methods usually leverage sample uncertainty to select reliable samples for model adjustment via entropy minimization (EM). However, sample uncertainty often relies on a plausible metric and leaves many unreliable samples into EM process, potentially leading to model collapse. Importantly, these excluded samples incur biased data features of the shifted distribution in TTA. This paper introduces SaTeen, a Structural Alignment-based Test-Time Adaptation method that performs two-fold aligning the structures of test samples with the reliable reference structures. Specifically, the two-fold alignments are 1) Intra-sample structure alignment, where SaTeen maximizes cross-entropy discrepancy between a sample (reference) and its structure-disrupted counterpart, with the assumption of stable dominant features; 2) Inter-sample structure alignment, where SaTeen minimizes the reconstruction error of test samples in the reference subspace spanned by the Incremental PCA on reliable samples, with the assumption of stale intrinsic data manifold. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that SaTeen achieves the state-of-the-art performance across various scenarios for both TTA and continual TTA.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model when incoming data differs from its training distribution. Many approaches select supposedly reliable samples and make their predictions more confident through entropy minimization. The paper identifies two problems: unreliable samples can still enter this process and destabilize the model, while excluding samples can bias the representation of the new distribution.

SaTeen instead aligns test-sample structure with reliable reference structure in two ways. Within a sample, it increases the cross-entropy discrepancy between a reference and a version whose structure has been disrupted, assuming dominant features remain stable. Across samples, it reduces reconstruction error in a reference subspace built using incremental principal component analysis on reliable samples. This second component assumes the underlying data manifold remains stable.

These complementary objectives use both the organization inside individual samples and the shared structure across samples to guide adaptation. The authors report state-of-the-art results across several test-time and continual test-time adaptation scenarios. The findings support structural alignment as an effective alternative adaptation signal under the stated structural assumptions.
summary.tldr: SaTeen improves test-time adaptation by aligning within-sample and between-sample structure with reliable references under stability assumptions.

title: SaTeen: Learning Structural Alignment for Continual Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: Structural nested mean models (SNMMs) are a principled approach to estimate the treatment effects over time. A particular strength of SNMMs is to break the joint effect of treatment sequences over time into localized, time-specific “blip effects”. This decomposition promotes interpretability through the incremental effects and enables the efficient offline evaluation of optimal treatment policies without re-computation. However, neural frameworks for SNMMs are lacking, as their inherently sequential g-estimation scheme prevents end-to-end, gradient-based training. Here, we propose DeepBlip, the first neural framework for SNMMs, which overcomes this limitation with a novel double optimization trick to enable simultaneous learning of all blip functions. Our DeepBlip seamlessly integrates sequential neural networks like LSTMs or transformers to capture complex temporal dependencies. By design, our method correctly adjusts for time-varying confounding to produce unbiased estimates, and its Neyman-orthogonal loss function ensures robustness to nuisance model misspecification. Finally, we evaluate our DeepBlip across various clinical datasets, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Understanding a sequence of treatments requires separating effects that occur at different times. Structural nested mean models do this through localized “blip” effects, which describe incremental treatment contributions. This decomposition supports interpretation and efficient offline evaluation of treatment policies. However, their sequential estimation procedure has made end-to-end neural training difficult.

DeepBlip introduces a double optimization technique that allows all blip functions to be learned simultaneously. This makes the framework compatible with sequence models such as LSTMs and transformers, allowing it to represent complex dependencies over time. The contribution connects the time-specific structure of these causal models with gradient-based neural learning.

The method is designed to adjust for time-varying confounding and produce unbiased treatment-effect estimates. It also uses a Neyman-orthogonal loss to provide robustness to misspecification in nuisance models, the supporting models used during estimation. Across several clinical datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art performance. The stated benefit is richer temporal modeling while retaining the interpretable decomposition and confounding adjustment central to the underlying statistical approach.
summary.tldr: DeepBlip enables joint neural learning of time-specific treatment effects while incorporating confounding adjustment and a robust estimation objective.

title: DeepBlip: Estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effects Over Time

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable capabilities, they remain susceptible to sophisticated, multi-step jailbreak attacks that circumvent conventional surface-level safety alignment by exploiting the internal generation process. To address these vulnerabilities, we propose Reflector, a principled two-stage framework that internalizes self-reflection within the generation trajectory. Reflector first leverages teacher-guided generation to produce high-quality reflection data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), establishing structured reflection patterns. It subsequently uses Reinforcement Learning (RL) with outcome-driven and reward-validity supervision to instill robust, autonomous self-reflection capabilities. Empirical results show that Reflector achieves Defense Success Rates (DSR) exceeding 90% against complex indirect attacks while generalizing robustly across diverse threat scenarios. Notably, the framework enhances both task-specific and general utility, yielding a 5.85% gain on GSM8K alongside improved performance on knowledge-intensive benchmarks. By internalizing trajectory-level safety, Reflector overcomes the fundamental limitations of surface alignment without significant computational overhead, offering an efficient and scalable solution for the development of safe and capable LLMs.

paragraphs: Complex indirect jailbreaks can exploit a model’s generation process over multiple steps, bypassing safety alignment focused on surface behavior. Reflector trains models to reflect within that process. The aim is to make checking part of the generation trajectory, so the model develops structured and increasingly autonomous reflection capabilities.

Training proceeds in two stages. First, teacher-guided generation supplies reflection examples for supervised fine-tuning, establishing the desired patterns. Second, reinforcement learning uses outcome-driven supervision together with reward-validity supervision to strengthen autonomous reflection. This links the initial demonstrations to training signals intended to support reliable behavior under attack.

The reported defense success rate exceeds 90% against complex indirect attacks, with generalization across diverse threat scenarios. Reflector also improves utility, including a 5.85% gain on GSM8K and gains on knowledge-intensive benchmarks. The authors report these benefits without significant computational overhead. The findings suggest that internalizing reflection can improve measured safety and task performance together, while the reported success rate remains an empirical result rather than a guarantee against every attack.
summary.tldr: Reflector trains step-wise self-reflection, reporting over 90% defense success against complex indirect attacks alongside utility gains.

title: Reflector: Internalizing Step-wise Reflection against Indirect Jailbreaks

abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are typically pre-trained with explicit load-balancing constraints to ensure statistically balanced expert routing. Despite this, we observe that even well-trained MoE models exhibit significantly imbalanced routing. This behavior is arguably natural—and even desirable—as imbalanced routing allows models to concentrate domain-specific knowledge within a subset of experts. Expert parallelism (EP) is designed to scale MoE models by distributing experts across multiple devices, but with a less-discussed assumption of balanced routing. Under extreme imbalance, EP can funnel a disproportionate number of tokens to a small number of experts, leading to compute- and memory-bound failures on overloaded devices during post-training or inference, where explicit load balancing is often inapplicable. We propose Least-Loaded Expert Parallelism (LLEP), a novel EP algorithm that dynamically reroutes excess tokens and associated expert parameters from overloaded devices to underutilized ones. This ensures that all devices complete their workloads within the minimum collective latency while respecting memory constraints. Across different model scales, LLEP achieves up to 5x speedup and 4x reduction in peak memory usage compared to standard EP. This enables faster and higher-throughput post-training and inference, with 1.9x faster for gpt-oss-120b. We support our method with extensive theoretical analysis and comprehensive empirical evaluations, including ablation studies. These results illuminate key trade-offs and enable a principled framework for hardware-specific hyper-parameter tuning to achieve optimal performance.

That imbalance may reflect useful specialization, but standard expert parallelism can overload particular devices during inference or post-training. Least-Loaded Expert Parallelism addresses the hardware imbalance without assuming that token routing itself will remain uniform.

The algorithm moves excess tokens together with their needed expert parameters from busy devices to underused ones. Its allocation respects memory constraints while seeking minimum collective completion latency. Theory, ablations, and hardware-sensitive tuning analysis examine the tradeoffs created by this dynamic redistribution.

These results concern execution under imbalanced routing. The contribution is a scheduling and placement strategy, rather than evidence that changing a model’s learned expert choices improves its predictive quality.
summary.tldr: Least-Loaded Expert Parallelism redistributes tokens and expert parameters to relieve device overload from imbalanced MoE routing.

title: Least-Loaded Expert Parallelism: Load Balancing An Imbalanced Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: We study layered models, including feedforward networks, ResNets, and transformers, by limiting each layer to a width of $d = 3$, i.e., $\mathbb{R}^3$ as representation space. This allows us to track how a neural network changes low-dimensional topological invariants through its layers. Just about any topological structure may be simplified or even trivialized by simply increasing dimension; e.g., any knot is equivalent to an unknot in $\mathbb{R}^4$. By restricting to $\mathbb{R}^3$, we not only isolate the effects of activation and depth from that of width, we work in a space that lends itself to easy visualization. We focus on linking number here, deferring other invariants like link groups, Milnor’s $\bar{\mu}$-invariants, knot types, ambient cobordisms, to a sequel. We provide full proofs and empirical experiments to justify the following insights: When measured by their power to effect changes in linking numbers, the layer-skipping feature in ResNets is as powerful as the attention mechanism in transformers; both ResNets and transformers are strictly more powerful than feedforward neural networks with monotonic activations, which are in turn more powerful than invertible and flow-based models; but replacing monotonic activation with a nonmonotonic one elevates a feedforward network into the same expressivity class as ResNets and transformers. These results suggest that low-dimensional topology can be a useful tool to guide designs of AI architectures. We also generalize our results from $d = 3$ to arbitrary $d > 3$.

It initially restricts every layer to a three-dimensional representation space. This isolates the effects of depth and activation from width, since adding dimensions can simplify structures that remain nontrivial in fewer dimensions. Three dimensions also make these transformations easier to visualize.

Measured by their ability to change linking numbers, residual connections and transformer attention have equal power. Both are strictly more powerful than feedforward networks with monotonic activations, which in turn exceed invertible and flow-based models. These comparisons concern the specified topological measure of expressivity.

Changing the activation can alter that hierarchy: nonmonotonic activations bring feedforward networks into the same expressivity class as ResNets and transformers. The authors support these claims with proofs and experiments and extend the results beyond three dimensions. The work suggests that topology can reveal architectural differences that help guide network design.
summary.tldr: A topology-based analysis ranks neural architectures by their ability to change linking numbers and shows how nonmonotonic activations alter that hierarchy.

title: Low-dimensional topology of deep neural networks

abstract: Diffusion models have excelled at generative tasks for both continuous and token-based domains, but their application to discrete ordinal data remains underdeveloped. We present CountsDiff, a diffusion framework designed to model distributions on the natural numbers. CountsDiff extends the Blackout diffusion framework by simplifying its formulation through a direct parameterization in terms of a survival probability schedule and an explicit loss weighting. This introduces flexibility through design parameters with direct analogues in existing diffusion modeling frameworks. Beyond this reparameterization, CountsDiff introduces features from modern diffusion models, previously absent in counts-based domains, including continuous-time training, classifier-free guidance, and churn/remasking reverse dynamics that allow non-monotone reverse trajectories. We propose an initial instantiation of CountsDiff and validate it on natural image datasets (CIFAR-10, CelebA), exploring the effects of the introduced design parameters in a complex, well-studied, and interpretable data domain. We then highlight biological count assays as a natural use case, evaluating CountsDiff on single-cell RNA-seq imputation in fetal and heart cell atlases. Remarkably, we find that even this simple instantiation matches or surpasses the performance of a state-of-the-art discrete generative model and leading scRNA-seq imputation methods, while leaving substantial headroom for further gains through optimized design choices in future work.

The paper addresses a gap between diffusion methods for continuous measurements or tokens and methods for discrete values with a numerical ordering. Biological assays provide a motivating application, particularly when the task is to impute single-cell RNA-sequencing data.

This makes its design choices easier to connect with those in other diffusion frameworks. Even this simple version matches or exceeds a state-of-the-art discrete generative model and leading single-cell imputation methods. The authors identify further optimization of the framework's design choices as an opportunity for additional gains.
summary.tldr: CountsDiff adapts modern diffusion techniques to count data and shows competitive generation and single-cell RNA-sequencing imputation results.

title: CountsDiff: A diffusion model on the natural numbers for generation and imputation of count-based data

abstract: Activation sparsity offers a compelling route to accelerate large language model (LLM) inference by selectively suppressing hidden activations, yet existing approaches exhibit severe accuracy degradation at high sparsity. We show that this failure stems from representational instability: activation sparsity disrupts input-dependent activation learned during pretraining, inducing distribution shifts in hidden states. We address this issue by reframing activation sparsity as a representational alignment problem and introducing Spontaneous Neurons (SPON), a lightweight mechanism inspired by spontaneous neural activity in biological systems. SPON injects a small set of learnable, input-independent activation vectors that act as persistent representational anchors for sparse computation. These vectors are trained via distribution matching to the dense model and can be absorbed into bias terms after training, incurring negligible inference overhead. Across multiple LLM backbones, SPON consistently restores performance, stabilizes latent representations, and preserves generalization. Our results establish SPON as an effective and principled solution for reliable activation-sparse inference, and offer new insights into knowledge retention in LLMs.
originalAbstract: Activation sparsity offers a compelling route to accelerate large language model (LLM) inference by selectively suppressing hidden activations, yet existing approaches exhibit severe accuracy degradation at high sparsity. We show that this failure stems from representational instability: activation sparsity disrupts input-dependent activation learned during pretraining, inducing distribution shifts in hidden states. We address this issue by reframing activation sparsity as a representational alignment problem and introducing Spontaneous Neurons (SPON), a lightweight mechanism inspired by spontaneous neural activity in biological systems. SPON injects a small set of learnable, input-independent activation vectors that act as persistent representational anchors for sparse computation. These vectors are trained via distribution matching to the dense model and can be absorbed into bias terms after training, incurring negligible inference overhead. Across multiple LLM backbones, SPON consistently restores performance, stabilizes latent representations, and preserves generalization. Our results establish SPON as an effective and principled solution for reliable activation-sparse inference, and offer new insights into knowledge retention in LLMs.

paragraphs: Suppressing hidden activations can reduce language-model inference work, but aggressive sparsity can substantially damage accuracy. This paper attributes that failure to instability in the model's internal representations. Removing activations disrupts input-dependent patterns learned during pretraining, shifting the hidden-state distributions on which the model relies.

Spontaneous Neurons, or SPON, addresses sparsity as a representation-alignment problem. It introduces a small collection of learned activation vectors that do not depend on the current input. These persistent additions act as anchors for sparse computation and are trained by matching distributions to those of the dense model.

After training, the vectors can be folded into bias terms, giving the mechanism negligible inference overhead. Across multiple language-model backbones, the authors report restored performance, more stable latent representations, and preserved generalization. The result suggests that retaining useful behavior under activation sparsity involves stabilizing the representations produced by the remaining computation, alongside reducing how much of the network is active.
summary.tldr: SPON stabilizes sparsified language models with learned input-independent activation anchors that add negligible inference overhead.

title: Resting Neurons, Active Insights: Robustifying Activation Sparsity in LLMs via Spontaneity

abstract: Federated graph anomaly detection (GAD) aims to identify abnormal nodes in distributed subgraphs through federated learning. However, existing methods suffer from two limitations. 1) Their reliance on neighborhood aggregation assumes that anomalous information can be sufficiently captured, which often fails in federated learning with partitioned client subgraphs. 2) They overlook the detection bottleneck caused by weak attribute or structural anomalies. To tackle these challenges, we revisit federated GAD and reveal that weak anomalies exhibit harder-to-detect signals compared to strong anomalies. Specifically, we propose MV-FGAD, an efficient and effective federated GAD framework for mining anomalies of varying strengths. MV-FGAD introduces a federated knowledge learning module to aggregate and broadcast shared knowledge, which is further exploited to optimize local topological structures. Moreover, it designs a multi-view learning mechanism to capture diverse anomaly patterns, and adopts Mahalanobis distance–based scoring strategy to quantify node abnormality across views. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets of varying types and scales demonstrate MV-FGAD’s efficiency and effectiveness. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Junyi-Yan/MV-FGAD.

paragraphs: Federated graph anomaly detection searches for unusual nodes across subgraphs held by different clients. Partitioning a graph can leave local neighborhood aggregation without enough information to expose an anomaly. The paper also identifies a second difficulty: weak irregularities in node attributes or graph structure are harder to detect than strong ones and can become a detection bottleneck.

MV-FGAD combines shared knowledge with multiple views of anomaly patterns. A federated knowledge-learning module aggregates information and broadcasts the resulting shared knowledge, which clients use to improve local graph topology. A multi-view learning mechanism then captures different kinds of anomalous behavior. Mahalanobis-distance-based scoring quantifies how abnormal a node appears across those views.

Experiments on real-world datasets covering different types and scales support the framework's efficiency and effectiveness. The approach matters because it addresses both incomplete local graph context and variation in anomaly strength. Shared knowledge helps improve the structures used locally, while multiple views give the detector several ways to recognize irregularity. Together, these components target signals that a single neighborhood-based representation may fail to capture.
summary.tldr: MV-FGAD combines federated knowledge sharing and multiple anomaly views to detect weak and strong irregularities in distributed graphs.

title: MV-FGAD: Towards Efficient and Effective Federated Graph Anomaly Detection via Multi-view Learning

abstract: UI-to-code aims to translate UI screenshots into executable front-end code. Despite progress with vision-language models (VLMs), most existing methods formulate UI-to-code as a single-pass generation, which mismatches real-world UI development that is inherently iterative and feedback-driven. We reformulate UI-to-code as an interactive visual optimization problem, where code generation is embedded in a closed-loop process of execution, visual inspection, and iterative refinement driven by rendered visual feedback. To address the non-differentiability of visual objectives and the noise of absolute visual evaluators, we propose Relative Visual Policy Optimization (RVPO), a preference-based reinforcement learning method that optimizes relative visual rankings among rendered candidates under execution feedback. We instantiate this paradigm in UI2Code$^{\text{N}}$, an open-source 9B model trained via continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on UI drafting, UI polishing, and UI editing benchmarks, even outperforming larger models, with performance consistently improving through iterative visual optimization. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/zai-org/UI2Code_N.

paragraphs: Generating front-end code from a screenshot is often treated as a single prediction. UI2Code-N instead makes it an iterative process: generate code, execute it, inspect the rendered result, and refine the implementation. This puts visual feedback inside the generation loop, matching the feedback-driven character of interface development.

The training method, Relative Visual Policy Optimization, learns from relative rankings among rendered candidates under execution feedback. This addresses two difficulties: visual objectives cannot be directly differentiated through the whole process, and absolute visual scores can be noisy. The authors build an open-source nine-billion-parameter model through continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results on interface drafting, polishing, and editing benchmarks, including performance above larger models. Results also improve consistently through iterative visual optimization. The findings support training models to respond to what their code actually renders: comparing candidate appearances and revising execution-tested output can be an effective part of UI generation, rather than leaving all visual correction to a later human workflow.
summary.tldr: UI2Code-N learns to iteratively render, compare, and refine interface code, achieving leading results on drafting, polishing, and editing benchmarks.

title: UI2Code$^\textN$: UI-to-Code Generation as Interactive Visual Optimization

abstract: Offline meta-reinforcement learning requires agents to generalize to unseen tasks from fixed datasets, yet existing sequence-based and MoE-based methods rely on implicit or token-level routing signals that fail to capture task-level structure. We propose the Task-Guided Router (TGR), a structured expert-routing framework that explicitly models inter-task relationships via multi-view task representations that combine semantic descriptors, behavioral summaries, and latent dynamics features. Using structure-guided routing, TGR assigns experts based on global task compatibility rather than local trajectory fragments, enabling stable specialization and effective knowledge transfer across tasks.Extensive experiments on continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate that TGR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline meta-RL methods in few-shot generalization, particularly under sparse data and heterogeneous dynamics. Our results highlight the importance of task-level priors for robust offline meta-reinforcement learning.

We propose the Task-Guided Router (TGR), a structured expert-routing framework that explicitly models inter-task relationships via multi-view task representations that combine semantic descriptors, behavioral summaries, and latent dynamics features. Using structure-guided routing, TGR assigns experts based on global task compatibility rather than local trajectory fragments, enabling stable specialization and effective knowledge transfer across tasks.Extensive experiments on continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate that TGR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art offline meta-RL methods in few-shot generalization, particularly under sparse data and heterogeneous dynamics. paragraphs: Offline meta-reinforcement learning seeks to transfer learning from fixed datasets to previously unseen tasks. Expert-based methods must decide which specialists should handle a new task, but routing based on individual tokens or short trajectory fragments can miss broader relationships between tasks. The Task-Guided Router makes those relationships explicit.

TGR represents tasks using several complementary views: semantic descriptions, summaries of behavior, and latent features describing dynamics. Its routing mechanism uses these representations to assess global task compatibility and assign experts accordingly. This structure is intended to support stable specialization while allowing useful knowledge to transfer between related tasks.

Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art offline meta-reinforcement-learning methods in few-shot generalization. The gains are especially evident when data are sparse and dynamics differ across tasks. These findings support task-level information as a useful routing prior: deciding which experts fit the overall task can improve transfer when local observations provide an incomplete or fragmented picture of what the agent needs to do.
summary.tldr: TGR routes experts using semantic, behavioral, and dynamics-based task representations to improve few-shot offline reinforcement-learning generalization.

title: Structured Expert Routing with Multi-View Task Priors for Offline Meta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Rapidly increasing AI capabilities have substantial real-world consequences, ranging from AI safety concerns to labor market consequences. The Model Evaluation & Threat Research (METR) report argues that AI capabilities have exhibited exponential growth since 2019. In this position paper, we argue that the data is insufficient to support exponential increase in AI capabilities. We propose an alternative hypothesis that existing exponential growth has been driven by (1) model and data scaling, and (2) the development of reasoning models. Barring major new breakthroughs, our hypothesis is that AI capabilities have already exhibited an inflection point or will do so in the near future. We call for more rigorous evaluation methodologies for AI forecasts and better academic discussion on this topic.

paragraphs: This position paper questions whether the available evidence supports a claim of exponential growth in AI capabilities. It responds to a METR report describing such growth since 2019. The authors argue that the data are insufficient to establish that pattern, an issue that matters because capability forecasts shape expectations about safety and labor markets.

They propose an alternative explanation for the apparent trajectory: progress has been driven by increasing model and data scale, together with the development of reasoning models. On this account, the observed gains may reflect these particular sources of improvement rather than establish an enduring exponential trend. Explaining past growth and predicting its continuation are separate questions.

The authors hypothesize that, without major new breakthroughs, capability growth has already reached an inflection point or will reach one soon. This is a conditional hypothesis, not a demonstrated slowdown or a claim that future breakthroughs cannot occur. The paper calls for more rigorous evaluation of AI forecasts and stronger academic discussion of the evidence behind competing growth scenarios.
summary.tldr: The paper challenges evidence for exponential AI capability growth and proposes a conditional hypothesis of an approaching or existing inflection point.

title: Position: AI Capabilities May Not Increase Exponentially

abstract: Foundation models, such as Diffusion Models (DMs) and Large Language Models (LLMs), are now widely integrated into digital systems. This widespread use introduces a specific security risk: generative backdoors. Unlike traditional models where backdoors cause simple classification errors, generative backdoors hide within the model’s output distribution. This makes them difficult to detect using standard pattern-based methods.This paper argues that current defensive strategies are insufficient for generative AI. We propose Distributional Integrity, a framework that focuses on maintaining the stability and accuracy of the model’s data distribution. We identify two primary threats: backdoors within the model supply chain and the contamination of synthetic data pipelines. To address these, we advocate for a shift toward cross-modal certification and parameter-level verification. These methods aim to secure the AI-generated content (AIGC) ecosystem against inherited vulnerabilities.

paragraphs: This position paper examines backdoor attacks in generative foundation models, including diffusion models and large language models. It argues that the security problem differs from backdoors that produce simple classification errors. A generative backdoor can be embedded in the distribution of possible outputs, making standard detection methods based on recognizable patterns less effective.

The authors propose Distributional Integrity as a framework centered on preserving the stability and accuracy of a model’s data distribution. This shifts attention toward the overall pattern of generated content. They identify two principal routes for concern: vulnerabilities introduced through the model supply chain and contamination of pipelines that use synthetic data.

To address these threats, the paper advocates certification across modalities and verification at the parameter level. These are proposed directions for securing the wider ecosystem of AI-generated content against vulnerabilities it may inherit. The central implication is that defensive strategies should account for how compromised generative behavior can persist through connected models and data pipelines, alongside examining individual outputs.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes Distributional Integrity to address generative backdoors across model supply chains and synthetic-data pipelines.

abstract: Most prevalent techniques in Support Vector Machine (SVM) feature selectionare based on the intuition that the weights of features that are close to zeroare not required for optimal classification. In this paper we show thatindeed, in the sample limit, the irrelevant variables (in a theoretical andoptimal sense) will be given zero weight by a linear SVM, both in the soft andthe hard margin case. However, SVM-based methods have certain theoreticaldisadvantages too. We present examples where the linear SVM may assign zeroweights to strongly relevant variables (i.e., variables required for optimalestimation of the distribution of the target variable) and where weaklyrelevant features (i.e., features that are superfluous for optimal featureselection given other features) may get non-zero weights. We contrast andtheoretically compare with Markov-Blanket based feature selection algorithmsthat do not have such disadvantages in a broad class of distributions andcould also be used for causal discovery.

We contrast andtheoretically compare with Markov-Blanket based feature selection algorithmsthat do not have such disadvantages in a broad class of distributions andcould also be used for causal discovery.

paragraphs: Feature selection with a linear support vector machine often treats small feature weights as evidence that the corresponding variables can be removed. This paper examines the theoretical basis of that practice. It establishes that, in the sample limit, theoretically irrelevant variables receive zero weight in both soft-margin and hard-margin linear SVMs.

That result does not make SVM weights a complete description of feature relevance. The authors construct examples in which strongly relevant variables receive zero weight, even though they are needed for optimal estimation of the target distribution. They also show that weakly relevant variables can receive nonzero weights despite being unnecessary for optimal feature selection when other features are available.

The paper compares these properties with Markov-blanket approaches to feature selection. For a broad class of distributions, those approaches avoid the identified disadvantages and may also support causal discovery. The findings distinguish a useful guarantee about irrelevant variables from stronger interpretations of SVM weights that the counterexamples undermine.
summary.tldr: Linear SVMs give irrelevant variables zero weight in the sample limit, but their weights can still misrepresent other forms of feature relevance.

title: A theoretical characterization of linear SVM-based feature selection

abstract: The standard model of supervised learning assumes that training and test data are drawn from the same underlying distribution. This paperexplores an application in which a second, auxiliary, source of data isavailable drawn from a different distribution. This auxiliary data is moreplentiful, but of significantly lower quality, than the training and testdata. In the SVM framework, a training example has two roles: (a) as a datapoint to constrain the learning process and (b) as a candidate support vectorthat can form part of the definition of the classifier. The paper considersusing the auxiliary data in either (or both) of these roles. This auxiliarydata framework is applied to a problem of classifying images of leaves ofmaple and oak trees using a kernel derived from the shapes of the leaves.Experiments show that when the training data set is very small, training withauxiliary data can produce large improvements in accuracy, even when theauxiliary data is significantly different from the training (and test) data. The paper also introduces techniques for adjusting the kernel scores of theauxiliary data points to make them more comparable to the training data points.

paragraphs: This paper studies supervised learning when plentiful auxiliary data come from a different distribution and are substantially lower quality than the main training and test data. The question is whether those additional examples can still improve an SVM, especially when the main training set is very small.

The authors separate two roles of an SVM training example. An example can constrain the learning problem, and it can be a candidate support vector used in the classifier's definition. They investigate assigning auxiliary examples either role or both. They also introduce adjustments to auxiliary kernel scores to make those scores more comparable with scores for the main training examples.

The framework is evaluated by classifying maple and oak leaf images using a kernel derived from leaf shapes. Experiments show that auxiliary data can produce large accuracy gains when the main training set is very small, even with substantial distribution differences. This is a conditional empirical benefit: the result supports using auxiliary data in that setting, rather than assuming all additional data are equally useful.
summary.tldr: Lower-quality auxiliary data can substantially improve SVM accuracy with very small training sets, as demonstrated in leaf-image classification.

title: Improving SVM accuracy by training on auxiliary data sources

abstract: Given observed data and a collection of parameterized candidate models, a 1 − α confidence region in parameter space provides useful insight as to those models which are a good fit to the data, all while keeping the probability of incorrect exclusion below α. With complex models, optimally precise procedures (those with small expected size) are, in practice, difficult to derive; one solution is the Minimax Expected-Size (MES) confidence procedure. The key computational problem of MES is computing a minimax equilibria to a certain zero-sum game. We show that this game is convex with bilinear payoffs, allowing us to apply any convex game solver, including linear programming. Exploiting the sparsity of the matrix, along with using fast linear programming software, allows us to compute approximate minimax expected-size confidence regions orders of magnitude faster than previously published methods. We test these approaches by estimating parameters for a cosmological model.

paragraphs: A confidence region identifies parameter values compatible with observed data while controlling the probability of incorrectly excluding the true value. Smaller expected regions offer greater precision, but finding procedures with this property can be computationally difficult for complex models. This paper focuses on making the Minimax Expected-Size confidence procedure more practical to compute.

The central calculation in that procedure is an equilibrium of a particular zero-sum game. The authors show that the game is convex and has bilinear payoffs, opening it to convex game solvers, including linear programming. This characterization connects the statistical objective to optimization methods that can be used to carry out the required computation.

The implementation exploits sparsity in the game's matrix and uses fast linear programming software. Together, these choices allow approximate minimax expected-size confidence regions to be computed orders of magnitude faster than previously published methods. The authors test the approaches by estimating parameters of a cosmological model. The reported advance concerns the computational accessibility of the confidence-region procedure, with the regions explicitly described as approximate.
summary.tldr: A convex-game formulation and sparse linear programming compute approximate minimax expected-size confidence regions orders of magnitude faster.

title: Efficiently computing minimax expected-size confidence regions

abstract: Most current multi-task learning frameworks ignore the robustness issue, which means that the presence of “outlier” tasks may greatly reduce overall system performance. We introduce a robust framework for Bayesian multitask learning, t-processes (TP), which are a generalization of Gaussian processes (GP) for multi-task learning. TP allows the system to effectively distinguish good tasks from noisy or outlier tasks. Experiments show that TP not only improves overall system performance, but can also serve as an indicator for the “informativeness” of different tasks.

We introduce a robust framework for Bayesian multitask learning, t-processes (TP), which are a generalization of Gaussian processes (GP) for multi-task learning. TP allows the system to effectively distinguish good tasks from noisy or outlier tasks. Experiments show that TP not only improves overall system performance, but can also serve as an indicator for the “informativeness” of different tasks.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning shares information across related learning problems. The paper focuses on a risk in that sharing: some tasks may be noisy or behave as outliers, and their presence can substantially reduce overall performance. It argues that robustness to such tasks deserves explicit treatment in the learning framework.

The authors introduce t-processes as a Bayesian framework for robust multi-task learning. These processes generalize Gaussian processes for the multi-task setting. Their stated role is to let the system distinguish useful tasks from noisy or outlying ones. The distinction concerns the tasks participating in shared learning, making task quality part of how the overall collection is understood.

Experiments show improvements in overall system performance and suggest a second use for the framework: indicating how informative different tasks are. This means the method can provide information about the contributors to shared learning as well as improve its results. The findings support robustness and task informativeness in the reported experiments, without asserting that every collection of tasks benefits equally.
summary.tldr: Bayesian t-processes distinguish useful tasks from noisy or outlier tasks, improving multi-task performance and indicating task informativeness in experiments.

title: Robust multi-task learning with t-processes

abstract: The problem of identifying the minimal gene set required to sustain life is of crucial importance in understanding cellular mechanisms and designing therapeutic drugs. This work describes several kernel-based solutions for predicting essential genes that outperform existing models while using less training data. Our first solution is based on a semi-manually designed kernel derived from the Pfam database, which includes several Pfam domains. We then present novel and general domain-based sequence kernels that capture sequence similarity with respect to several domains made of large sets of protein sequences. We show how to deal with the large size of the problem � several thousands of domains with individual domains sometimes containing thousands of sequences � by representing and efficiently computing these kernels using automata. We report results of extensive experiments demonstrating that they compare favorably with the Pfam kernel in predicting protein essentiality, while requiring no manual tuning.

paragraphs: Predicting which genes are essential helps investigate the minimal requirements for life and informs work on cellular mechanisms and therapeutic drugs. This paper develops kernel-based approaches to predicting essentiality from protein sequences. The authors report solutions that outperform existing models while using less training data, making sequence comparison central to the prediction task.

The first approach uses a partly hand-designed kernel derived from several domains in the Pfam database. The paper then introduces general domain-based sequence kernels that compare sequences with respect to domains containing large collections of protein sequences. This replaces the semi-manual construction with a broader mechanism for expressing domain-related sequence similarity.

Computing these kernels presents a scale challenge: there can be thousands of domains, with thousands of sequences in some individual domains. The authors use automata to represent and efficiently compute the kernels. Extensive experiments show that the general kernels compare favorably with the Pfam kernel for essentiality prediction while requiring no manual tuning, linking computational tractability with useful predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Domain-based sequence kernels use automata for efficient protein-essentiality prediction and compare favorably with a semi-manual Pfam kernel without manual tuning.

title: Sequence kernels for predicting protein essentiality

abstract: In the absence of explicit queries, an alternative is to try to infer users' interests from implicit feedback signals, such as clickstreams or eye tracking. The interests, formulated as an implicit query, can then be used in further searches. We formulate this task as a probabilistic model, which can be interpreted as a kind of transfer learning and meta-learning. The probabilistic model is demonstrated to outperform an earlier kernel-based method in a small-scale information retrieval task.
