The interests, formulated as an implicit query, can then be used in further searches. We formulate this task as a probabilistic model, which can be interpreted as a kind of transfer learning and meta-learning. The probabilistic model is demonstrated to outperform an earlier kernel-based method in a small-scale information retrieval task.

paragraphs: The paper studies information retrieval when a user has not supplied an explicit query. Instead, interests may be inferred from implicit feedback, such as clickstreams or eye-tracking signals. Those inferred interests can be expressed as an implicit query and used to support further searches.

The authors formulate this inference task as a probabilistic model. They explain that the model can be interpreted through both transfer learning and meta-learning, connecting query inference to these broader learning ideas. The central task is therefore to turn observed behavior into a representation of interests that a retrieval system can use.

In a small-scale information retrieval experiment, the probabilistic model outperforms an earlier kernel-based method. This provides evidence for the proposed formulation in that evaluated setting, with the small scale of the task defining the scope of the reported result. The contribution is a probabilistic route from implicit behavioral signals to usable search queries, supported by a direct comparison with an earlier approach.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model infers implicit search queries from behavioral feedback and outperforms an earlier kernel method on a small retrieval task.

title: Learning to learn implicit queries from gaze patterns

abstract: In this paper, we investigate a new machine learning framework called ``Online Transfer Learning (OTL) that aims to transfer knowledge from some source domain to an online learning task on a target domain. We do not assume the target data follows the same class or generative distribution as the source data, and our key motivation is to improve a supervised online learning task in a target domain by exploiting the knowledge that had been learned from large amount of training data in source domains. OTL is in general challenging since data in both domains not only can be different in their class distributions but can be also different in their feature representations. As a first attempt to this problem, we propose techniques to address two kinds of OTL tasks: one is to perform OTL in a homogeneous domain, and the other is to perform OTL across heterogeneous domains. We show the mistake bounds of the proposed OTL algorithms, and empirically examine their performance on several challenging OTL tasks. Encouraging results validate the efficacy of our techniques.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we investigate a new machine learning framework called ``Online Transfer Learning (OTL) that aims to transfer knowledge from some source domain to an online learning task on a target domain. We do not assume the target data follows the same class or generative distribution as the source data, and our key motivation is to improve a supervised online learning task in a target domain by exploiting the knowledge that had been learned from large amount of training data in source domains. OTL is in general challenging since data in both domains not only can be different in their class distributions but can be also different in their feature representations. As a first attempt to this problem, we propose techniques to address two kinds of OTL tasks: one is to perform OTL in a homogeneous domain, and the other is to perform OTL across heterogeneous domains. We show the mistake bounds of the proposed OTL algorithms, and empirically examine their performance on several challenging OTL tasks. Encouraging results validate the efficacy of our techniques.

paragraphs: The paper studies how knowledge learned from substantial source-domain training data can help a supervised learner operating online in a target domain. The target learner receives data over time, and the proposed Online Transfer Learning framework aims to use previously learned knowledge to improve that continuing learning process.

A central challenge is that the source and target need not share class distributions or the same data-generating distribution. They may also describe examples through different features. The authors address both homogeneous transfer, involving compatible feature representations, and heterogeneous transfer, where the representations differ. This distinction makes feature mismatch an explicit part of the transfer problem.

The paper proposes algorithms for these two settings and establishes mistake bounds, providing theoretical statements about their prediction errors during online learning. It also evaluates the techniques on several challenging transfer tasks and reports encouraging results. Together, the analysis and experiments support the usefulness of transferring prior knowledge in the studied settings despite differences between source and target data.
summary.tldr: Online Transfer Learning uses source-domain knowledge to support online target learning even when distributions or feature representations differ.

title: OTL: A Framework of Online Transfer Learning
